# socketley

> One Linux daemon and CLI that runs your servers, proxies, caches, storage, databases, DNS, sign-in, MQTT, mail, metrics, tunnels and MCP: each a runtime made with one command.

socketley is a single Linux binary. `socketley daemon` supervises runtimes; every other invocation is the CLI that talks to the daemon over a unix socket. A runtime is a network service of one of 15 types, made with `socketley create <type> <name> [flags]`, each in its own worker process on an io_uring event loop, scriptable in Lua. The manual page man/socketley.1 is the source of truth; these files are generated from it and from the site's own pages (https://docs.smileygames.online/).

Every page below is plain Markdown. llms-full.txt is all of them in one file (large).


---

# socketley

One Linux daemon and CLI that runs your servers, proxies, caches, storage, databases, DNS, sign-in, MQTT, mail, metrics, tunnels and MCP: each a runtime made with one command.

```
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HiImSmiley/Socketley/main/install.sh | sudo sh
socketley create cache store -p 6379 -s          # a Redis-compatible cache
socketley create server api -p 9000 --lua api.lua -s
socketley create proxy edge -p 8080 --backend api -s
socketley ls
```

## What it is

socketley is one binary. As `socketley daemon` it runs **runtimes**: network services, each made with one command and each in its own worker process on an io_uring event loop. Anything else you type is the CLI that talks to that daemon, as `docker` talks to `dockerd`.

A runtime has a type, which decides what it speaks, and a name, by which others reach it (`--backend api`). Every type is created, started and removed the same way.

## The runtimes

- [cache](rt-cache.txt): In-memory store on the Redis protocol: strings, lists, sets, hashes, sorted sets, streams, pub/sub (compared with Redis, Valkey)
- [client](rt-client.txt): Dials a server and holds the connection: TCP, UDP or a unix socket, over TLS, reconnecting (compared with Go, Node.js, Python asyncio, tcpkali, socat)
- [db](rt-db.txt): JSON documents owned by accounts, over HTTP, with indexes, queries, replicas and backups (compared with MongoDB, PocketBase)
- [dns](rt-dns.txt): Authoritative name server for its zones, over UDP and TCP, with DNSSEC and transfers (compared with NSD, Knot)
- [idp](rt-idp.txt): OpenID Connect provider with its own accounts, second factors, app passwords and SSH certificates (compared with Keycloak)
- [mail](rt-mail.txt): Mail server: SMTP, submission, IMAP, POP3, JMAP and webmail, mailboxes in a storage (compared with Postfix and Dovecot)
- [mcp](rt-mcp.txt): A Model Context Protocol server: the tools, resources and prompts its script declares, for AI clients (compared with the MCP Python and TypeScript SDKs)
- [metrics](rt-metrics.txt): Time series for years, answered with PromQL over the Prometheus API, with alert rules and logs (compared with Prometheus, VictoriaMetrics)
- [mqtt](rt-mqtt.txt): MQTT 3.1, 3.1.1 and 5.0 broker on TCP, TLS and WebSocket, with sessions and rules (compared with Mosquitto)
- [proxy](rt-proxy.txt): HTTP and TCP reverse proxy: routes by name and path, health checks, retries, mTLS, FastCGI (compared with HAProxy, nginx)
- [server](rt-server.txt): TCP, UDP, WebSocket and HTTP on one port, answered by Lua or by a built-in path (compared with Node.js (ws, uWebSockets.js), Go, nginx)
- [storage](rt-storage.txt): S3 object storage over a directory, with versioning, replication, a web drive and git (compared with MinIO)
- [sync](rt-sync.txt): One job that carries a directory to a storage, from it, or both ways (compared with rclone, mc)
- [tunnel](rt-tunnel.txt): Makes a machine without an address of its own reachable through an edge it dials (compared with frp)
- [web](rt-web.txt): Static site of files for browsers: a docs site, a blog, a single-page app; caching and compression built in (compared with nginx)

## Benchmarks

Each runtime's headline result against the server people run instead; method and every set are on the [benchmarks](bench.txt) page.

- cache: 3.9× against Redis (GET)
- server: 5.5× against nginx (1 KiB file, keep-alive, 256 connections)
- proxy: 2.0× against HAProxy (HTTP, 1 KiB, keep-alive, 256 connections)
- web: 4.9× against nginx (page 4 KiB, keep-alive, 256 connections)
- dns: 1.2× against NSD (A queries over UDP)
- mqtt: 21.6× against Mosquitto (fan-out: 1 publisher to 50 subscribers, QoS 1, 64 B)
- storage: 18.2× against MinIO (GET 4 KiB, 64 connections)
- db: 2.5× against MongoDB (mixed: 90% reads, 10% writes, 64 clients)
- tunnel: 2.3× against frp (throughput, 512 MiB echoed through the tunnel)
- metrics: 2.5× against Prometheus (CPU per sample ingested)
- sync: 2.1× against rclone (first copy, 2000 files of 64 KiB and 50 of 1 MiB)
- idp: 24.9× against Keycloak (refresh token, 256 clients)
- mail: 4.4× against Postfix 3.10.6 + Dovecot (SMTP in, 4 KiB messages, 64 connections, 10 a connection)
- mcp: 29.4× against MCP Python SDK 2.3.0 (uvicorn 0.54.0) (tools/call add(a, b), 64 sessions)
- client: 1.1× against Go (request-answer: 1 connection, 64 B each way)

# Install

From source, the install script or a Debian package; the daemon then runs as a systemd service.

socketley runs on Linux 5.19 or newer, on x86_64 and aarch64. Install it one of four ways, join the group, then check it.

## A release package

```
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HiImSmiley/Socketley/main/install.sh | sudo sh
```

Installs the newest release `.deb`, asking before each missing dependency (ffmpeg is offered for the storage runtime's thumbnails and video). If the package was built for a newer distribution than yours, the script stops without changing anything.

| Option | Does |
|---|---|
| `--deb FILE` | Installs a package you have. |
| `--yes` | Takes every default. |
| `--uninstall` | Removes socketley. |

## From source, in one step

```
git clone https://github.com/HiImSmiley/Socketley
cd Socketley
bash scripts/install-from-source.sh
```

Checks the kernel, architecture and compiler (GCC 12 or newer), builds liburing and Release, installs the binary, man page and service, and starts the daemon.

| Option | Does |
|---|---|
| `--dry-run` | Prints every command, runs none. |
| `--uninstall` | Removes what it installed. |
| `--prefix` | Installs elsewhere; only `/usr` gives a system service. |

## From source, by hand

1. Dependencies.

   ```
   sudo apt install build-essential libssl-dev libluajit-5.1-dev git
   ```
2. liburing, if yours is older than 2.7.

   ```
   bash scripts/install-liburing.sh          # liburing >= 2.7, only if yours is older
   ```
3. The third-party archives.

   ```
   ./bin/build-thirdparty.sh                 # the static archives the tree links, HTTP/3 included
   ```
4. Build.

   ```
   ./bin/premake5 gmake2
   make -C make config=release_x64 -j$(nproc)
   ```
5. Optionally, install system-wide.

   ```
   sudo bash packaging/install.sh            # optional: system-wide, with the service
   ```

Without installing, `./bin/Release/socketley daemon &` starts a development daemon on `/tmp/socketley.sock` with state under your home directory; see [environment & files](env.txt).

## A Debian package of your own

```
bash packaging/build-deb.sh
sudo apt install ./socketley_*.deb
```

Build it on the release it is for: a package built on Ubuntu 24.04 does not install on Debian 12.

## Join the socketley group

```
sudo usermod -aG socketley $USER
```

Only root and the `socketley` group reach the installed daemon; anyone else silently gets a private daemon of their own. Log in again after joining.

## Check it

```
systemctl status socketley
socketley ls
socketley --help          # the interactive help
man socketley
```

[The manual's installation section →](man-installation.txt)

# Ten-minute tour

Make a server, a cache and a proxy, script one of them, and look at all three.

Ten minutes, three runtimes, on a fresh install. The only file you write is one short script. You also need `nc`, `curl` and, for the cache, `redis-cli`.

## 1. A server

1. Create a server; `-s` starts it.

   ```
   socketley create server chat -p 9000 -s
   socketley ls
   ```
2. In two terminals, run `nc 127.0.0.1 9000`. What you type in one appears in the other.
3. Send to both from the CLI: `socketley send chat "hello"`.

## 2. A script

1. Write `echo.lua`.

   ```
   function on_client_message(id, msg)
       self.send(id, "you said: " .. msg)
   end
   ```
2. Run a server with it.

   ```
   socketley create server echo -p 9001 --lua echo.lua -s
   printf 'hi\n' | nc -q1 127.0.0.1 9001
   ```
3. Edit the file, then `socketley reload-lua echo`. Connections stay open.

All callbacks: the [Lua page](lua.txt).

## 3. A cache

```
socketley create cache store -p 6379 -s
redis-cli -p 6379 SET visits 0
redis-cli -p 6379 INCR visits
```

It speaks the Redis protocol, and plain text lines too:

```
printf 'get visits\n' | nc -q1 127.0.0.1 6379
```

## 4. A proxy

```
mkdir -p site && echo '<h1>hello</h1>' > site/index.html
socketley create server web -p 9100 --http ./site -s
socketley create proxy gw -p 8080 --backend web -s
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/gw/index.html
```

The proxy finds `web` by its name, so it follows the server if its port changes. It takes its own name off the path: `/gw/index.html` reaches `web` as `/index.html`.

## 5. Look at it

```
socketley ls                 # every runtime, its state and port
socketley stats gw           # live counters
socketley show echo          # its configuration as JSON
socketley edit gw --backend-timeout 5s --restart
socketley stop chat; socketley remove chat
```

After `sudo systemctl restart socketley`, every running runtime comes back by itself. The [dashboard](man-dashboard.txt) shows it all in a browser.

## Where next

- Each runtime's page: [server](rt-server.txt), [proxy](rt-proxy.txt), [cache](rt-cache.txt), and the ten others.
- [How it works](how.txt) for what happened behind each command, [concepts](concepts.txt) for what runtimes share, [deployment](deploy.txt) before running it for real.

# Concepts

The daemon, its runtimes and the few rules every one of them follows.

The rules every runtime follows, whatever its type. For what happens behind a command, step by step, see [How it works](how.txt).

## A runtime

A runtime is one network service. It has a **type**, which decides what it speaks (a server, a proxy, a cache, …; see [registered types](man-registered-types.txt)), and a **name**, unique on its daemon, by which commands and other runtimes refer to it.

| Command | What it does to a runtime |
|---|---|
| `create type name [flags]` | Checks the flags and saves the runtime. With `-s` it also starts it. |
| `start` / `stop` | Starts its worker process / ends it. The runtime itself is kept. |
| `edit name [flags]` | Changes flags. Without flags it opens the runtime's JSON in your editor. |
| `reload-lua name` | Loads the changed script without dropping connections. |
| `remove` | Stops it and deletes it. |

A runtime is always in one of four states: `created` (saved, never started), `running`, `stopped`, or `failed` (it could not start; `ls` shows why).

## State that survives

Each runtime is saved as a JSON file in the daemon's state directory. When the daemon starts, it brings every runtime back and starts the ones that were running before. Runtimes survive restarts and reboots without any setup.

| Command | Use it to |
|---|---|
| `show name` / `import name` | Print a runtime's configuration as JSON / replace it from JSON, so `show a \| import b` copies one. |
| `export dir` | Write the daemon's whole setup as Lua files into a directory. |
| `export --full file` | Archive setup and data together, for a backup; `restore` puts it back. |

- More in the manual: **State persistence** (man-state-persistence.txt): The daemon persists runtime configurations as JSON files.

## Names, ports and addresses

- **Runtimes find each other by name.** `--backend api` or `--cache store` names a runtime, not a port, so the link holds when its port changes.
- **Public names go through the entrance.** A runtime's `--domain` names are served by the entrance, the one proxy on ports 80 and 443, which also gets their certificates.
- **A port can be kept local.** `--bind 127.0.0.1` binds it to one address; `--listen unix:/path` uses a unix socket instead of a port.
- **One address, one runtime.** Two runtimes on the same port and address are refused, so a typo cannot silently split traffic.

- More in the manual: **The node beside the port** (man-common-flags.txt): A server or an unsharded cache that listens on a TCP port also listens on an AF_UNIX node.
- More in the manual: **Between runtimes on one machine** (man-common-flags.txt): Requests from one runtime to another include socketley.send , self.route , and a server's --cache name .
- More in the manual: **Which port a runtime is on** (man-common-flags.txt): ls , ps , stats and the metrics endpoint report the port a runtime binds , which is not always the port it was configured with.
- More in the manual: **One address, one runtime** (man-common-flags.txt): A runtime's start is refused when another runtime on this daemon is already serving the address it would bind: a TCP port, a UDP port, or a --listen unix: path.

## TLS

A server, cache, proxy or mqtt broker encrypts its own port with `--tls --cert file --key file`. Add `--ca file` to require client certificates. `--acme name` gets a Let's Encrypt certificate and renews it.

When socketley connects out (a client runtime, a proxy's `https://` backend), it always verifies the server's certificate; that check cannot be turned off. What is not supported is listed under [TLS limitations](man-limitations.txt).

## Several cores

A runtime's worker uses one core. `--shards N` runs N workers that share the port, and `--cpus` chooses the cores they may run on. On a cache, each key belongs to one shard. More shards do not always mean more speed: read [sharding](man-server-flags.txt) before choosing N.

## Scripts

Most types take `--lua file`: a script whose callbacks (`on_client_message`, `on_http_request`, …) answer instead of the built-in behaviour. It is loaded when the runtime starts and replaced with `reload-lua`. A callback that never returns is ended by its [deadline](man-lua-configuration.txt). See [Lua scripting](lua.txt).

## More than one machine

Daemons that share a cluster directory see each other's runtimes, and a proxy's `@group` backend reaches group members on every machine. See [Cluster](cluster.txt).

## Watching it

`socketley ls` lists runtimes and their states; `socketley stats name` and `socketley daemon stats` print live counters. The daemon also serves a web [dashboard](man-dashboard.txt) and Prometheus `/metrics`. A [metrics](rt-metrics.txt) runtime keeps the history and sends alerts.

- More in the manual: **Dashboard** (man-dashboard.txt): When daemon.metrics_port is set in the daemon configuration file, the metrics endpoint serves the following routes: GET / # Serves the web dashboard, which has the storage interface's look and takes i

# How it works

What happens, and where, from the command you type to the answer a client gets.

Every fact on this page is from the [manual](man.txt), and each section links the part with the details.

## The pieces

socketley is one binary. Started as `socketley daemon` it is the **daemon**: a supervisor that keeps every runtime alive. Started any other way it is the **CLI**: it sends one command to the daemon over a unix socket (`/run/socketley/socketley.sock` when installed, `/tmp/socketley.sock` in development) and prints the answer.

```
  you
   │  socketley create cache store -p 6379 -s
   ▼  one command over the control socket
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ daemon                               │
  │ checks the flags, saves the runtime, │
  │ forks a worker and watches it        │
  └─────┬────────────┬────────────┬──────┘
        ▼            ▼            ▼
  ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐
  │ worker   │ │ worker   │ │ worker   │
  │ server   │ │ cache    │ │ proxy    │
  │ api      │ │ store    │ │ edge     │
  │ :9000    │ │ :6379    │ │ :8080    │
  └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────┘
  each worker: one process, one io_uring
  event loop on one thread
```

- **A runtime** is one network service of one type (server, proxy, cache, storage, …) with a name that is unique on the daemon.
- **Every runtime you create runs in its own worker process**, the entrance proxy included. The worker binds the port, serves every byte and runs the runtime's Lua script. The daemon keeps a placeholder with the name, port and state, so `ls` and `stats` can answer. The one exception: a server, client, proxy, cache, storage or dns runtime that a Lua script makes with `socketley.create` runs inside the daemon. [Out-of-process runtimes →](man-limitations.txt)
- **Opening the control socket is an administrative right**: whoever can open it can run code as the daemon's user. That is why the installed socket belongs to the `socketley` group. [The IPC socket →](man-files.txt)

## What `create` does

1. **The CLI sends the command** to the daemon. A relative path in a flag (a script, a directory) is made absolute first, so it means what it meant in your shell.
2. **The daemon checks it**: the type, the name, every flag and its value. If a `--lua` script does not parse, `create` refuses it on the spot. `--test` stops here and keeps nothing.
3. **The daemon saves the runtime** as a JSON file in its state directory. From now on the runtime survives restarts of the daemon and reboots.
4. **With `-s`, the daemon forks a worker.** The worker binds the port, reads the TLS certificate, resolves its backends and runs the script's top level.
5. `create` waits for the worker's verdict and tells you through its exit status:

   | Exit | Meaning |
   |---|---|
   | `0` | The worker is serving. |
   | `1` | The worker refused, or could not bind, resolve or load its certificate. The reason is in the daemon's log; the runtime is left `failed`, so `ls` still shows it. One exception: if only the script's `on_start` raised an error, the runtime is running and the command names the callback. |
   | `2` | A fatal error, or no answer in time: the daemon could not be reached, or the worker said nothing within two seconds. The runtime stays supervised and may still come up; `ls` shows the state it settles on. |

## The path of a request

A client connects to the runtime's port. The worker's event loop reads the bytes and answers them, either with a built-in path (a static file, a cache command, a relayed message) or by calling the runtime's Lua handler. The daemon is not on this path at all.

For a public website, the **entrance** sits in front: one proxy on ports 80 and 443 that a [dns runtime](rt-dns.txt) creates with `--proxy`. It gets certificates itself and routes each request by its host name to the runtime that has that name in `--domain`.

```
  browser: https://shop.example.com/cart
   │
   ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ entrance proxy, port 443             │
  │ TLS with an ACME certificate         │
  │ shop.example.com → runtime "shop"    │
  └──────────────────┬───────────────────┘
                     │ a unix socket beside its
                     │ port, when it has one
                     ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ worker: server "shop", port 9100     │
  │ on_http_request(req) in Lua,         │
  │ or the static files of --http        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘
```

A proxy that names its backend by runtime name (`--backend shop`) follows the runtime if its port changes. On the same machine it reaches a server or an unsharded cache over an AF_UNIX node beside the port, which only the daemon's user can open. [The node beside the port →](man-common-flags.txt)

## Runtimes talking to each other

A script can reach another runtime: `socketley.send`, `self.route`, or a server's `--cache name`. The first such request between two runtimes goes through the daemon. The daemon then hands both workers the two ends of a private socket pair, and later requests go straight across. If that link ever breaks, requests go through the daemon again; only speed is lost.

`socketley stats name` shows `peer_links`, `peer_direct` and `peer_relayed`. [Between runtimes on one machine →](man-common-flags.txt)

## What is stored where

| What | Installed (package) | Development |
|---|---|---|
| Control socket | `/run/socketley/socketley.sock` (0660, group `socketley`) | `/tmp/socketley.sock` (0600) |
| Runtimes, one JSON file each | `/var/lib/socketley/runtimes/` | `~/.local/share/socketley/runtimes/` |
| Daemon configuration | `/etc/socketley/config.lua` | `~/.config/socketley/config.lua` |
| Registered types | `/etc/socketley/types/*.toml` | `~/.config/socketley/types/*.toml` |

A runtime's JSON file holds its flags and whether it was running. It can hold a master password and key paths, so it is readable by the daemon's user alone. A daemon on another socket (`SOCKETLEY_SOCKET`) gets a state directory of its own, and logs which one at startup. [Files →](man-files.txt)

## When something stops or fails

| Event | What happens |
|---|---|
| A worker crashes | The daemon restarts it and the runtime stays `running`. What the worker held only in memory is lost: a cache keeps only what `--persistent` saved. Other runtimes release the connections routed to or from it. |
| It crashes more than five times in ten seconds | The runtime is left `failed` instead of being forked again in a loop. Fix the cause, then `socketley start` it again. |
| A Lua callback never returns | Its deadline ends it. [Callback deadline →](man-lua-configuration.txt) |
| The daemon is restarted (`systemctl restart`, or a package upgrade, which restarts a running service) | Every runtime is stopped cleanly with the daemon, so their connections close; a cache with `--persistent` writes its file. When the daemon is back, it restores every saved runtime and starts the ones that were running. |
| The daemon itself crashes | Its workers end with it: a worker never outlives its daemon. systemd starts the daemon again after five seconds, and it restores the runtimes as above. |
| The machine reboots | The service starts at boot and restores the runtimes as above. |
| The power fails | What was only in memory is gone, and so can be the last writes the kernel had not written to disk yet. A cache's journal is not synced to disk; a storage runtime's `--fsync` decides when its writes are. |
| You run `stop` | The worker ends; the runtime is kept as `stopped`. With `--drain` it first finishes what is in flight. |

A runtime's state is always one of `created`, `running`, `stopped` or `failed`; `ls` shows it, and a failed runtime shows the reason.

## One thread per worker

A worker serves everything on one event loop, on one thread. That is what makes it cheap, and it has one consequence: a call that waits stops that worker's whole loop. The manual lists the few calls that can; `socketley.http` outside a callback that can wait is the one most scripts meet. [What can stop the event loop →](man-limitations.txt)

To use more cores, `--shards N` runs N workers that share the port. A cache gives each key one owning shard. [Concepts: several cores →](concepts.txt)

## More than one machine

Daemons that share a cluster directory see each other's runtimes, and a proxy's `@group` backend reaches members on every machine. An opt-in Raft mode adds elections and replicas. [Cluster →](cluster.txt)


---

# Lua scripting

Callbacks per message, connection and request, the runtime methods a script calls, and what a script may not do.

A runtime created with `--lua file` runs that script: LuaJIT, Lua 5.1 syntax, the runtime as `self`, callbacks as global functions. It loads at `start`; `socketley reload-lua name` replaces it and keeps connections.

```
-- a server that answers each line, counts clients and says the time every minute
local n = 0
function on_connect(id)    n = n + 1 end
function on_disconnect(id) n = n - 1 end
function on_client_message(id, msg)
    self.send(id, "you said: " .. msg)
end
socketley.set_interval(60000, function()
    self.broadcast(os.date("%H:%M") .. ", " .. n .. " online")
end)
```

> Callbacks run on the runtime's single thread. Inside a callback that can wait, such as `on_message`, `on_client_message` or an [mcp](rt-mcp.txt) tool's handler, `socketley.http` waits without blocking that thread. Anywhere else, `on_http_request` included, it blocks the whole runtime until the answer arrives; see [what blocks a runtime](operate.txt). A callback that never ends is stopped by its [deadline](man-lua-configuration.txt).

## Callbacks

#### `on_start()`

Called when the runtime starts.

#### `on_stop()`

Called when the runtime stops.

#### `on_message(msg)`

Called when a message is received (server and client). A client passes the connection id as a second argument, 1 unless **--connections** is given; see there. When a server defines this callback, it takes over message handling: the default broadcast (in **inout** and **master** modes) is suppressed. Use **self.broadcast(msg)** to relay messages yourself.

#### `on_client_message(client_id, msg) -> true`

Called when a message is received, with the sender's id (server only). It fires alongside on_message, and first. Returning **true** says the script has handled the message, so nothing is sent automatically: not the relay of **--mode inout** or of the master's messages, and not what **--send-to** names for a non-master. Returning anything else, or nothing, leaves those as they are. On a UDP server, client_id names the peer that sent the datagram; see **--udp**. A handler still waiting on **self.cache** when the relay runs has not returned yet, so its message is relayed; define on_message to stop the relay for such a script.

#### `on_messages(chunk, id)` / `on_client_messages(client_id, chunk) -> true`

The batch forms of on_message (client) and on_client_message (server): every complete line of one read in one call, instead of one call per line. **chunk** is the bytes as they arrived, up to and including the read's last newline, so every line in it ends with its '\n', a CRLF line keeps its '\r' and an empty line is a bare '\n'. An unfinished last line is kept and arrives at the start of the next call. When a script defines both forms, only the batch one is called.

A client calls on_messages for its TCP, unix-socket and TLS reads, with the connection's id after the chunk (see **--connections**). A server calls on_client_messages for a TCP line connection; returning **true** answers for every line in the chunk, as on_client_message's **true** does for one. A route or pipe the script sets from on_client_messages carries the next read on: the lines of the chunk it was handed are its own and are not sent on as well. Where there is no read to batch, each message is a chunk of one line with its '\n' added, and a message that itself holds a newline reads as more than one line there, so a script for such a runtime is better written with on_message: a datagram (**--udp**), a WebSocket message, a server in **--mode master** or with **--rate-limit** or **--global-rate-limit**, which judge each line on its own. **-w**, bash output and an interactive attach still see each line, exactly as with on_message.

A call per read instead of per line pays where the script takes the chunk whole: measured on one core, a server echoing 64 connections of 16 pipelined 64-byte lines with one **self.send** per chunk answered 1.6 times as many as with on_client_message. A script that walks the chunk line by line in Lua spends about what the calls it saves cost: counting 64-byte lines with string.find as below came to 5 per cent fewer than with on_message, and with 4 KiB lines, where copying the chunk into Lua is the cost, a third fewer. Counting the lines of a chunk:

```
local n = 0
function on_messages(chunk)
    local i = 1
    while true do
        local j = string.find(chunk, "\n", i, true)
        if not j then break end
        n = n + 1      -- the line is chunk:sub(i, j - 1)
        i = j + 1
    end
end
```

#### `on_read(view, id)`

A client's read without a string made of it: the same bytes on_messages would be handed, every complete line of one TCP, unix-socket or TLS read up to and including its last newline, as one **view** of the buffer they arrived in, with the connection's id after it (see **--connections**). When a script defines on_read, on_messages and on_message are not called; on_messages wins over on_message in the same way. Where there is no read to batch, as for a datagram (**--udp**), the view is one message with its '\n' added, as on_messages has it. **-w**, bash output, an interactive attach and **total_messages** see each line exactly as with on_message.

A view is valid only inside the call it was given to, until on_read returns or waits for an answer, as **self.cache** does: the buffer is the next read's after that, so a method called on a view kept past it raises *a view is valid only inside the on_read call it was given to; copy what you keep with view:sub*. Indexes count from 1 and are inclusive, negative ones from the end, as for a string, and no method reads outside the view.

#### `view:len()`

The number of bytes.

#### `view:byte(i)`

The byte at *i*, as string.byte, and nil outside the view.

#### `view:find(s [, init])`

Where *s* first occurs from *init*, as start and end, as string.find with plain set; nil if it does not. Patterns are not supported.

#### `view:sub(i [, j])`

Bytes *i* to *j* as a new string, as string.sub: the only method that copies, and how a script keeps any of a view.

#### `view:eq(i, j, s)`

Whether bytes *i* to *j* are the string *s*, which is view:sub(i, j) == s without the copy.

#### `view:lines()`

An iterator over the lines, yielding the start and end of each without its '\n', or the '\r' before it: the lines on_message would be handed, so an empty line is skipped.

A view's methods are LuaJIT FFI reads, which a compiled loop keeps in its trace, so a script that walks a read byte by byte or line by line makes no string for a line it does not keep, and v:find("\n", i) steps from line to line on the newlines the read was already searched for. Where the trace compiler stays shut, in a runtime embedded through the SDK with a callback deadline, the view is a string of the read underneath: the same methods and rules, slower than on_messages there. Counting lines and answering a line END:

```
local n = 0
function on_read(v)
    local i = 1
    while true do
        local j = v:find("\n", i)
        if not j then break end
        if v:eq(i, j - 1, "END") then
            self.send("done " .. n)
            n = 0
        else
            n = n + 1
        end
        i = j + 1
    end
end
```

#### `on_http_body(client_id, chunk, remaining)`

Called with each piece of a request body and the number of bytes still to come after it. **remaining** therefore reaches 0 exactly once per body. Defining this callback is the opt-in. A server whose script defines it streams request bodies to the callback instead of collecting them. A server whose script does not define it keeps its usual behaviour, including the 413 for a body larger than **--read-buffer**.

This callback is what makes a body larger than memory possible. The bytes are handed over and erased as they arrive. So **req.body** in the **on_http_request** that follows is deliberately EMPTY: keeping the bytes a second time is the memory cost this callback exists to avoid. Measured on one worker, one connection at a time:

```
start             19,796 kB
after 50 MB #1    37,344 kB
after 50 MB #2    37,344 kB     unchanged
after 50 MB #3    37,344 kB     unchanged
after 200 MB      37,428 kB     +84 kB
after 500 MB      37,444 kB     +16 kB
```

The first upload costs 17.5 MB once, which is the provided-buffer ring being faulted in. Every upload after it costs nothing: half a gigabyte is received inside 37 MB resident.

Keep per-upload state keyed by **client_id**, and clear it in **on_disconnect**. An abandoned body never reaches **on_http_request**, so nothing there can reset the state. **on_disconnect** is the only signal an abandoned body produces. It does fire, however much of the body arrived. That is what a script writing to a temporary file needs in order to remove the file.

```
local st = {}
function on_http_body(id, chunk, remaining)
    st[id] = (st[id] or 0) + #chunk
    if remaining == 0 then ... end
end
function on_disconnect(id) st[id] = nil end
```

**A body of unknown length.** A client that cannot say how long its body is sends **Transfer-Encoding: chunked**. Examples are fetch() with a ReadableStream body, anything piping a process's output, and anything that cannot stat what it is sending. With **on_http_body** defined, such a body is decoded and delivered like any other, without a limit, because there is no length to limit it by. Without the callback, it is answered 501.

**remaining** is **nil** for every chunk of such a body, because how much is still to come is genuinely unknowable. The end of the framing produces ONE final call, with an empty chunk and **remaining = 0**. So "remaining reaches 0 exactly once per body" holds for both forms, and a script written for **Content-Length** needs no change. Measured with 62 MB in 1000 chunks: 1708 calls, 1707 of them nil and one zero. 250 MB more after that costs 148 kB more resident memory.

Only chunked is decoded. **Transfer-Encoding: gzip, chunked** can be framed, because the chunk sizes do delimit it, but its contents are still compressed. Removing the framing and handing the bytes on as the body would hand on gzip and call it the body. That stays 501. A coding that is not chunked at all leaves the message with no way to say where the body ends, and is answered 400.

Trailers are consumed, limited to 8 KB, and discarded. Turning them into headers after the request has been dispatched is how a trailer becomes request smuggling. Framing that contradicts itself is a 400, because nothing after it can be trusted to be payload. Examples are a chunk not followed by CRLF, a size that is not hex, and a size line longer than 256 bytes.

Header names keep the case the client sent them in, so use **req.headers["Host"]** and not **req.headers["host"]**.

#### `on_upstream_writable(conn_id)`

Called when an upstream's write queue has come back under **self.watermark()**. A producer that stopped because **self.upstream_pending(conn_id)** was high can then carry on. This is a separate callback from **on_writable** because upstream ids and client ids are different spaces. One function taking both would have to be told which kind of id it had been given.

#### `on_writable(client_id)`

Called when this connection's write queue has come back under **self.watermark()**. A producer that stopped because **self.pending(client_id)** was high can then carry on. The callback is edge-triggered: it fires once per crossing, not once per completed write.

A client runtime passes its connection id, **on_writable(id)**. It is 1 unless **--connections** is given. A client's refusal to send also names its real cause. A connected **--mode out** client whose server has stopped reading is refused with a reason that names the backlog. It is not told it "is not connected to its server, or was created --mode in and does not send", three statements that are all false of it. Measured with 400 chunks of 64 KB sent to a peer reading nothing: 129 taken, 271 refused, 8,396,928 bytes queued.

This callback is what makes a body larger than the queue limit sendable at all. Without it, a script had only the hard limit, with nothing leading up to it: at 8 MiB the connection is closed. The only safe strategy was to know the limit in advance and never approach it. Measured with a client reading in 256 KB bites with a 5 ms pause, sending 200 chunks of 64 KB (13,107,400 bytes):

```
unpaced   8,454,273 bytes delivered, then the connection closed
paced    13,107,400 bytes delivered, on_writable fired 3 times
```

Pace against **self.watermark()**, not against a number of your own. It is a call and not a field because **--write-buffer** can be edited, and a number copied into the script's table at load would go stale as soon as the setting changed. The callback fires on the crossing. A producer that stops below the watermark never crosses it, so it is never called back. It would wait for an event that its own caution prevented:

```
local function pump(id)
    while remaining > 0 do
        if (self.pending(id) or 0) >= self.watermark() then return end
        if not self.send(id, next_chunk()) then return end
        remaining = remaining - 1
    end
end

function on_writable(id) pump(id) end
```

The call is made one loop turn after the write that emptied the queue, not on that write's completion. A connection that closes in between is simply not called.

#### `on_connect(client_id)`

Called when a client connects (server and client). It is also called on a sub-server when a connection is routed to it. The client_id is opaque. For this runtime's own clients, it is the file descriptor. For a connection routed here from another runtime, it is a handle above 16777216 that names the connection wherever it lives. Pass it back to **self.send()**, **self.owner_send()**, or anything else that takes a client_id. Do not compare it against a descriptor or assume anything about its value.

#### `on_disconnect(client_id)`

Called when a client disconnects (server and client). A client's **on_connect** and **on_disconnect** are given the descriptor and then the connection id; see **--connections**.

#### `on_rcpt(rcpt, default) -> bool`

Decides, in a mail runtime, whether to accept each recipient as the client names it. Each message the runtime accepts is then passed to **on_message(msg)**. See **Lua** under **MAIL FLAGS**.

#### `on_publish(client, msg) -> bool | table` / `on_subscribe(client, filter, qos) -> bool`

Decide, in an mqtt runtime, which publishes and subscriptions pass. In that runtime, **on_auth**, **on_connect** and **on_disconnect** are given a client table. See **Lua** under **MQTT FLAGS**.

#### `on_send(msg)`

Called when a message is sent. Under **--shards**, it is called on each shard that sends the message to its own clients, so a broadcast that reaches the siblings, like a **send** from the command line, calls it once per shard.

#### `on_route(method, path, backend_path)`

Chooses the backend for a request by returning its index (0-based). It is called by a proxy only, and only with **--strategy lua**. It answers only "where does this go". To accept or refuse a request before any backend is chosen, see **Proxy Filter Chain**.

The strategy decides whether the callback is consulted. A proxy created without **--strategy lua** keeps round-robin (or **random**, if that was requested) and never looks the callback up. A script that defines **on_route** on such a proxy loads without any report, and the proxy routes exactly as if the function were not there. That is the usual reason why an **on_route** that was tested and works appears to do nothing.

*path* is the path *as the client sent it,* including this proxy's own **/***name***/** prefix. *backend_path* is the same path with that prefix removed, which is what the backend will actually receive. A proxy named **gw** that is handed **/gw/api/users** sees both:

```
function on_route(method, path, backend_path)
    -- path         == "/gw/api/users"
    -- backend_path == "/api/users"
    if backend_path:match("^/api/") then return 0 end
    return 1
end
```

Both are offered because each is the truth about a different thing. The filter chain judges the request the client made, so it is handed *path*. A routing decision is usually about the endpoint being addressed, which is *backend_path*.

*backend_path* exists so that scripts stop computing it. Doing it by hand means stripping **"/" .. self.name .. "/"** and getting the bare case right, and the bare case is the one nobody gets right. The gateway's own root arrives as **/gw**, three characters against a five-character prefix, and must become **/**. A **sub()** past the end yields the empty string, which matches no pattern at all.

The arguments are passed with **--protocol http** only. A TCP proxy has no request line to read them from, and calls **on_route** with none. So a body written for HTTP, such as `**return hash(path) % n**`, raises on the first request when it is moved to a TCP proxy.

A handler that declares only two parameters is unaffected. Lua discards arguments that a function does not name, so every **on_route** written before this existed behaves exactly as it did.

If a call raises, or returns anything other than an index inside the backend list, it selects nothing. The proxy reports the error on stderr and falls back to the selection it would have made without the callback. The request is forwarded either way. Refusing a request is the filter chain's job, not this callback's.

#### `filters`

Not a callback but an array of them, for a proxy only: see **Proxy Filter Chain**.

#### `routes`

Not a callback either, but a table in which this runtime declares what it answers. The daemon publishes it to the proxies in front of the runtime: see **Declared Routes**.

#### `on_proxy_request(client_id, data) -> string | nil`

Called for every chunk forwarded from a client to a backend (proxy only). Return a modified string to replace the data, or **nil** to drop the chunk entirely, so that the backend never receives it.

Returning nothing at all forwards the chunk unchanged, which is not the same as returning **nil**. A hook written to watch traffic (**function on_proxy_request(id, data) log(data) end**) ends without a return. If that were read as **nil**, the most natural three lines in this API would discard every byte through the proxy. The filter chain draws the same distinction: a filter that returns nothing has no opinion, and the chain continues.

The hook fails closed, like the filter chain and for the same reason. If it raises a Lua error, or returns anything other than a string or **nil**, the request is refused. The connection to the client and the one to the backend are both closed, and the reason is logged. The hook is where a script strips a header or rejects a request. Forwarding the unmodified bytes when it could not run would admit exactly what it was there to refuse. And **return false** is a rejection, not a value to guess at.

The refusal closes the connections rather than answering with a status. This callback is on the byte path: it is called with body chunks as well as with the request head, and it carries TCP as readily as HTTP. To refuse a request with a status line, use the filter chain; see **Proxy Filter Chain**.

#### `on_proxy_response(client_id, data) -> string | nil`

Called for every chunk forwarded from a backend to a client (proxy only). It works like **on_proxy_request**. Returning nothing forwards the chunk unchanged, a replacement string replaces it, and nil drops it. An error, or a return of any other type, refuses. Here the refusal closes the client connection, because the response this hook was to redact must not be delivered unredacted.

#### `on_master_auth(client_id, password) -> bool`

Decides whether a client gets the master role, on a server in master mode. Return **true** to grant the master role. If this callback is defined, it overrides **--master-pw**, so it is the entire gate on that server.

Its result is read strictly, and it fails closed: only the boolean **true** grants. Anything else denies: **false**, **nil**, no return at all, and every truthy non-boolean, such as a string, the number 0 or a table. If the callback raises a Lua error, the attempt is denied and the error is logged. A denial from this callback is counted against the source address exactly as a wrong **--master-pw** is, so the per-address lockout described there applies here too.

#### `on_auth(client_id) -> bool`

Decides whether to admit a client, right after it is accepted (server only). It is called before **on_connect** fires. Return **true** to admit the client, or **false** to reject it and close the connection. If the callback raises a Lua error, the client is also rejected (fail-closed). When no **on_auth** callback is defined, all clients are admitted.

#### `on_websocket(client_id, headers)`

Called right after a WebSocket upgrade handshake completes (server only). By then, **on_connect** has already fired. The *headers* argument is a Lua table with any subset of these keys from the HTTP upgrade request: **cookie**, **origin**, **protocol** (Sec-WebSocket-Protocol) and **authorization**. Only keys present in the request are set; absent headers are nil. This callback never fires for plain TCP clients.

#### `on_http_request(req) -> table`

Called when the server receives an HTTP request (server only): the HTTP side of a server of messages, such as a webhook it relays to its clients. A site whose **.lua** files answer their own addresses is a **web** runtime's **--lua-pages**; see **Lua Pages**. The server detects HTTP from the first bytes; see **Multi-Protocol Auto-Detection**. The *req* argument is a table with these fields:

```
method      string   HTTP method ("GET", "POST", etc.)
path        string   Request path (e.g. "/api/users")
query       string   Query string without leading ? (empty if none)
body        string   Request body (empty for GET)
client_id   number   File descriptor of the client
version     string   HTTP version (e.g. "1.1")
headers     table    Request headers {["Host"]="...", ...}
```

Header names arrive as the client spelled them. Values arrive with optional whitespace (spaces and tabs) removed from both ends, so **X-Token: abc** reaches the callback as **abc**. A request whose framing this server refuses never reaches the callback. See **Request Framing** above for those requests and how they are answered.

Return a table with the HTTP response:

```
{
    status  = 200,                              -- HTTP status code
    headers = {["Content-Type"] = "text/html"}, -- response headers
    body    = "<h1>Hello</h1>"                  -- response body
}
```

If no **on_http_request** callback is defined, the server falls back to static file serving (**--http**) or returns 404. Returning nothing, or anything that is not a table, has the same effect: the request falls through to the static file or the 404. Only **nil** and no return at all do this silently; they are how a handler declines. Any other value means the script meant to answer, so the daemon's log names the fall-through as **[lua <runtime>] on_http_request returned a string; expected a table or nil ...**.

In the returned table, **status** must be a number, **body** a string, and **headers** a table of string to string. A field the script did not set takes its default: 200, an empty body, and no headers. A **status** or **body** that is present but of the wrong type makes a response this server cannot build. The request is then answered **500 Internal Server Error**, and the field and the type it arrived as are written to the daemon's log. A header whose name or value is not a string costs the client only that one header, not the whole answer, and is logged the same way.

HTTP/1.1 keep-alive is supported: the connection is reused for later requests unless the client's **Connection** header asks to close. That request is honoured for a Lua response exactly as it is for a static file.

A callback that **raises** is not a callback that declined. The request is answered **500 Internal Server Error**, and the error is written to the daemon's log as **[lua <runtime>] on_http_request error: ...**. Falling through to the 404 would make a broken handler look the same, to the client, as one that had no answer.

Example:

```
function on_http_request(req)
    if req.method == "GET" and req.path == "/health" then
        return {status = 200, body = "ok"}
    end
    return {
        status  = 200,
        headers = {["Content-Type"] = "application/json"},
        body    = '{"method": "' .. req.method .. '", "path": "' .. req.path .. '"}'
    }
end
```

#### `on_tick(dt)`

Called at a configurable interval while the runtime is running. *dt* is the actual time elapsed since the last tick, in milliseconds (a double). The interval is set by a top-level **tick_ms** global in the Lua script: a whole number of milliseconds, 10 or more. Default: 100, when the global is omitted. A value below 10, or one that is not a whole number, makes the script refuse to load, with a reason; it is not rounded into something else. 10 is the shortest interval **on_tick** can be armed at, and the daemon will not do what a script asking for less requests. Example:

```
tick_ms = 50
function on_tick(dt)
    self.broadcast("ping")
end
```

#### `on_miss(key) -> value [, ttl_seconds]`

Called when **GET** finds nothing (cache only), so the script can fetch the value from somewhere else. What it returns is stored and answered as a hit. See **Database Backend** for the four cache callbacks in full, with their ordering and their failure behaviour.

#### `on_write(key, value, ttl)`

Called after a successful **SET**/**SETEX**/**SETNX**/**MSET** (cache only).

#### `on_delete(key)`

Called after a **DEL** that removed something (cache only).

#### `on_expire(key)`

Called after the TTL sweep removes a key (cache only).

#### `on_upstream(conn_id, data)`

Called for each newline-delimited message received from an upstream connection (server only). Use -u to configure upstreams.

#### `on_upstream_connect(conn_id)`

Called when an upstream connects, including automatic reconnects (server only).

#### `on_upstream_disconnect(conn_id)`

Called when an upstream disconnects (server only).

#### `on_cluster_join(daemon)`

Called when a new remote daemon is discovered (cluster only). See **Cluster Event Callbacks**.

#### `on_cluster_leave(daemon)`

Called when a remote daemon becomes stale or disappears (cluster only).

#### `on_group_change(group, members)`

Called when the member count of a group changes (cluster only).

## What a script calls

- More in the manual: **Runtime Methods (in Lua)** (man-lua-configuration.txt): -- Every type self.name -- Runtime name (read-only) self.port -- Port number (read-only) self.state -- Current state (read-only) self.type -- Runtime type (read-only) self.connections() -- Current con

- More in the manual: **Global Functions** (man-lua-configuration.txt): socketley.log(msg) # Writes one line to the daemon's log at INFO level, prefixed with the name of the runtime that wrote it: [12:04:31] [INFO] [lua my-server] ...

- More in the manual: **Runtime Management API** (man-lua-configuration.txt): Create, start, stop, and remove runtimes from Lua scripts: socketley.create(type, name, config) -- Create runtime socketley.start(name) -- Start runtime socketley.stop(name) -- Stop runtime socketley.

## Making runtimes from a script

A script can create, start, stop and remove other runtimes. Each call returns `true`, or `false` and a sentence saying why, so `assert(...)` prints the reason.

```
function on_start()
    assert(socketley.create("server", "child", { port = 9010, lua = "/etc/socketley/child.lua", start = true }))
end
```

- The new runtime is **owned** by the one whose script made it (`ls` shows it under OWNED BY). When the owner stops, it is stopped too; `on_parent_stop = "remove"` removes it instead.
- A server, client, proxy, cache, storage or dns runtime made this way **runs inside the daemon**, not in a worker of its own; other types get their own worker as usual.
- Such runtimes are saved like any other and are back after a daemon restart.
- A runtime that is `failed` cannot be started from a script; `socketley start` on the command line can.

## The rest

- More in the manual: **Configuration File Format** (man-lua-configuration.txt): -- Optional: configure the daemon itself daemon = { name = "node1", cluster = "/shared/cluster" } runtimes = { { type = "server", name = "api", port = 9000, group = "api", config = "handler.lua", star

- More in the manual: **A machine's setup** (man-lua-configuration.txt): A setup is a machine's runtimes, written as Lua files.

- More in the manual: **Handler Privileges** (man-lua-configuration.txt): A Lua handler runs with the daemon's full privileges.

- More in the manual: **Callback Deadline** (man-lua-configuration.txt): Every invocation of a Lua callback has a wall-clock time budget.

- More in the manual: **Proxy Filter Chain** (man-lua-configuration.txt): This applies to a proxy in HTTP mode only.

- More in the manual: **Declared Routes** (man-lua-configuration.txt): routes is a global array in which a runtime states what it answers: each entry is a path and the methods allowed on it.

- More in the manual: **Cluster Introspection API** (man-lua-configuration.txt): When the daemon runs in cluster mode ( --cluster ), the socketley.cluster table provides read-only introspection into the full cluster topology.

- More in the manual: **Cluster Event Callbacks** (man-lua-configuration.txt): These optional callbacks fire when the cluster topology changes.

More script APIs: [storage](man-storage-flags.txt), [socketley.storage](man-storage-flags.txt), [mqtt](rt-mqtt.txt), [mail](rt-mail.txt). Working scripts for every type are in the repository's `examples/`.

# Deployment

Running socketley on a machine that matters: the service, permissions, TLS, state, backups and limits.

What to settle before socketley runs something that matters.

## The service and who may use it

- The installed daemon is the systemd unit `socketley`; it restores every runtime at boot and logs to the journal.
- The `socketley` group can create, stop and script every runtime: treat membership like sudo.
- The unit grants `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`, so runtimes may bind ports below 1024.

## What is exposed

- Keep local things on `--bind 127.0.0.1` or `--listen unix:`. A cache is local unless created `--public`.
- Put public HTTP behind the entrance: `--domain` names, ACME certificates, `--auth` and an [idp](rt-idp.txt) for sign-in.
- Cap what a client may cost: `--max-connections`, `--rate-limit`, `--global-rate-limit`, `--idle-timeout`, `--read-buffer`, `--write-buffer`.

## State and backups

- A runtime's state file can hold secrets such as a master password; see [a state file is a secret](man-state-persistence.txt).
- Back up from a timer with `socketley export --full file`; `socketley restore file` puts it back.

| Runtime | Durability flag |
|---|---|
| cache, mqtt | `--persistent` |
| storage | `--fsync` |
| metrics | `--durable` |

## Watching it

- A [metrics](rt-metrics.txt) runtime raises alerts; the daemon sends them per `daemon.alert_webhook` and `daemon.alert_mail`.
- The [dashboard](man-dashboard.txt) shows every runtime, its log and its figures.

## Recipe: a public HTTPS site with a Lua handler

The goal: `https://shop.example.com` answered by a Lua script, with a real certificate, on one machine with the public address 203.0.113.7.

1. **Serve the domain's DNS from this machine.** The dns runtime writes a zone whose name servers `ns1` and `ns2` point here, and makes the **entrance**: a proxy on 443 (with a redirect from 80) that gets its own certificates.

   ```
   socketley create dns ns --zone example.com --publish 203.0.113.7 -s
   ```
2. **Delegate the domain.** At your registrar, set `ns1.example.com` and `ns2.example.com` as the name servers, both with the glue address 203.0.113.7. The entrance asks Let's Encrypt for the certificates by itself, and asks again until the delegation is visible.
3. **Write the handler**, `shop.lua`:

   ```
   function on_http_request(req)
       if req.path == "/" then
           return { status = 200, headers = { ["Content-Type"] = "text/plain" }, body = "hello\n" }
       end
       return { status = 404, body = "not found\n" }
   end
   ```
4. **Create the site.** `--domain shop` becomes `shop.example.com` under the zone; `--bind 127.0.0.1` keeps its own port off the network, since visitors come through the entrance.

   ```
   socketley create server shop -p 9100 --bind 127.0.0.1 --lua shop.lua --domain shop -s
   curl https://shop.example.com/
   ```

A request now goes browser → entrance on 443 (TLS ends here) → the server `shop` → `on_http_request`. See [How it works](how.txt) for the path, and the [dns runtime](rt-dns.txt) for `--publish` behind NAT.

**If your DNS stays with another provider**, the entrance has no names to route, because it learns them from the dns runtime. Point an A record for `shop.example.com` at this machine instead, and let the server hold port 443 and its certificate itself; it proves the name on that port.

```
socketley create server shop -p 443 --acme shop.example.com --acme-email you@example.com --lua shop.lua -s
```

Only one runtime can hold 443 on an address, so for several sites the entrance is the better way.

## Recipe: moving to a new machine

1. **On the old machine, archive everything**: every runtime, their data (buckets, mailboxes, a cache's file, zones, keys and certificates) and the daemon's configuration.

   ```
   socketley export --full /var/backups/socketley.tar.gz
   ```
2. **On the new machine**, [install socketley](install.txt), copy the archive over, and restore it with the daemon stopped. Each runtime comes back running where it ran.

   ```
   systemctl stop socketley
   socketley restore /var/backups/socketley.tar.gz
   systemctl start socketley
   socketley ls
   ```
3. **Check what it names.** The archive leaves out logs, output files, backup directories and what sync runtimes carry, and `restore` leaves paths under `/etc`, `/usr` and the like for you to take out with `tar`; both commands list these when they finish.
4. **If the new machine has another public address**, three places still name the old one: the glue at your registrar, the dns runtime's `--publish`, and the zone file it wrote (its `ns1`, `ns2` and the zone's own address, under the state directory's `zones/`). Edit the zone file, then give the runtime the new address:

   ```
   echo '{"publish":"198.51.100.4"}' | socketley import ns --restart
   ```

## Reference

- More in the manual: **System Mode (installed via package)** (man-files.txt): /usr/bin/socketley # The socketley binary.
- More in the manual: **Development Mode (no system install)** (man-files.txt): /tmp/socketley.sock # The Unix domain socket for daemon IPC.
- More in the manual: **The IPC socket** (man-files.txt): Every socketley command travels over the socket above, and through it a client can reach everything the daemon can do.
- More in the manual: **Where state lives** (man-files.txt): The two directories above are where a daemon's runtimes live when the daemon serves the default socket.
- More in the manual: **Daemon Configuration** (man-files.txt): The daemon configuration file is a Lua script that sets a daemon table: daemon = { name = "node1", -- this daemon's name in a cluster cluster = "/shared/dir", -- cluster directory; needs name log_leve

- More in the manual: **WebSocket and other protocol upgrades** (man-limitations.txt): A proxy in http mode relays a connection that has switched protocols.
- More in the manual: **What can stop the event loop** (man-limitations.txt): A process serves its runtimes on one thread: a worker serves its one runtime, and the daemon serves the runtimes that scripts make in it.
- More in the manual: **Out-of-process runtimes** (man-limitations.txt): Every runtime made with create or restored at boot, of any type, runs in its own supervised worker process.
- More in the manual: **TLS** (man-limitations.txt): Every runtime type speaks TLS.

- More in the manual: **Daemon flags** (man-daemon-flags.txt): These flags configure the running daemon through IPC commands.

# Operating it

Is it running, where the log is, why a runtime failed, and what blocks it.

The day-to-day questions once runtimes are running: is it up, where is the log, why did it fail, what is slow. For the first setup, see [Deployment](deploy.txt).

## Symptoms

| You see | Usually because | Do |
|---|---|---|
| `404` on `/` through a proxy | A proxy with `--backend` forwards only `/<proxy-name>/…`. | Ask for `/name/…`, or reach the runtime by its `--domain` name through the entrance. |
| `504` from a proxy | The backend did not begin its answer within `--backend-timeout` (2 s). | Find what is slow in the backend, or raise the timeout. |
| Requests to one backend fail at once | Five errors in a row opened its circuit breaker. | It is tried again after `--circuit-timeout`; fix the backend. |
| `create` exits 1, runtime `failed` | The worker could not bind, load its certificate, or run its script. | Read `ls` and the log, fix, then `socketley start name`. |
| `NOT RESPONDING` in `ls` | A Lua callback that does not return. | See below; the deadline ends it. |
| A cache lost data | Its worker crashed without `--persistent-interval`, or the power failed. | Add `--persistent-interval`; see [what survives what](how.txt). |
| `not permitted to open the daemon socket` | You are not in the `socketley` group. | `sudo usermod -aG socketley $USER`, then log in again. |

## Is it running?

| Command | Shows |
|---|---|
| `socketley ls` | Every runtime with its port, connections and status. A running one shows its uptime and notes: `(N restarts)` means its worker died and was replaced N times; `NOT RESPONDING` means it is alive but stuck. A `failed` one shows why. |
| `socketley ps` | The same, for running runtimes only; `ps -a` shows them all. |
| `socketley stats name` | Live counters of one runtime: connections, messages, bytes, and its type's own figures. |
| `socketley daemon stats` | The daemon's own figures. |

## Where the log is

- **Installed:** `journalctl -u socketley`. Every worker's output reaches the daemon, which passes each line on to the journal.
- **Development:** the terminal where `socketley daemon` runs.
- **In a browser:** with `daemon.metrics_port` set in the configuration file, the [dashboard](man-dashboard.txt) shows each runtime's own log and a failed runtime's last error.

```
journalctl -u socketley -f                  # follow it
journalctl -u socketley --since "10 min ago"
```

## A runtime failed

1. **Read the reason**: `socketley ls` shows it beside the runtime, and the log has the full line.
2. **Know which kind it is.** Either the worker could not start (a port in use, an unreadable certificate, a script error), or it died more than five times in ten seconds.
3. **Fix the cause and start it again.** A failed runtime keeps its configuration; nothing has to be created anew.

   ```
   socketley start name
   ```

A worker that crashed loses what it held only in memory. A cache keeps what `--persistent` saved; see [How it works](how.txt).

## Slow under load

Look in this order:

1. **A Lua call that waits** in a callback that cannot wait, typically `socketley.http` in `on_http_request`, holds up every client of that runtime. See **What blocks a runtime** below.
2. **One core is full.** A worker uses one core; `socketley stats name` and the dashboard show its CPU. Near one full core, the runtime is at its limit: `--shards N` spreads it over N workers, though not every workload gains (see [sharding](man-server-flags.txt)).
3. **A slow backend behind a proxy.** A backend that has not begun its answer within `--backend-timeout` (2 seconds by default) gets the client a 504. After five errors in a row, its circuit breaker opens and requests to it fail at once for a while.
4. **A limit you set.** `--max-connections`, `--rate-limit` and `--global-rate-limit` refuse or slow clients by design.

## Restarts and upgrades

- **A package upgrade restarts the service** if it was running, onto the new binary. Restarting the daemon stops every worker, so connections close for the moment it takes; the runtimes then come back as they were.
- **A worker never outlives its daemon.** If the daemon crashes, systemd starts it again after five seconds.
- **One runtime alone**: `socketley restart name`. Other runtimes are not touched.

Everything else that can happen, and what survives it, is in the table under [How it works](how.txt).

## `NOT RESPONDING`: a stuck worker

`ls` and `ps` show this when a worker has said nothing for fifteen seconds while using at least half a core. It is almost always a Lua callback that does not return. Its [deadline](man-lua-configuration.txt) (10 seconds by default) ends the callback; nothing is killed for being slow.

## What blocks a runtime

A worker serves its runtime on one thread. A Lua call that waits for something outside, such as `socketley.http`, either suspends the callback or blocks the whole runtime, depending on where it is made:

| Called from | What a waiting call does |
|---|---|
| `on_message`, `on_client_message` | Suspend the callback; the runtime keeps serving everyone else. |
| The storage hooks, an mcp tool's handler | Suspend the callback, as above. |
| `on_http_request` | **Block the whole runtime** until the answer arrives or `timeout_ms` (default 5000) runs out. |
| `on_start`, `on_stop`, timers, filters | Block the whole runtime, as above. Keep such calls to `on_start`, `on_stop` or a rare `on_tick`. |

Other runtimes are not affected: each has its own worker. The full list of calls that can stop a loop is under [What can stop the event loop](man-limitations.txt).

## Settings you may actually change

Every setting has a default that suits a normal deployment. These are the ones worth knowing; set them in the `settings` table of `/etc/socketley/config.lua`, or as environment variables of the service. `socketley settings` lists every one with its value and where it came from. The `settings` table is the simpler place: it needs no change to the service unit.

| Variable | What it changes |
|---|---|
| `SOCKETLEY_CPUS` | The CPUs the daemon may run on; every worker inherits the set. |
| `SOCKETLEY_LUA_TIMEOUT_MS` | The callback deadline, 10000 ms by default. |
| `SOCKETLEY_ACME_DIRECTORY` | The ACME CA, for example Let's Encrypt's staging CA while testing. |
| `SOCKETLEY_PROXY_HTTP2`, `SOCKETLEY_PROXY_HTTP3` | `0` turns HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 off at the entrance. |

The rest are tuning knobs for unusual workloads, and the ones the manual calls test hooks exist for socketley's own test suite. All are on [Environment & files](env.txt).

## Alerts

Set `daemon.alert_webhook`, `daemon.alert_mail` or `daemon.events` in the configuration file, and the daemon creates a [metrics](rt-metrics.txt) runtime whose built-in rules raise an alert when, among others:

- a runtime failed, or was started again three times within the hour;
- a certificate a runtime serves expires within two weeks;
- a disk under a storage runtime or the state directory, or the host's memory, is at 90%;
- a mail runtime has a hundred messages waiting.

The full list, and how to change it with `--rules`, is under [Dashboard](man-dashboard.txt).

# Cluster

Daemons on several machines that see each other's runtimes, and the opt-in Raft mode.

Daemons that share a directory form a cluster. Each writes its state there every two seconds; one silent for ten seconds is left out. Then `socketley ls` shows every daemon's runtimes, and a proxy's `@group` backend reaches members wherever they run.

```
# on every machine, the same shared directory
socketley daemon --name node-a --cluster /mnt/cluster
socketley create server api -p 9000 -g api -s
# anywhere in the cluster
socketley create proxy gw -p 8080 --backend @api -s
socketley daemons
```

> Warning: Whoever can write to the cluster directory decides where `@group` traffic goes. Protect it like the control socket.

- More in the manual: **Cluster mode** (man-cluster-mode.txt): The cluster directory is as privileged as the daemons that read it.

- More in the manual: **Raft mode (experimental, opt-in)** (man-cluster-mode.txt): Experimental.

- More in the manual: **Cluster Introspection API** (man-lua-configuration.txt): When the daemon runs in cluster mode ( --cluster ), the socketley.cluster table provides read-only introspection into the full cluster topology.

- More in the manual: **Cluster Event Callbacks** (man-lua-configuration.txt): These optional callbacks fire when the cluster topology changes.

## Service mesh

The proxy's health checks, circuit breaker, deadlines, retries and mTLS are what a service mesh gives each call. `--sidecar` turns on health checks, the circuit breaker, retries and draining in one flag.

- More in the manual: **Health Checks** (man-service-mesh.txt): Active health checks probe backends at a regular interval ( --health-interval ) using either a TCP connect or an HTTP GET ( --health-check ).
- More in the manual: **Circuit Breaker** (man-service-mesh.txt): The circuit breaker prevents cascading failures by tracking consecutive errors per backend.
- More in the manual: **Response Deadline** (man-service-mesh.txt): A backend that accepts connections and then stops answering fails no check.
- More in the manual: **Request Framing** (man-service-mesh.txt): In HTTP mode the proxy is strict about how a request's header block is framed.
- More in the manual: **Retries** (man-service-mesh.txt): When --retry is set, failed requests are automatically retried on the next backend in the load balancer pool.
- More in the manual: **mTLS** (man-service-mesh.txt): Both legs can be encrypted.
- More in the manual: **Sidecar Deployment** (man-service-mesh.txt): The --sidecar flag enables a production-ready set of defaults: TCP health checks, a circuit breaker (threshold 5, timeout 30s), 2 retries, and graceful drain.

# C++ SDK

Control a daemon, embed the engine, or attach a process of your own to a daemon.

The C++ SDK in `include/linux/socketley/` has three tiers. Examples are in `sdk/examples`, and the test suite builds each one.

Socketley ships a modular C++ SDK in three tiers, in **include/linux/socketley/**. Tiers 1 and 3 are self-contained, header-only files. Copy them anywhere and compile with **g++ -std=c++17**; no library is needed. Tier 2 must be built from source.

| Tier | Header | Use Case | Dependencies |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | socketley/control.h | Control a running daemon | None (POSIX) |
| 2 | socketley/{server,cache,proxy,client}.h | Embed the full engine | libsocketley_sdk.a |
| 3 | socketley/attach.h | Register with a daemon | None (Tier 1) |

- More in the manual: **Tier 1: Daemon Control (header-only)** (man-c-sdk.txt): socketley/control.h gives a program full control over a running daemon.
- More in the manual: **Tier 2: Embed Engine (build from source)** (man-c-sdk.txt): Tier 2 embeds the full io_uring event loop and all four runtime types in your own binary.
- More in the manual: **Cross-Platform SDK (Windows / macOS)** (man-c-sdk.txt): These header-only TCP clients connect to Socketley runtimes from non-Linux platforms.
- More in the manual: **Tier 3: Daemon Attach (header-only)** (man-c-sdk.txt): socketley/attach.h registers your own process as a runtime with a running daemon.
- More in the manual: **Mixed: Engine + Daemon Attach (Tier 2 + 3)** (man-c-sdk.txt): Embed the full engine for maximum performance, and register with the daemon for fleet monitoring.

# CLI

Every command socketley takes, with its options.

`socketley --help` is the same reference, interactive, in the terminal. A runtime's own verbs are `socketley <name> <verb>`, as in `socketley store get key`.

#### `daemon`

Start the socketley daemon. When socketley is installed system-wide (with the .deb package or install.sh), systemd manages the daemon and starts it automatically, so you do not need to run this command yourself. Use **systemctl start socketley** or **systemctl enable socketley** to control the service.

When running from the build directory (development mode), start the daemon manually: **./bin/Release/socketley daemon &**

The daemon creates its IPC socket at /run/socketley/socketley.sock (system install) or /tmp/socketley.sock (development mode). On startup, it restores the saved runtime configurations. Runtimes that were running when the daemon last stopped are started again automatically.

The daemon ignores **SIGHUP**, so closing the terminal or a stray **kill -HUP** does not stop it.

**daemon** accepts **--cpus** *set***,** the ring setting described under **COMMON FLAGS**. Here it sets the CPUs of the ring this daemon is about to create, rather than stating what a runtime requires of its ring. It is the command-line form of **SOCKETLEY_CPUS**; when both are given, the flag wins. **daemon** also accepts **--fast-lo**, **--fast-lo-limit** (below) and the experimental Raft flags described under **CLUSTER MODE**. It refuses any other argument.

These flags cannot be combined with **--name** or **--cluster**, which configure a running daemon. When none is running, they start one without these flags first. A ring's CPU set is fixed when the ring is created, so there would be nothing left for them to change.

Every runtime runs in its own process and inherits this CPU set, so the set also decides how many runtimes share a core. In a test with fifty idle servers beside one server doing a ping-pong, the median round trip did not change (30.2 against 29.4 microseconds), but the 99th percentile did: 156.5 microseconds on six cores against 51.7 on twelve. Idle runtimes still cost something, because each one wakes on its own stats interval. That cost shows up in the tail latency of whichever runtime is working, and a wider CPU set is the way to reduce it. The daemon itself stayed under one per cent of a core with fifty runtimes. Creating a runtime took the same fourteen milliseconds with five runtimes as with fifty. Neither of these is worth watching.

#### `daemon --fast-lo [own|all|trust]`

Put TCP connections whose two ends are both 127.0.0.1 or ::1 on a kernel shortcut. A BPF **sockops** program adds both sockets to a sockhash when the connection is established. An **sk_msg** program then places every send directly into the peer's receive queue, skipping TCP/IP, the loopback device and its softirq. Off by default.

**all** is the mode used when no mode is given. It accelerates any local client that connects to a port one of this daemon's runtimes listens on, and the connections of the runtimes among themselves. It also accelerates every connection a runtime makes to a listener on 127.0.0.1, whoever owns that listener. Examples are a proxy with **--backend 127.0.0.1:8080** in front of a local application, a client runtime, or a Lua HTTP call to a local service.

**own** accelerates only pairs whose two ends are both this daemon's runtimes, such as a client runtime connected to a server runtime.

**trust** is **all** without the receiver rule described below: it also redirects a send into a foreign receiver. A foreign client of a cache and a proxy's foreign backend are then accelerated in both directions. It is meant for an operator who knows that every local process reading a socket of such a pair reads with **recv**, **read** or **recvmsg**.

**Warning:** a byte redirected into a socket waits in an ingress queue that only **recvmsg** drains. A local process never sees those bytes if it reads with **splice**(2), **sendfile**(2) or **TCP_ZEROCOPY_RECEIVE**, or through a relay built on them (such as Go's **io.Copy** between two TCP connections, or HAProxy with splicing). Under **trust**, the bytes are lost, and neither side gets an error. In a test, a backend reading with **splice** behind a proxy echoed 0 of 500 bytes. Such readers cannot be detected from the outside, which is why **all** never redirects into a foreign socket. Use **all** unless you know every local client and backend. **socketley daemon stats** reports which mode is running.

Under **own** and **all**, a send is redirected only when the socket that will *receive* it belongs to one of this daemon's workers. That is either the socket of a runtime that connects (the socket is marked when it connects), or a socket accepted on a runtime's listener. A send to a foreign receiver goes over ordinary TCP. Each direction of a pair is decided by its own receiver. The reason is that a socket receiving through the kernel's ingress queue can only be read with **recvmsg**. A foreign reader that uses **splice**(2), **sendfile**(2), Go's **io.Copy** between two TCP connections, or HAProxy's splicing would lose the redirected bytes, and such readers cannot be detected from the outside. So the shortcut accelerates only what it can accelerate safely: sends into a runtime always, and sends out to a foreign peer never (unless **trust** is given).

Results for common setups, measured on one machine with alternating passes:

- Runtime to runtime (a client runtime to a server runtime, both ends this daemon's) is accelerated in both directions under every mode. 64 B round trips are 1.3–1.4x faster with one connection and with eight, and 16 KB round trips about 1.2–1.5x. For a client runtime against a cache with one request in flight, off against **all**: 110–116K against 83–85K round trips a second.
- A foreign client of a cache is accelerated only on the requests it sends; the replies come back over TCP. So a workload of small requests and large replies gains little under **all**. **redis-benchmark** (50 connections, 4 threads, six alternating passes) measured these requests per second, off / **all** / **trust**. **GET** **-P1**: 240–279K / 222–250K / 387–667K. **SET** **-P1**: 222–286K / 197–273K / 462–632K. GET **-P16**: 2.3–4.0M / 2.7–3.4M / 5.3–6.9M. A bulk reader of 64 KiB values: 1377–1488 / 1276–1322 / 2464–3040 MB/s. A request that carries the payload does gain under **all**: a 64 KiB **SET** pipelined 8 deep made 49.9K against 59.1K, 1.18x. Only **trust** gives a foreign client the full gain.
- For a proxy in front of a foreign local backend, **all** accelerates the two legs that end in the proxy. It leaves the two legs that end in a foreign socket on TCP, so a foreign backend that reads with **splice** keeps every byte. Under **trust**, both kinds of leg are redirected. 64 B round trips through a proxy to a C echo backend, over one connection: 44–48K off, 41–45K under **all**, and 86–88K under **trust**.

The shortcut needs **CAP_BPF** and **CAP_NET_ADMIN** (root, or **setcap cap_bpf,cap_net_admin+ep** on the binary) and cgroup v2 at /sys/fs/cgroup. Without them the daemon logs **fast-lo: unavailable, serving without it** with the reason, and serves on the ordinary path. **own** attaches to the daemon's cgroup; **all** and **trust** attach to the root cgroup. The daemon's own processes are the workers its supervisor forked, and the daemon keeps their pids in a map. Under **all** and **trust**, the program runs for every process on the host, so it accepts only sockets in the daemon's own network namespace. The namespace's netns cookie is built into the program at load time, so a container's identical 127.0.0.1 tuple is left alone. This needs **SO_NETNS_COOKIE** in the kernel. Without it, the shortcut refuses to attach rather than serve across namespaces. The programs and maps are anonymous, and they are detached when the daemon exits.

What it costs:

- The redirected backlog is bounded by **daemon --fast-lo-limit** *per-pair-MiB*,*global-MiB* (default 4,64). A redirected send does not wait for the receiver, so the program counts each pair's sends.
