The file uses the **resolv.conf**(5) format, so a test can point the resolver at a nameserver of its own. Default: /etc/resolv.conf (see What can stop the event loop). A mail runtime's SPF, DKIM and DMARC lookups also ask these nameservers.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_MAIL_MX_PORT`

A test aid that sets the port on which a mail runtime hands mail to a domain's exchangers. Default: 25. A test's own server can then act as an exchanger.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_MAIL_TLS_CA`

A test aid that names the CA file a mail runtime checks an exchanger's certificate against. It applies where DANE or MTA-STS asks for that check. Default: the system's roots. A test's own exchanger can then be trusted.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_MAIL_STS_CA`

A test aid that names the CA file a mail runtime checks an MTA-STS policy server against. Default: the system's roots.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_MAIL_STS_CONNECT`

A test aid that sets the *host*:*port* from which every MTA-STS policy is fetched. The name in the policy's URL is still the one checked. A test can thus serve the policies of domains it does not own. Default: each policy's own host.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_MAIL_DELAY_NOTICE_MS`

A test aid that sets how many milliseconds a mail runtime tries a message before it tells the sender the message is late. This applies only to senders who asked for the notice (NOTIFY=DELAY). Default: four hours.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_MAIL_SPOOL_MOVE_MS`

A test aid that sets how many milliseconds a sealed spool segment waits before it is used again. Before the segment is reused, the few messages still in it are moved. Default: one minute.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_MAIL_DEAD_DOMAIN_MS`

A test aid that sets how many milliseconds a mail runtime holds on to a domain that cannot take mail. This covers a domain it found not to exist or to take no mail. After this time, the runtime looks the domain up again. Default: ten minutes.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_MAIL_PUSH_CONNECT`

A test aid that sets the *host*:*port* to which every JMAP push is posted. The certificate is still checked for the name in the push URL. A test can thus receive the pushes of a URL it does not own. Default: the URL's own host.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_MAIL_PUSH_CA`

A test aid that names a file of CA certificates for checking a JMAP push URL's certificate. Default: the system's CA certificates.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_MAIL_IDLE_MS`

A test aid that sets how many milliseconds a connection to a mail runtime may stay quiet before it is closed. The same limit applies to how long a TLS handshake may take. The runtime tells the client before it closes the connection. Defaults: five minutes for SMTP, POP3 and ManageSieve, thirty minutes for IMAP, and thirty seconds for a handshake.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_MAIL_BAYES_FOLD_MS`

A test aid that sets how many milliseconds new spam filter learning stays in a mail runtime's journal. After this time, the first shard folds it into the filter's file. Default: ten minutes.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_MAIL_LET_GO_MS`

A test aid that sets how many milliseconds a shard of a mail runtime, other than the first, keeps a user's index in memory after nothing on that shard asked for it. The index is read again from its files when it is next asked for. Default: ten minutes.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_IDP_CLIENT_CA`

A test aid that names a file of CA certificates for checking the client metadata documents an idp fetches. The certificate served with each such document is checked against this file. Default: the system's CA certificates.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_IDP_CLIENT_CONNECT`

A test aid that sets the host:port from which every client metadata document is fetched. The name in the document's address is still the one sent and checked. Default: the host in that address.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_IDP_COMPACT_AFTER`

A test aid that sets how many account changes an idp runtime journals before it folds them into its snapshot. A test can thus see the snapshot written while changes go on. Default: 1000.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_MAIL_SPOOL_FROZEN_US`

A test aid that names every message of a mail runtime after this fixed microsecond instead of the clock. Writers in two shards then produce the same name, as they would if they wrote in the same microsecond. Default: the clock.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_MAIL_QUEUE_SCALE`

A test aid that runs a mail runtime's retries and **--queue-lifetime** this many times faster. A test can then see a message tried again and given up within seconds. Default: 1.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_MAIL_BUSY_HOLD_MS`

A test aid that sets how many milliseconds a mail runtime pauses a domain after one of its exchangers answered 421. During the pause, the runtime opens no new connection to that domain. Each further 421 doubles the pause, up to fifteen minutes, until a message is taken. Default: thirty seconds.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_MAIL_SPOOL_KEEP_BYTES`

A test aid that sets how many bytes of message bodies a mail spool keeps in memory beside its segments. Default: 64 MiB. A small value lets a test have bodies read back from disk.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_NOTIFY_HOSTS`

A test aid that names a hosts file for a storage runtime's notification webhooks. The file holds one *name address* pair per line. The webhooks' resolver reads it before the system resolver, on every resolve, so a test can point a webhook's host name at another address. Unset, a name is asked of the resolver on the loop and then of the system's resolver (see Event notifications).

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_NOTIFY_QUEUE`

Sets the most undelivered events a storage shard holds. Beyond that, a new event is dropped and counted in **notify_dropped**. Default: 10000. A test lowers it to reach the bound.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_CLUSTER_QUEUE`

Sets the most changes a storage shard queues for another node of its cluster. Beyond that, the shard lets the queued changes go. Once that node answers, the shard sends it everything instead (see Cluster). Default: 100000. A test lowers it to reach the bound with a few writes.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_REPLICATION_HOSTS`

A test aid that names a hosts file for a storage runtime's replication targets. The file holds one *name address* pair per line. The targets' resolver reads it before the system resolver, on every resolve, so a test can name a target by a host name. Unset, a name is asked of the resolver on the loop and then of the system's resolver (see Replication).

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_STOP_HOLD_MS`

A test aid that makes a storage shard's stop wait before it lets go of its directory. The value is in milliseconds, 0 to 3000. The wait starts after the shard's in-flight work has finished, and it is multiplied by the shard's number plus one. A test can thus start a runtime beside shards that are still stopping. Unset, a stop waits only for its own work. It slows every stop and restart, so never use it on a runtime in use.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_START_SPIN_MS`

A test aid that makes a storage shard's start keep the CPU busy before it opens its store. The value is in milliseconds, 0 to 30000. The shard uses CPU the way reading a large store's files does.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_START_SLEEP_MS`

A test aid that makes a storage shard's start wait idle before it opens its store. The value is in milliseconds, 0 to 60000. This imitates a wedged start.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_LOG_FLUSH_MS`

A test aid that sets how long a storage shard holds server access log lines before it delivers them. The value is in milliseconds, 100 to 3600000. Default: one minute.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_RECOVERY_THREADS`

Sets how many threads a storage worker uses to read its object headers when it starts after an unclean stop. The range is 1 to 64. Default: the number of CPUs the worker may run on, at most 16. The threads end before the listener opens. This changes how long such a start takes, never what it finds.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_RECOVERY_DEPTH`

Sets how many opens and header reads each recovery thread keeps in flight on an io_uring of its own. The range is 0 to 256. Both this value and the thread count are lowered to fit within half of what **RLIMIT_NOFILE** leaves. Default: **32**; **0** reads one file at a time without a ring. This changes how long a start from a cold cache takes, never what it finds.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_STORAGE_RECV_BUFS`

Sets how many 16 KiB buffers a storage worker's receive ring holds; the value must be a power of two. Default: **64**; **0** removes the ring, and every connection reads into a buffer of its own. A connection borrows a buffer only for the length of one completion, so an idle keep-alive connection holds none. When a receive finds the ring empty, it uses a buffer of its own for that one read. Such reads are counted as **recv_fallbacks** in **stats**. This changes the memory a worker holds, never what it returns.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_TLS_FAILURE_REPORT_SECS`

Sets how often a runtime serving TLS logs one line counting the inbound handshakes that failed since its last report. Default: every 60 seconds; the range is 1 to 3600. A failed handshake comes from a port scanner far more often than from a client, so each one is counted rather than logged.

#### `SOCKETLEY_TLS_TICKET_SECS`

A test aid that sets how many seconds one session ticket key seals new tickets. The key still opens its tickets for as long again, and is then wiped. The range is 1 to 86400. Default: an hour.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_WRITE_STALL_SECS`

A test aid that sets how many seconds a server or proxy client with no **--idle-timeout** may take nothing of its answer before the connection is reset. The range is 1 to 86400. Default: 120 seconds.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_ACME_DIRECTORY`

Sets the directory URL of the ACME CA that **--acme** and **acme issue** use. Default: Let's Encrypt, **https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory**. Its staging CA is **https://acme-staging-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory**. Each CA has an account of its own.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_ACME_CHALLENGE`

Sets the challenge type that **acme issue** and **--acme** use to prove a name when no type is requested. The values are **http-01** (the default), **tls-alpn-01** and **dns-01**. A wildcard name is always proven over DNS-01, whatever this variable says.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_ACME_DNS_WAIT`

Sets the seconds between publishing a DNS-01 answer and telling the CA to look for it. The answer is published where the **dns** runtimes serve it. The wait is the time a secondary of the zone has to take the new serial, and the delegation probe gives the secondary the same time. Default: 10, at most 3600. A secondary that is told by NOTIFY and transfers on it takes seconds. For a secondary that waits for its refresh, set this to the minutes the refresh takes.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_ACME_DNS_PROBE`

Names the resolver that **acme issue** asks whether a zone is delegated to this daemon's **dns** runtimes. The value has the form *host*[:*port*]. **acme issue** asks about a zone of **--dns-zones** before it proves anything there over DNS-01. It then asks each name server of the zone, by its IPv4 addresses, the way a CA would. **off** asks nothing and treats every zone as delegated. Default: the first **nameserver** of */etc/resolv.conf*.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_ACME_CA`

Names a PEM file of root certificates for checking the ACME CA's own HTTPS. Use it for a CA whose certificate no system store holds, such as Pebble. Default: the system's roots.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_GIT_ACCESS_KEY`

Holds the access key that **git-sync** uses to write into a library. A storage runtime that starts git-sync gives it temporary credentials of the user for whom the repository is kept.

#### `SOCKETLEY_GIT_SECRET`

Holds the secret of that access key.

#### `SOCKETLEY_GIT_SESSION_TOKEN`

Holds the session token of temporary credentials, sent as x-amz-security-token.

#### `SOCKETLEY_GIT_TOKEN`

Holds a GitHub token that **git-sync** uses to read a private repository. git-sync gives it to git as an http.extraHeader in git's environment, never on a command line.

#### `SOCKETLEY_FFMPEG`

Names the ffmpeg that a storage runtime uses to make thumbnails and streams under **/~media/**. The runtime reads what a film is with the **ffprobe** beside that ffmpeg, or the one on **PATH**. Default: the first **ffmpeg** on **PATH**. With neither, a media request is answered **501**. The runtime reads this variable at its first media request.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_MEDIA_HWACCEL`

Selects where a storage runtime encodes its renditions. **off** always uses x264 on the CPU. A render node such as **/dev/dri/renderD129** uses that GPU. The default is **/dev/dri/renderD128**.

At its first medium, a worker runs one second of test picture through the GPU's whole chain (upload, scale, H.264 encode). It tries the full encoder and then the low-power one. The worker uses the GPU for renditions only when one of them works; until it knows, renditions use x264. A rendition keeps the encoder that its first job chose. If a rendition's first GPU job fails before anything is made, that rendition continues with x264. HLG is tone-mapped on the CPU, HDR10 on the GPU. **vaapi-unchecked:***node* skips the test run, for testing that fallback.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_MEDIA_CACHE_MB`

Sets the size in MiB beyond which a storage runtime removes the media it made from *dir*/.media/. It removes the least recently requested media first. Default: 10240. The medium made last is kept even when it alone is larger, and no medium is removed while it is being made.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_CACHE_TTL_SWEEP_MS`

Sets the interval in milliseconds between periodic sweeps for expired cache keys. Default: **500**. This never affects correctness: an expired key is not served no matter when the sweep runs, because every read path checks the expiry itself. The interval controls only how quickly keys that are never accessed again release their memory.

#### `SOCKETLEY_CACHE_SNAPSHOT_MB`

Sets how many MiB a cache shard's journal (**--persistent-interval**) may hold before the shard snapshots, unless its last dump is larger, in which case that size is the bound. Default: **64**. The snapshot is written by a forked child, so the shard goes on serving; the journal is then cut to what came after the snapshot began.

#### `SOCKETLEY_LUA_TIMEOUT_MS`

Sets how long, in milliseconds, one Lua callback invocation may hold the event-loop thread. Default: **10000**. **0** switches the bound off entirely: nothing is armed or written for a callback. LuaJIT's trace compiler is on either way. The budget is measured from the start of the callback's loop turn and checked every 100 milliseconds, and a compiled callback that cannot be interrupted is ended by replacing its worker. See **Callback Deadline**.

This is the default for every script that does not declare its own **callback_timeout_ms** global; a script that declares one overrides it. A value that is not a whole number of milliseconds in 0–3600000 is refused with a warning, and the default is used.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_HTTP_REVALIDATE`

Set to **0** to switch off the response cache of plain **--http**. Each request then costs an open, a read and a close again. Any other value, or leaving the variable unset, keeps the cache on. The variable is read when the runtime starts, so a **restart** picks up a change. The server serves the same content either way, because the cache is revalidated on every request. The switch exists for measurement, and for ruling the cache out when diagnosing something else.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_KERNEL_TLS`

Set to **0** to keep every TLS record in this process. Otherwise, some TLS 1.3 connections hand their sending to the kernel's TLS layer. This happens in six cases. A server, storage or proxy connection sends a file or object over 256 KiB. A TCP proxy's backend streams that much to the client. An HTTP/1.1 proxy sends a client an answer body of that known length. A cache connection is owed 2 MiB or more at once. An mqtt client is sent a packet of 256 KiB or more. A mail client is sent a reply of 4 MiB or more, without COMPRESS.

The connection then changes its send key and hands the new key to the kernel's TLS layer. The kernel encrypts what is sent, by sendfile from the page cache or spliced from the backend, at about half the CPU of encrypting a copy in this process. A cache's answer is in memory and has no sendfile to gain, so the kernel only spares it the copies OpenSSL makes: measured over loopback, 2 MiB answers cost 0.83 and 8 MiB 0.53 of the CPU, while 1 MiB and smaller cost the same or more, which is why a cache waits for 2 MiB. A connection that never sends that much stays as it was, because for small answers encrypting a copy here costs less. An mqtt payload under kernel TLS is not copied at all, so the broker gains from 256 KiB: measured over loopback, a 1 MiB publish to 20 TLS subscribers costs 0.56 of the CPU, a 256 KiB one 0.68. A mail FETCH of 8 MiB costs 0.61, of 4 MiB 0.79, while at 1 and 2 MiB the move gains nothing it can hold to, so mail waits for 4 MiB. The move is for the rest of the connection: a 1 KiB answer on a moved cache connection costs what it did, a 256 KiB one about a tenth more. HTTP/2 connections are never moved.

This needs the kernel's **tls** module (**modprobe tls**). Without the module, the connection continues in user space under its new key, and the runtime says so once in its log. The variable is read when the runtime starts.

Inherited by worker processes, which have no command line of their own.

#### `SOCKETLEY_PROXY_SPLICE`

Makes a **--protocol tcp** proxy splice a pair from its first byte to its last, not only while a side streams. Unset by default; any value other than **0** turns it on. It is read once per process and inherited by worker processes.

Without the variable, each side of a pair decides for itself. A side copies through a buffer until four reads in a row have filled it, which marks a stream. It then moves its bytes with **splice**(2) through a pipe. The splice is called on the event loop, with both sockets non-blocking for the call. It never goes through io_uring, whose splice is an io-wq hand-off per transfer. Four splices in a row that would not have filled the buffer mark messages. The side then goes back to copying and gives its pipe back. Each switch waits until nothing of the other path is in flight or queued, so no byte overtakes another. Measured on one core, over loopback, through the proxy:

```
                        copy             adaptive         from the first byte
4 GB stream             3.4-4.2 GB/s     9.3-9.9 GB/s     10.1 GB/s
  CPU per GB            0.24-0.30 s      0.08-0.11 s      0.08-0.10 s
64 B messages, 32 conns 6.95 us           6.86 us          10.36 us
4 KB messages           7.41 us           7.37 us          9.28 us
```

So the variable is for measuring, not for speed. A TLS listener or TLS backend never splices. Neither does a pair with a 127.0.0.1 leg while the daemon runs with **--fast-lo**. A proxy with an **on_proxy_request** or **on_proxy_response** hook never splices either, because the kernel would move those bytes without the script ever seeing them. Nor does a proxy with a **--rate-limit** or **--global-rate-limit**, which is charged per read.

#### `SOCKETLEY_FAST_LO`

Set by a daemon started with **--fast-lo** once the shortcut is attached; it is not a setting. The value is **own**, **all** or **trust**. It tells the daemon's workers to keep a proxied pair with a 127.0.0.1 leg off splice. The daemon clears any inherited value at startup.

#### `SOCKETLEY_NAPI_BUSY_POLL_US`

Enables io_uring NAPI busy polling with this timeout in microseconds. Unset by default. It trades CPU for lower receive latency on busy links.

#### `SOCKETLEY_HUGEPAGE`

Set to **0** to stop cache workers from asking glibc for transparent huge pages. On by default, and only a cache asks for them. A cache's hot path walks a keyed structure larger than the TLB covers, which is what a huge page is for. A server showed no measured gain for the extra resident memory. glibc reads the tunable at process startup, and a running process cannot ask for itself. The daemon therefore puts it in the worker's environment at exec.

#### `SOCKETLEY_RECV_MULTISHOT`

Set to **0** to arm one read at a time instead of a multishot receive. On wherever the kernel supports it. A multishot arm is one submission for a stream of messages instead of one per message. The switch exists so that the two can be measured against each other on one binary. A dns runtime's TCP connections read one at a time either way: a client's pipelined queries arrive several to a read, and there a multishot receive cost more CPU per query than the submissions it saved.

#### `SOCKETLEY_RECV_BUNDLE`

Set to **0** to stop packing several provided buffers into one receive (**IORING_RECVSEND_BUNDLE**). On where the kernel supports it. Support is probed once rather than assumed, and the receive falls back to the plain multishot arm wherever the flag is refused.

Both of these variables read **only** the exact string **0**. **SOCKETLEY_RECV_MULTISHOT=off** leaves multishot on, which is the opposite of what it looks like. The **SOCKETLEY_NO_*** switches below follow the other rule: any value except **0** turns the feature off.

#### `SOCKETLEY_NO_SHARD_MESH`

Any value but **0** stops shards from linking to each other directly. The shards then relay through the daemon, and the daemon logs at startup that the mesh is off. This is the measurement control for the mesh: the two paths differ only in the route, not in the build. A request or answer longer than the 8 MiB one frame holds goes in pieces, through the daemon as over a link, up to 256 MiB. Requests and answers for a shard that has not read them yet wait on each side of the daemon up to 64 MiB, and beside that one of up to 256 MiB; past that, an asker is answered at once, as **the runtime is overloaded: its request backlog is full**, not as no such runtime. Everything else the daemon and a shard tell each other (configuration, publishes, deliveries) waits up to 4 MiB of its own beside them.

#### `SOCKETLEY_CACHE_HANDOFF`

**0** stops a sharded cache from handing a client connection to the shard that owns its keys; it then relays each of that connection's commands there instead. On by default for every cache with two or more shards. A connection is handed once 28 of its last 32 single-key commands named one other shard, over the link between the two shards, and only between commands: never inside MULTI or WATCH, while subscribed, blocked or replicating, with a reply or crossing outstanding, or over TLS, a unix socket or a per-shard port. A connection handed on waits a second at its new shard before it may move again, twice as long after each further move. **stats** shows **handoff_out**, **handoff_in**, **handoff_aborted** and **handoff_busy** per shard while it is on.

#### `SOCKETLEY_NO_PEER_LINKS`

Any value but **0** stops runtimes from opening direct links to their peers. It exists for the same reason as **SOCKETLEY_NO_SHARD_MESH** and is read the same way.

#### `SOCKETLEY_NO_COMPANION`

Any value but **0** stops a unix-socket listener from being placed beside a port.

#### `RES_OPTIONS`

Passes options to glibc's resolver; socketley itself does not read it. If you have not set it, socketley sets it for worker processes to **timeout:1 attempts:2**.

It is set because **getaddrinfo**(3) blocks the thread that calls it. In a worker, that thread is the event loop, with the daemon's control socket armed on the same ring. While a lookup waits, **stop** and **stats** go unanswered. glibc's own default is five seconds, twice. Against a nameserver that drops packets, that measured 10.0 s for one lookup. And a client re-resolves on every reconnect once its cached address stops accepting. One second twice has the same ceiling as two seconds once, and still retries a lost packet.

If you set it yourself, your value is used unchanged, for the daemon and every worker. Raise it if a slow but working nameserver is being given up on. The cost of giving up is one more reconnect round, not a failed runtime.

#### `EDITOR , VISUAL`

Name the editor that **socketley edit** opens when given no flags. **VISUAL** is tried first.

#### `TMPDIR`

Sets where that editor's temporary file is written. While the editor is open, the file holds the runtime's entire configuration; for a cache, that includes **master_pw**. If */tmp* is shared, point this at a directory of your own. The file is created 0600 and removed when the editor exits.

#### `SOCKETLEY_DNS_CACHE_MS`

Sets how long, in milliseconds, **socketley.http()** reuses a resolved address before it asks the resolver again. Default: **60000**. **0** disables reuse and makes every call resolve.

This is a ceiling, not a promise. If a connect to the cached address is refused or times out, the entry is dropped at once. An endpoint that moved is then followed on the next call. So this value only decides how long the cache stays wrong about an endpoint that moved *without* refusing, which is when something else answers on the old address.

The cache exists because **getaddrinfo**(3) blocks the thread that calls it, glibc caches nothing of its own, and in a worker that thread is the event loop. Every other resolver in this daemon is bounded by something. A client and a server re-resolve at most once per second of reconnect backoff, a proxy once per thirty-second sweep, and the rest once at start. Without the cache, **socketley.http()** would resolve on every call. It resolves on a thread of its own and gives up at the call's deadline. A resolver that does not answer therefore costs a call its timeout, rather than costing the loop every retry the resolver makes.

#### `SOCKETLEY_RAFT_TICK_MS`

Sets the Raft tick, in milliseconds, of a daemon started with **--raft-listen**. Default: **100**. The election timeout is ten to twenty ticks, and a heartbeat is sent every tick. Every member of one cluster should therefore use the same value.

#### `SOCKETLEY_RAFT_COMPACT_EVERY`

Sets how many applied Raft entries go by between snapshots. Default: **1000**. A small value makes a joining node catch up through a snapshot; the test suite sets it for that purpose.

#### `SOCKETLEY_CONFIG`

Sets the path to the daemon configuration file.

- More in the manual: **System Mode (installed via package)** (man-files.txt): /usr/bin/socketley # The socketley binary.
- More in the manual: **Development Mode (no system install)** (man-files.txt): /tmp/socketley.sock # The Unix domain socket for daemon IPC.
- More in the manual: **The IPC socket** (man-files.txt): Every socketley command travels over the socket above, and through it a client can reach everything the daemon can do.
- More in the manual: **Where state lives** (man-files.txt): The two directories above are where a daemon's runtimes live when the daemon serves the default socket.
- More in the manual: **Daemon Configuration** (man-files.txt): The daemon configuration file is a Lua script that sets a daemon table: daemon = { name = "node1", -- this daemon's name in a cluster cluster = "/shared/dir", -- cluster directory; needs name log_leve

- More in the manual: **State persistence** (man-state-persistence.txt): The daemon persists runtime configurations as JSON files.

# cache runtime

In-memory store on the Redis protocol: strings, lists, sets, hashes, sorted sets, streams, pub/sub

A **cache** is an in-memory data store that speaks the Redis protocol, so `redis-cli` and Redis libraries work unchanged. `nc` works too, in plain text.

```
socketley create cache store -p 6379 -s
redis-cli -p 6379 SET greeting hello
redis-cli -p 6379 GET greeting

socketley create cache sessions -p 6380 --maxmemory 512M --eviction allkeys-lru \
    --persistent /var/lib/socketley/sessions.bin -s
socketley create cache copy -p 6381 --replicate 10.0.0.5:6380 -s
```

> Warning: A cache has no password: whoever reaches it reads and writes everything. So it serves this machine only, unless created with `--public` or mutual TLS (`--tls --cert --key --ca`), where the client certificate is the credential. `--public` opens it to every machine that reaches its address; keep it on a private one with `--bind` and a firewall.

## What it does

- **Redis data types**: Strings, lists, sets, hashes, sorted sets, streams; see [commands](man-cache-flags.txt).
- **Redis features**: TTLs, pub/sub and transactions over [RESP](man-cache-flags.txt).
- **Bounded memory**: `--maxmemory` with an `--eviction` policy.
- **Persistence**: `--persistent file` saves at a clean stop; `--persistent-interval` journals writes, so a crashed worker loses at most that interval (a power cut can lose more).
- **Replication**: `--replicate` makes a read-only [follower](man-cache-flags.txt).
- **Several cores**: `--shards N`, one keyspace; `--cluster` for cluster-aware clients.
- **Database backing**: Lua `on_miss` reads through, `on_write` writes behind; see [database backend](man-cache-flags.txt).

## Works with

A [server](rt-server.txt) with `--cache` lets its clients and scripts reach it.

## Flags

Every flag a cache runtime takes, by group.

**Basics**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `-p` | int | Port: The port it listens on (a client: the port of its target). |
| `-s` |  | Start now: Start it as soon as it is made. |
| `-g` (--group) | text | Group: Puts it in a group; a proxy with --backend @group reaches every member. |
| `--lua` | path | Lua script: A script with the runtime's callbacks, run at start. |
| `--lua-ffi` |  | Lua FFI: Let the script require("ffi"): LuaJIT's calls into C and raw memory, where a wrong pointer ends the runtime's process. |

**Network**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--bind` | text | Bind address: Bind the port to this address only, such as 127.0.0.1 when only a proxy on this machine should reach it. |
| `--listen` | text | Unix socket: Listen on a unix socket instead of a port. |
| `--shards` | int | Shards: Worker processes sharing the port: the way one runtime uses more than one core. |
| `--domain` | list | Names: The names it is reached by through the entrance; empty for its own name. |
| `--cpus` | text | CPUs: The CPUs its I/O may run on, as 0-3,6. |

**TLS**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--tls` |  | TLS: Encrypt its transport: terminate TLS on its port, or dial over it. |
| `--cert` | path | Certificate: The PEM certificate (chain allowed) a listener presents. |
| `--key` | path | Key: The PEM key of the certificate. |
| `--ca` | path | CA: On a listener: require client certificates from this CA (mutual TLS). On a client or proxy: the CA its servers are checked against. |
| `--acme` | list | ACME names: Names to get a Let's Encrypt certificate for, renewed by itself. |
| `--acme-email` | text | ACME e-mail: The address the CA writes to about the certificate. |

**Limits**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--max-connections` (--max-conn) | int | Max connections: The most clients at once. |
| `--rate-limit` | int | Rate limit: Messages a second per connection. |
| `--global-rate-limit` | int | Global rate limit: Messages a second over all connections. |
| `--congestion` | text | Congestion control: The kernel's congestion control for its connections, such as bbr, which keeps its rate up under packet loss. |
| `--idle-timeout` | duration | Idle timeout: Close a connection that has received nothing for this long; off unless given. |
| `--read-buffer` | size | Read buffer: How much data may pile up from one connection before it is refused; 1M unless given. |
| `--write-buffer` | size | Write buffer: How much unsent data may queue up for one connection before it is dropped; 8M unless given. |
| `--drain` |  | Drain on stop: Finish what is in flight before stopping. |

**Output**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--log` | path | State log: A file it appends each state change to. |

**Cache**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--mode` | one of readonly, readwrite, admin | Access: What its clients may do: read, read and write, or everything. |
| `--persistent` | path | Persist to: The file it is kept in across restarts. |
| `--persistent-interval` | duration | Journal every: How often accepted writes reach the journal. |
| `--maxmemory` | size | Max memory: The most memory its data may take. |
| `--eviction` | one of noeviction, allkeys-lru, allkeys-random | When full: Refuse writes, or evict keys. |
| `--resp` |  | Redis protocol only: Speak RESP to every client, without detecting it. |
| `--replicate` | text | Follow: The leader cache it follows, host:port. |
| `--public` |  | Public: Serve clients on other machines too. |
| `--cluster` |  | Cluster map: Publish a slot map so cluster clients go straight to each shard (the default above one shard). |
| `--no-cluster` |  | No cluster map: Keep the shards on the one port: no per-shard ports, no slot map. |

## Benchmarks

A ratio (×) is how many times better socketley did: more per second, or less time, memory or CPU; above 1× socketley is ahead. The range in brackets is the lowest and highest ratio across the passes.

### Redis protocol, one command per round trip

Redis 8.0.5, Valkey 9.0.4, 3 passes, 2026-11-10, socketley 0174a7a1.

| case | socketley | Redis | Valkey | socketley vs Redis | socketley vs Valkey |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SET | 289 K /s (1.00 cores) | 165 K /s (1.00 cores) | 172 K /s (1.00 cores) | 1.78× (1.72–1.79) | 1.66× (1.55–1.86) |
| GET | 283 K /s (1.00 cores) | 167 K /s (1.00 cores) | 174 K /s (1.00 cores) | 1.63× (1.57–1.71) | 1.64× (1.49–1.76) |
| LPUSH | 272 K /s (1.00 cores) | 191 K /s (1.00 cores) | 169 K /s (1.00 cores) | 1.42× (1.42–1.44) | 1.70× (1.49–1.75) |
| LPOP | 275 K /s (1.00 cores) | 187 K /s (1.00 cores) | 174 K /s (1.00 cores) | 1.47× (1.43–1.72) | 1.60× (1.48–1.63) |
| SADD | 274 K /s (1.00 cores) | 178 K /s (1.00 cores) | 180 K /s (1.00 cores) | 1.58× (1.51–1.66) | 1.57× (1.52–1.84) |
| HSET | 282 K /s (1.00 cores) | 175 K /s (1.00 cores) | 164 K /s (1.00 cores) | 1.61× (1.36–1.72) | 1.73× (1.53–1.75) |
| ZADD | 196 K /s (1.00 cores) | 164 K /s (1.00 cores) | 163 K /s (1.00 cores) | 1.17× (1.13–1.26) | 1.19× (1.14–1.43) |

How it was measured: 3 redis-benchmark processes × 50 connections; servers on one core, clients on 20 others. Each server on one pinned core, every row at a full core: the rate is one core divided by the cost of an operation. SET and GET draw their keys at random from about a million, as a cache's clients spread them. At depth 1 that cost is mostly the kernel's per-message price, which all three pay alike, so the differences are small and the ranges wide; this VM halts idle vCPUs and every wakeup of a client costs the server a VM exit, which moves a server that answers each command with its own write more than one that batches.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SET | 9.69 M /s (1.00 cores) | 2.31 M /s (1.00 cores) | 2.68 M /s (1.00 cores) | 4.18× (4.17–4.19) | 3.62× (3.60–3.63) |

| SADD | 5.76 M /s (1.00 cores) | 2.91 M /s (1.00 cores) | 2.55 M /s (1.00 cores) | 2.00× (1.96–2.04) | 2.23× (2.23–2.28) |
| HSET | 4.64 M /s (1.00 cores) | 2.33 M /s (1.00 cores) | 2.11 M /s (1.00 cores) | 1.99× (1.98–2.00) | 2.18× (2.18–2.21) |

How it was measured: 3 redis-benchmark processes × 50 connections; servers on one core, clients on 20 others. The per-message price divided by a hundred: what remains is parsing and executing commands, where the servers differ. SET and GET draw their keys at random from about a million, more than a core's caches hold, so each lookup waits on memory; SADD, HSET and ZADD put random members into one big collection each.

### Four cores, a cluster-aware client

Redis Cluster 8.0.5, 4 masters, 3 passes, 2026-11-10, socketley 0174a7a1.

| case | socketley | Redis Cluster 8.0.5, 4 masters | socketley vs Redis Cluster 8.0.5, 4 masters |
|---|---|---|---|
| SET | 24.96 M /s (3.25 cores) | 12.70 M /s (3.95 cores) | 1.97× (1.89–2.05) |
| GET | 27.23 M /s (3.35 cores) | 13.97 M /s (3.86 cores) | 1.95× (1.79–2.04) |
| LPUSH | 27.92 M /s (3.47 cores) | 13.97 M /s (3.91 cores) | 2.00× (2.00–2.00) |
| LPOP | 25.40 M /s (2.99 cores) | 12.15 M /s (3.92 cores) | 2.09× (2.09–2.09) |

How it was measured: 3 redis-benchmark processes × 50 connections, 100 commands a message; socketley as four shards and Redis Cluster as four masters, each shard or master pinned to one of the same four cores; five redis-benchmark --cluster processes on 20 others. SET and GET draw their keys at random from 1,048,576, 64 behind each of the 16,384 slot tags, preloaded so every GET finds its key (the hit rate is counted every pass). Every shard's mesh counters are read around every timed run: no command crossed between shards in any pass, so the client sent each to its owner. redis-benchmark --cluster's threads spin while they wait, so its client cores are no reading of headroom.

### Four cores, a plain client at one address

Valkey 9.0.4, --io-threads 4, 3 passes, 2026-11-10, socketley 0174a7a1.

| case | socketley | Valkey 9.0.4, --io-threads | socketley vs Valkey 9.0.4, --io-threads |
|---|---|---|---|
| SET | 12.55 M /s (3.97 cores) | 3.49 M /s (3.99 cores) | 3.59× (3.54–3.63) |
| GET | 13.17 M /s (3.97 cores) | 5.05 M /s (3.99 cores) | 2.61× (2.60–2.64) |
| LPUSH | 9.76 M /s (1.00 cores) | 4.63 M /s (3.99 cores) | 2.11× (2.11–2.12) |
| LPOP | 11.67 M /s (1.00 cores) | 3.50 M /s (3.99 cores) | 3.35× (3.33–3.40) |
| SADD | 12.03 M /s (1.00 cores) | 6.17 M /s (3.99 cores) | 1.95× (1.94–1.97) |
| HSET | 10.35 M /s (1.00 cores) | 4.88 M /s (3.99 cores) | 2.12× (2.11–2.13) |
| ZADD | 9.92 M /s (1.00 cores) | 4.70 M /s (3.99 cores) | 2.12× (2.09–2.14) |

How it was measured: 3 redis-benchmark processes × 50 connections, 100 commands a message; socketley as four shards on one port and Valkey with four I/O threads, on the same four cores; five redis-benchmark processes on 20 others. SET and GET draw their keys at random from 1,048,576, three in four of them owned by another shard than the one a connection landed on: socketley carries those over its shard mesh, many commands a frame. LPUSH to ZADD name one key, which one shard owns, so socketley runs those on one of its four cores (see the cores column) and Valkey on its four I/O threads.

## In the manual

Every flag in full, and Cache Protocol, RESP Protocol (Redis Compatibility), Database Backend, Replication: man-cache-flags.txt


---

# client runtime

Dials a server and holds the connection: TCP, UDP or a unix socket, over TLS, reconnecting

A **client** dials a TCP or UDP peer and keeps the connection. What arrives is printed, saved or handled in Lua.

```
socketley create client feed -t 10.0.0.5:9000 --reconnect 0 -b -s   # print what arrives, reconnect for ever
socketley send feed "subscribe prices"
socketley create client probe -t unix:/run/app.sock --lua probe.lua -s
```

## What it does

- **Any target**: `-t host:port` or `-t unix:/path`; `--udp` for datagrams.
- **Verified TLS**: `--tls`, checked against `--ca` or the system store; no way to skip it.
- **Reconnects**: `--reconnect [n]` backs off up to 16 seconds; `0` retries for ever.
- **Output**: `-b` prints messages (`-bpt` adds name and time); `-w file` saves them.
- **Lua**: `on_connect`, `on_message`, `on_disconnect`; `on_writable` paces sending.

## Works with

Any [server](rt-server.txt) or TCP service. `socketley send` writes through it from the shell.

## Flags

Every flag a client runtime takes, by group.

**Basics**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `-p` | int | Port: The port it listens on (a client: the port of its target). |
| `-s` |  | Start now: Start it as soon as it is made. |
| `-g` (--group) | text | Group: Puts it in a group; a proxy with --backend @group reaches every member. |
| `--lua` | path | Lua script: A script with the runtime's callbacks, run at start. |
| `--lua-ffi` |  | Lua FFI: Let the script require("ffi"): LuaJIT's calls into C and raw memory, where a wrong pointer ends the runtime's process. |

**Network**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--cpus` | text | CPUs: The CPUs its I/O may run on, as 0-3,6. |

**TLS**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--tls` |  | TLS: Encrypt its transport: terminate TLS on its port, or dial over it. |
| `--cert` | path | Certificate: The PEM certificate (chain allowed) a listener presents. |
| `--key` | path | Key: The PEM key of the certificate. |
| `--ca` | path | CA: On a listener: require client certificates from this CA (mutual TLS). On a client or proxy: the CA its servers are checked against. |

**Limits**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--read-buffer` | size | Read buffer: How much data may pile up from one connection before it is refused; 1M unless given. |
| `--write-buffer` | size | Write buffer: How much unsent data may queue up for one connection before it is dropped; 8M unless given. |
| `--reconnect` | int | Reconnect: Reconnect with backoff when the connection drops: the most attempts, 0 for no limit. |

**Output**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--log` | path | State log: A file it appends each state change to. |
| `-w` | path | Message file: A file every received message is written to. |
| `-b` |  | Print messages: Print every received message. |
| `-bp` |  | …with name: Print them with the runtime's name before each. |
| `-bt` |  | …with time: Print them with the time before each. |
| `-bpt` (-btp) |  | …with time and name: Print them with the time and the name before each. |

**Server**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--udp` |  | UDP: Datagrams instead of a stream. |

**Client**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `-t` | text | Target: The server it connects to, host:port. |
| `--mode` | one of inout, in, out | Mode: Both ways, receive only or send only. |
| `--connections` | int | Connections: How many connections it holds to the target, each with its own id; changing it opens or closes them. |

## Benchmarks

A ratio (×) is how many times better socketley did: more per second, or less time, memory or CPU; above 1× socketley is ahead. The range in brackets is the lowest and highest ratio across the passes.

| request-answer over UDP: 1 socket, 64 B datagrams, round trip p50 | 28.5 µs (0.54 cores) | 32.1 µs (0.66 cores) | 35.6 µs (0.73 cores) | 42.8 µs (0.79 cores) | 1.13× (1.12–1.14) | 1.25× (1.25–1.26) | 1.50× (1.48–1.53) |
| request-answer over UDP: 1 socket, 64 B datagrams, round trip p99 | 41.2 µs (0.54 cores) | 46.3 µs (0.66 cores) | 50.4 µs (0.73 cores) | 59.1 µs (0.79 cores) | 1.12× (1.12–1.12) | 1.22× (1.21–1.24) | 1.44× (1.42–1.46) |
| connect: 200 connections dialled and held | 38 K conn/s (1.90 cores) | 7.0 K conn/s (0.37 cores) | 5.5 K conn/s (0.46 cores) | 9.0 K conn/s (0.98 cores) | 5.52× (3.92–6.08) | 6.35× (5.74–7.03) | 4.38× (3.13–4.47) |
| connect: 200 TLS connections, each a full verified handshake | 5.6 K conn/s (2.02 cores) | 2.7 K conn/s (1.28 cores) | 2.1 K conn/s (1.96 cores) | 2.5 K conn/s (2.27 cores) | 2.14× (1.97–2.14) | 2.61× (2.56–2.65) | 2.26× (2.21–2.40) |
| held: 200 idle connections, memory per connection | 62.8 KiB (0.00 cores) | 23.9 KiB (0.00 cores) | 269.0 KiB (0.00 cores) | 78.6 KiB (0.00 cores) | 0.38× (0.37–0.43) | 4.28× (4.14–4.81) | 1.25× (1.21–1.41) |
| held: 10,000 idle connections, memory per connection | 2.3 KiB (0.00 cores) | 9.6 KiB (0.00 cores) | 9.6 KiB (0.00 cores) | 9.5 KiB (0.00 cores) | 4.14× (4.06–4.17) | 4.17× (4.15–4.17) | 4.12× (4.04–4.14) |

How it was measured: clientgen target (Go) on 2-5, every client arm on core 8, 3 s windows; every client arm on one core, the Go target (clientgen) on four others. Every client on the same one core, the target (a Go program) on four others with headroom: every row records the target's cores, and none used all four. socketley is one client runtime holding every connection (--connections N) with its Lua on_message as the handler; the others are one process with the same logic. Every count is taken at the target: a consumer's count must equal the lines sent, every request's size is checked, and a round trip is the interval between one connection's requests as the target sees them. The firehose rows are bound by the client's core, and every line differs (each carries its index). socketley's script reads them with on_read, walking a view of the read buffer with view:lines(), which makes no string, as Go's ReadSlice hands out a slice of its buffer; Node and Python make a string or a bytes object per line. Written with on_message instead, a Lua string per line, the 64 B row makes about 12.7 million lines a second, and with on_messages, one string per read, about 52 million. Over TLS the 64 B row is bound by the target, whose one goroutine encrypting the stream uses a whole core while socketley's runtime decrypts at about four fifths of its own; the target's cores beside the row say so. Connecting is that one runtime dialling all of them, as the others dial from one process; the memory row is socketley's daemon and the runtime's process together, by proportional set size, divided by the connections, so at 200 it is mostly the two processes' fixed cost. One runtime per connection instead, each made with socketley create ... -s from a shell loop, is a process each: 386 created and connected a second, 243 with TLS, and 1,546 KiB each held.

### Generating load: lines as fast as the connection takes them

tcpkali 1.1.1, Go 1.24.6, 3 passes, 2026-11-10, socketley 0174a7a1.

| case | socketley | tcpkali | Go | socketley vs tcpkali | socketley vs Go |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| send: 64 B lines as fast as the connection takes them, TCP | 126.03 M lines/s (1.00 cores) | 102.03 M lines/s (1.00 cores) | 67.64 M lines/s (1.00 cores) | 1.15× (1.07–1.27) | 1.86× (1.63–1.86) |
| send: 4 KiB lines, TCP | 2.45 M lines/s (1.00 cores) | 1.62 M lines/s (1.00 cores) | 1.35 M lines/s (1.00 cores) | 1.48× (1.45–1.57) | 1.94× (1.74–2.83) |

How it was measured: clientgen target (Go) on 2-5, every client arm on core 8, 3 s windows; every sender on one core, the Go sink on four others. Sending as fast as the connection takes it, counted at a sink on other cores. socketley paces with self.pending() and on_writable and sends one line per self.send call; tcpkali repeats its message into large writes; Go makes one buffered write call per line. All are bound by the client's core.

### Generating load over a unix socket and TLS

|---|---|---|---|

The same over a unix socket and over TLS 1.3, which tcpkali does not speak. Over TLS Go's rate takes one of two levels from pass to pass in every run, about 18-21 or 33-38 million lines a second, while socketley's stays within a few per cent of its median; the ratio falls on whichever level most of Go's passes took.

### Driving a Redis-protocol server

redis-benchmark 8.0.5, 3 passes, 2026-11-10, socketley 0174a7a1.

| case | socketley | redis-benchmark | socketley vs redis-benchmark |
|---|---|---|---|
| pipelined INCR to a socketley cache, depth 32, 1 connection | 966 K /s (0.57 cores) | 916 K /s (0.62 cores) | 1.06× (1.05–1.06) |
| pipelined INCR to a socketley cache, depth 32, 4 connections | 5.91 M /s (0.84 cores) | 6.89 M /s (0.99 cores) | 0.86× (0.81–0.86) |

How it was measured: clientgen target (Go) on 2-5, every client arm on core 8, 3 s windows; each client on one core, the socketley cache on another. A socketley client runtime sending 32 INCR commands as one message and the next 32 on the 32nd reply, the replies counted with on_read and view:lines() as redis-benchmark counts them in C, against redis-benchmark -P 32 with one thread, both to the same socketley cache on its own core, counted by the cache's own counter. At one connection both wait on the round trip; at four, socketley's runtime holds four connections, as redis-benchmark's one thread does, and the cache is the bound under socketley's client at a whole core, where redis-benchmark is at its own.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

# db runtime

JSON documents owned by accounts, over HTTP, with indexes, queries, replicas and backups

A **db** keeps JSON documents for applications, such as a game's characters or a shop's orders. Each document belongs to an [idp](rt-idp.txt) account. Nobody writes another account's documents; who may read them is set per collection.

```
socketley create db data -p 9500 --domain data --idp auth \
    --schema /etc/socketley/db.schema --keys /etc/socketley/db.keys -s
socketley data query characters '{"where":{"level":{"gte":5}},"limit":10}'
```

## What it does

- **Documents over HTTP**: GET, PUT, PATCH, DELETE at `/c/collection/id`, each versioned for safe writes.
- **Queries**: `POST /c/collection/_query` filters, sorts and pages on the indexes in `--schema`.
- **Access per collection**: `private`, `owner`, `shared`, `public` or `catalog`; services use `--keys`.
- **Transactions and changes**: Several writes as one, and a live stream of changes.
- **Replicas**: `--replicate` keeps a read-only copy of another db.
- **Backups**: Scheduled with `--backup-dir`, or now with `socketley <db> backup|restore`.

## Works with

Users sign in through an [idp](rt-idp.txt). Pictures and other large files belong in a [storage](rt-storage.txt).

## Flags

Every flag a db runtime takes, by group.

**Basics**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `-p` | int | Port: The port it listens on (a client: the port of its target). |
| `-s` |  | Start now: Start it as soon as it is made. |

**Network**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--bind` | text | Bind address: Bind the port to this address only, such as 127.0.0.1 when only a proxy on this machine should reach it. |
| `--shards` | int | Shards: Worker processes sharing the port: the way one runtime uses more than one core. |
| `--domain` | list | Names: The names it is reached by through the entrance; empty for its own name. |
| `--cpus` | text | CPUs: The CPUs its I/O may run on, as 0-3,6. |

**Limits**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--max-connections` (--max-conn) | int | Max connections: The most clients at once. |

**Database**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--schema` | path | Schema: The collections, a line each: name, access (private, owner, shared, public, catalog) and indexed fields. |
| `--keys` | path | Keys: Service keys a backend sends as Authorization: Bearer, one name and secret per line. |
| `--idp` | text | Identity provider: The idp runtime whose accounts own documents and sign in by its cookie or access tokens. |
| `--idp-audience` | list | Token clients: The idp's clients whose access tokens it takes; a token of any other is refused. |
| `--origins` | list | Web origins: Web origins whose pages may call it with the user's sign-in; * lets any page call it, without the sign-in. |
| `--max-bytes` | size | Quota: The most bytes the documents hold. |
| `--cache` | size | Cache: Memory for the documents read most recently; the rest are read from disk. |

**Replication**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--replicate` | text | Copy of: The http or https address of the database this one follows; a copy answers reads. |
| `--replicate-key` | path | Its key: A file holding a key of that database. |

**Backups**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--backup-dir` | path | Backups: The directory backups are written into. |
| `--backup-every` | duration | Back up every: How often a backup is taken. |
| `--backup-keep` | int | Keep: How many backups are kept. |

## Benchmarks

A ratio (×) is how many times better socketley did: more per second, or less time, memory or CPU; above 1× socketley is ahead. The range in brackets is the lowest and highest ratio across the passes.

### JSON documents over HTTP

MongoDB 9.0.4, PocketBase 0.40.5, 3 passes, 2026-11-10, socketley 0174a7a1.

| case | socketley | MongoDB | PocketBase | socketley vs MongoDB | socketley vs PocketBase |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| read one document by id, 64 clients | 689 K req/s (3.46 cores) | 153 K req/s (3.87 cores) | 36 K req/s (3.86 cores) | 4.42× (4.36–11.45) | 19.23× (18.89–20.06) |
| replace one document, 64 clients | 133 K req/s (3.11 cores) | 105 K req/s (3.94 cores) | 12 K req/s (2.72 cores) | 1.26× (1.26–1.27) | 11.37× (10.82–11.82) |

| mixed: 90% reads, 10% writes, 64 clients | 339 K req/s (3.62 cores) | 134 K req/s (3.90 cores) | 39 K req/s (3.62 cores) | 2.48× (2.44–2.65) | 8.90× (8.41–9.48) |

How it was measured: loadgen, 4s a run, 100,000 documents, data on tmpfs; all three on the same four cores (socketley as four shards), loadgen on 20 others. 100,000 documents, data on tmpfs. MongoDB through its wire protocol with journaled writes, PocketBase over its REST API with request logs off, socketley over its HTTP API with a key. A sharded socketley db hands every write to shard 0, so its writes are at most what one shard takes, at more cores; reads and queries spread over all four.

# dns runtime

Authoritative name server for its zones, over UDP and TCP, with DNSSEC and transfers

A **dns** runtime is an authoritative name server for the zones you give it, over UDP and TCP on one port. It answers nothing else and is never an open resolver.

```
socketley create dns ns --zone example.com --publish 203.0.113.7 -s   # writes a zone file to start from
dig @127.0.0.1 example.com SOA
socketley create dns ns2 --zone /etc/socketley/example.com.zone \
    --publish 203.0.113.7 --transfer 203.0.113.53 --notify 203.0.113.53 --dnssec -s
```

## Good to know first

|  |  |
|---|---|
| `--publish` | Your public address. Needed when no interface has one, as behind NAT. |
| `--proxy none` | Skips the entrance `create` makes, which asks Let's Encrypt for certificates. Use it for a lab with real names. |
| `--rrl 0` | Lifts the default of 100 answers a second per client network, for a load test from one host. |

## What it does

- **Zone files**: RFC 1035 format; an edited file is served within a second.
- **UDP and TCP**: On port 53 unless `-p`; large answers move to TCP.
- **Secondaries**: AXFR to `--transfer`, NOTIFY to `--notify`.
- **DNSSEC**: `--dnssec` signs zones; `socketley <name> dnssec` prints the DS record.
- **Runtimes' names**: Answers for the `--domain` names of your runtimes ([how](man-dns-flags.txt)).

## Works with

Its entrance is a [proxy](rt-proxy.txt). A [mail](rt-mail.txt) runtime publishes its records through it.

## Flags

Every flag a dns runtime takes, by group.

**Basics**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `-p` | int | Port: The port it listens on (a client: the port of its target). |
| `-s` |  | Start now: Start it as soon as it is made. |
| `-g` (--group) | text | Group: Puts it in a group; a proxy with --backend @group reaches every member. |

**Network**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--bind` | text | Bind address: Bind the port to this address only, such as 127.0.0.1 when only a proxy on this machine should reach it. |
| `--shards` | int | Shards: Worker processes sharing the port: the way one runtime uses more than one core. |
| `--cpus` | text | CPUs: The CPUs its I/O may run on, as 0-3,6. |

**Output**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--log` | path | State log: A file it appends each state change to. |

**DNS**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--zone` | list | Zones: Zone names (a file is written) or zone files. Required. |
| `--publish` | list | Public addresses: The addresses runtimes' names are answered with. |
| `--proxy` | text | Entrance: The entrance proxy it creates; none for no entrance. |
| `--proxy-port` | int | Entrance port: The entrance's port; 443 also makes the redirect on 80. |
| `--transfer` | list | Transfer to: Addresses that may copy the zones (AXFR): secondaries. |
| `--notify` | list | Notify: Secondaries told of each change. |
| `--rrl` | int | Rate limit: Response rate limit: answers a second to one network; 0 turns it off. |
| `--dnssec` |  | DNSSEC: Signs its zones; the parent takes the DS that socketley <name> dnssec prints. |

## Benchmarks

A ratio (×) is how many times better socketley did: more per second, or less time, memory or CPU; above 1× socketley is ahead. The range in brackets is the lowest and highest ratio across the passes.

### Authoritative DNS, one zone of 10,000 names

NSD 4.14.0, Knot 3.5.3, 3 passes, 2026-11-10, socketley 0174a7a1.

| case | socketley | NSD | Knot | socketley vs NSD | socketley vs Knot |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A queries over UDP | 475 K q per core·s (1.00 cores) | 392 K q per core·s (0.83 cores) | 305 K q per core·s (0.86 cores) | 1.21× (1.17–1.33) | 1.55× (1.50–1.62) |
| A queries over TCP, 128 connections | 193 K q per core·s (0.99 cores) | 59 K q per core·s (0.87 cores) | 60 K q per core·s (0.98 cores) | 3.29× (3.21–3.36) | 3.22× (2.89–3.23) |

How it was measured: dnsperf 8 threads, 32 sockets, 4 s a run, zone of 10000 names; each server one worker on one core, dnsperf on 20 others. Queries answered per second of server CPU (rate ÷ cores), because NSD and Knot do not fill their cores at a window of 500 outstanding queries, and with more they drop UDP from their default socket buffers and dnsperf waits out each loss. socketley runs with --rrl 0 --proxy none: its response rate limit, on by default, would throttle one client host, and NSD and Knot have none by default. 90% of queries find a name, 10% are NXDOMAIN.

# idp runtime

OpenID Connect provider with its own accounts, second factors, app passwords and SSH certificates

An **idp** is an OpenID Connect provider with its own accounts. A user signs in once, and your applications, [proxy](rt-proxy.txt) routes, [storage](rt-storage.txt), [db](rt-db.txt), [mail](rt-mail.txt) and the dashboard know who they are.

```
socketley create idp auth -p 9400 --domain auth.example.com \
    --clients /etc/socketley/idp.clients --cookie-domain example.com -s
socketley auth user add smiley --password - --groups admins
```

## What it does

- **OpenID Connect**: Authorization code flow with PKCE, refresh tokens, discovery at `/.well-known/openid-configuration`.
- **Accounts**: Fields without a schema; fields it does not use are kept for your applications.
- **Sign-in**: Passwords, a second step and app passwords; users manage themselves at `/account`.
- **Applications**: Listed in `--clients` with an id, a secret or `-`, and redirect addresses.
- **Tokens for other servers**: `--resources` gives tokens for, say, an [mcp](rt-mcp.txt) runtime, to MCP clients like Claude Code too, once the user allows it.
- **SSH certificates**: `--ssh-ca hours` signs short-lived SSH certificates for signed-in users.

## Works with

Put routes behind it with a [proxy](rt-proxy.txt)'s `--auth idp:`. A [db](rt-db.txt), [mail](rt-mail.txt) or [mqtt](rt-mqtt.txt) runtime takes its users with `--idp`.

## Flags

Every flag a idp runtime takes, by group.

**Basics**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `-p` | int | Port: The port it listens on (a client: the port of its target). |
| `-s` |  | Start now: Start it as soon as it is made. |

**Network**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--bind` | text | Bind address: Bind the port to this address only, such as 127.0.0.1 when only a proxy on this machine should reach it. |
| `--shards` | int | Shards: Worker processes sharing the port: the way one runtime uses more than one core. |
| `--domain` | list | Names: The names it is reached by through the entrance; empty for its own name. |
| `--cpus` | text | CPUs: The CPUs its I/O may run on, as 0-3,6. |

**Limits**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--max-connections` (--max-conn) | int | Max connections: The most clients at once. |

**Identity**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--clients` | path | Clients: The applications that sign users in through it, one per line: id, secret (or -) and redirect addresses. |
| `--issuer` | text | Issuer: The https address it is reached at; https://<first name> when not given. |
| `--cookie-domain` | text | Cookie domain: The domain whose names share one sign-in, for a proxy's --auth idp:. |
| `--resources` | list | Resource servers: Resource servers an access token may be issued for, by their https address. With any set, an application may also sign in by the URL of its metadata document. |
| `--ssh-ca` | int | SSH certificates: Sign SSH certificates for signed-in users, valid for this many hours; off unless given. |

## Benchmarks

A ratio (×) is how many times better socketley did: more per second, or less time, memory or CPU; above 1× socketley is ahead. The range in brackets is the lowest and highest ratio across the passes.

### OpenID Connect provider

Keycloak 26.8.1, 3 passes, 2026-11-10, socketley 0174a7a1.

| case | socketley | Keycloak | socketley vs Keycloak |
|---|---|---|---|
| sign-in: authorization code with a password, 16 clients | 265.0 req/s (3.95 cores) | 223.0 req/s (3.90 cores) | 1.19× (1.18–1.24) |
| refresh token, 256 clients | 59 K req/s (2.91 cores) | 2.4 K req/s (3.86 cores) | 24.85× (24.10–25.84) |
| userinfo, 512 clients | 513 K req/s (3.75 cores) | 21 K req/s (3.83 cores) | 24.87× (24.11–26.34) |
| JWKS, 256 connections (wrk) | 510 K req/s (3.99 cores) | 29 K req/s (3.91 cores) | 17.30× (15.83–17.73) |

How it was measured: idpgen, 4s a run, 200 accounts; both on the same four cores (socketley as four shards; Keycloak with its PostgreSQL), idpgen and wrk on 20 others. 200 accounts. A sign-in is the authorization code flow with PKCE and a password, so it also compares the password hashes each uses by default: scrypt here, PBKDF2 in Keycloak. Keycloak's CPU includes PostgreSQL's. Refresh and userinfo come from four idpgen processes and JWKS from wrk, with as many clients as fill socketley's four cores; refresh stays near the same rate from 256 to 512 clients, bound by the durable write of each rotated token family through shard 0. Sign-ins come four at a time from each of four addresses: socketley refuses a fifth from one address while four are being checked, and four connections alone may land on two of its four shards, which would measure where the kernel put them. Both are warmed with sign-ins before the passes until a 5 s run gains under 3% on the best before it: Keycloak's JIT compiles the flow over its first half minute, from about 100 to 190 sign-ins a second.

## In the manual

Every flag in full, and the rest: man-idp-flags.txt

# mail runtime

Mail server: SMTP, submission, IMAP, POP3, JMAP and webmail, mailboxes in a storage

A **mail** runtime is a mail server: it receives mail for your domains, sends your users' mail, and keeps their mailboxes. Other runtimes, the CLI and the daemon's alerts can send through it.

```
socketley create mail m -p 25 --dns ns --no-reply -s            # only sends: alerts, notices
socketley send m --to ops@example.com --subject "Backup done" --text ok

socketley create mail m -p 25 --dns ns --idp auth --storage files/mail \
    --submission 587 --imap 143 --tls -s
```

## What it does

- **Receiving**: SMTP with SPF, DKIM, DMARC and ARC checks, optional greylisting and blocklists, and Sieve filters per user.
- **Safe spool**: A message is synced to disk before the sender is told 250.
- **Sending**: `--submission` and `--submissions` ports, DKIM signing, DANE and MTA-STS, or a `--relay` smarthost.
- **Reading**: IMAP, POP3, JMAP, and webmail on `--web`.
- **DNS records**: Publishes MX, SPF, DKIM, DMARC, MTA-STS and more through `--dns`.
- **Operating it**: `socketley mail m queue`, `show`, `flush`, `trace`; `on_rcpt` and `on_message` in [Lua](lua.txt).

## Works with

- [dns](rt-dns.txt) publishes its domains' records.
- [idp](rt-idp.txt) provides its users.
- [storage](rt-storage.txt) holds the mailboxes.

## Flags

## Benchmarks

A ratio (×) is how many times better socketley did: more per second, or less time, memory or CPU; above 1× socketley is ahead. The range in brackets is the lowest and highest ratio across the passes.

### Mail: delivery in, IMAP and POP3 out

Postfix 3.10.6 + Dovecot 2.4.2, 3 passes, 2026-11-10, socketley 0174a7a1.

| case | socketley | Postfix 3.10.6 + Dovecot | socketley vs Postfix 3.10.6 + Dovecot |
|---|---|---|---|
| SMTP in, 4 KiB messages, 64 connections, 10 a connection | 569.0 msg/s (0.14 cores) | 129.0 msg/s (0.30 cores) | 4.43× (3.88–4.43) |
| SMTP in, 64 KiB messages, 64 connections, 10 a connection | 345.0 msg/s (0.23 cores) | 75.5 msg/s (0.21 cores) | 4.62× (3.98–5.25) |
| IMAP: LOGIN and LOGOUT, 8 clients | 127.0 sign-ins/s (0.99 cores) | 65.2 sign-ins/s (0.99 cores) | 1.94× (1.94–1.95) |
| IMAP: LOGIN, SELECT, FETCH every header of 10,000, 8 clients | 484 K msg/s (0.99 cores) | 125 K msg/s (0.99 cores) | 3.88× (3.87–3.94) |
| IMAP: LOGIN, SELECT, FETCH 1,000 whole 64 KiB messages, 8 clients | 21 K msg/s (0.99 cores) | 14 K msg/s (0.99 cores) | 1.51× (1.43–1.56) |
| POP3: USER, PASS, RETR 1,000 64 KiB messages one by one, 8 clients | 13 K msg/s (0.99 cores) | 7.0 K msg/s (0.99 cores) | 1.82× (1.82–1.88) |

How it was measured: smtp-source (64 processes x 1 connections); mailload.py (8 asyncio processes x 1 connection), 4 s a run; every process of each on the same one core (socketley's daemon, idp, storage and mail; Postfix and Dovecot); smtp-source and mailload on 20 others; data on the VM's ext4 disk. Postfix hands each message over LMTP to Dovecot's Maildir and index; socketley's mail runtime writes it into its storage runtime. Both sync to disk (about 4 ms a sync here) before a message counts, so the SMTP rows are bound by syncs, not cores, and are timed until the last message is in its mailbox. Every sign-in hashes the password: scrypt in socketley, yescrypt in Dovecot. Dovecot 2.4's lmtp_user_concurrency_limit is set to unlimited, 2.3's default, since 10 made Postfix wait out five-minute retries.

# mcp runtime

A Model Context Protocol server: the tools, resources and prompts its script declares, for AI clients

An **mcp** runtime is a Model Context Protocol server: an AI client such as Claude Code gets the tools, resources and prompts its Lua script declares.

```
printf 'claude %s\nops %s admin\n' "$(openssl rand -hex 16)" "$(openssl rand -hex 16)" > /etc/socketley/mcp.keys
socketley create mcp shop -p 9600 --keys /etc/socketley/mcp.keys \
    --lua shop.lua --tools daemon --instructions "Ask about the shop's orders." -s
claude mcp add --transport http shop http://127.0.0.1:9600/mcp \
    --header "Authorization: Bearer <claude's secret>"
```

The script declares what is offered:

```
mcp.tool{
    name = "order_status",
    description = "The state of one order: paid, sent or unknown.",
    read_only = true,
    input = { type = "object", properties = { id = { type = "string" } }, required = { "id" } },
    -- the handler and the rest: examples/mcp/shop.lua in the repository
}
```

## What it does

- **Your tools in Lua**: Tools, resources and prompts from the script; `--instructions` says what the server is for.
- **The daemon as tools**: `--tools daemon` lists runtimes for any key; an admin key may start and stop them.
- **Streamable HTTP**: At `/mcp`, one JSON-RPC message per POST, stateless; revision 2026-07-28, and 2025-11-25, 2025-06-18, 2025-03-26.
- **Who may ask**: `--keys`, OAuth sign-in with `--idp`, or `--anonymous` on a local-only port.

## Works with

The entrance [proxy](rt-proxy.txt) terminates TLS in front of it. An [idp](rt-idp.txt) signs people in; its `admins` are admins here.

## Flags

Every flag a mcp runtime takes, by group.

**Basics**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `-p` | int | Port: The port it listens on (a client: the port of its target). |
| `-s` |  | Start now: Start it as soon as it is made. |
| `--lua` | path | Lua script: A script with the runtime's callbacks, run at start. |
| `--lua-ffi` |  | Lua FFI: Let the script require("ffi"): LuaJIT's calls into C and raw memory, where a wrong pointer ends the runtime's process. |

**Network**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--bind` | text | Bind address: Bind the port to this address only, such as 127.0.0.1 when only a proxy on this machine should reach it. |
| `--shards` | int | Shards: Worker processes sharing the port: the way one runtime uses more than one core. |
| `--domain` | list | Names: The names it is reached by through the entrance; empty for its own name. |
| `--cpus` | text | CPUs: The CPUs its I/O may run on, as 0-3,6. |

**Limits**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--max-connections` (--max-conn) | int | Max connections: The most clients at once. |

**Output**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--log` | path | State log: A file it appends each state change to. |

**MCP**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--keys` | path | Keys: The keys that may call it, one per line: name and secret, plus admin for a key that may change the daemon. |
| `--anonymous` |  | Anonymous: Anyone may call it without a key; only for a port no other machine can reach. |
| `--origins` | list | Origins: The web origins a browser may call it from, or * for any. |
| `--tools` | one of none, daemon | Daemon tools: This daemon's runtimes as tools: listed and read by every key, started and stopped by an admin's. |

## Benchmarks

### MCP server over Streamable HTTP

How it was measured: mcpgen (Streamable HTTP, 2025-11-25), 64 sessions, 4s a run; each server on one core, mcpgen on 20 others. Against the official MCP SDKs' own servers: the Python SDK under uvicorn with one worker, and the TypeScript SDK on Node as its JSON-response example. All three are driven on revision 2025-11-25 with the initialize handshake, every answer checked. socketley is stateless and issues no session id, so its new session is three requests to the SDKs' four.

# metrics runtime

Time series for years, answered with PromQL over the Prometheus API, with alert rules and logs

A **metrics** runtime keeps years of what socketley and nearby machines measure. It answers PromQL over the Prometheus HTTP API, so Grafana reads it as a Prometheus.

```
socketley create metrics metrics -p 9090 --scrape /etc/socketley/targets -s
socketley metrics query 'rate(socketley_runtime_messages_total[5m])'
socketley metrics query_range 'up' --start -6h --step 5m
```

## What it does

- **Collects**: This daemon's series with no setup; `--scrape` targets; remote write with `--receive`.
- **Stores compactly**: One to three bytes a sample, with coarser tiers (`--downsample`) for long ranges.
- **Stays bounded**: `--keep` limits age, `--max-series` cardinality; `--durable` loses nothing in a crash.
- **Alerts**: `--rules` in Prometheus's format, sent by webhook, mail or events (`--notify`).
- **Logs**: `--logs` keeps the daemon's log lines and answers LogQL as Loki does.
- **Archives**: `--archive` copies old blocks to an S3 bucket.

## Works with

The dashboard draws its history from it. A [storage](rt-storage.txt) runtime can hold its archive.

## Flags

Every flag a metrics runtime takes, by group.

**Basics**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `-p` | int | Port: The port it listens on (a client: the port of its target). |
| `-s` |  | Start now: Start it as soon as it is made. |

**Network**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--bind` | text | Bind address: Bind the port to this address only, such as 127.0.0.1 when only a proxy on this machine should reach it. |
| `--domain` | list | Names: The names it is reached by through the entrance; empty for its own name. |
| `--cpus` | text | CPUs: The CPUs its I/O may run on, as 0-3,6. |

**Output**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|

# mqtt runtime

MQTT 3.1, 3.1.1 and 5.0 broker on TCP, TLS and WebSocket, with sessions and rules

An **mqtt** runtime is an MQTT broker (3.1, 3.1.1 and 5.0) for devices, apps and browsers. A client that disconnects keeps its session and the messages it missed until it returns or the session expires.

```
socketley mqtt passwd /etc/socketley/mqtt.users sensor-17
socketley create mqtt broker --users /etc/socketley/mqtt.users \
    --acl /etc/socketley/mqtt.acl --ws 8083 --persistent on -s
mosquitto_sub -h 127.0.0.1 -u sensor-17 -P secret -t 'home/#'
```

## What it does

- **Full protocol**: QoS 0, 1 and 2, retained messages, wills, shared subscriptions and the 5.0 properties.
- **TCP, TLS, WebSocket**: Port 1883, or 8883 with `--tls`, and WebSocket on `--ws`.
- **Users**: A password file (`--users`), client certificates (`--ca`), [idp](rt-idp.txt) tokens, or `--anonymous`.
- **Topic rights**: Per user in `--acl`.
- **Survives restarts**: `--persistent` keeps sessions and retained messages.
- **Routes**: `--routes` hands matching messages to other runtimes.

## Works with

Routes deliver to a [cache](rt-cache.txt), [db](rt-db.txt), [storage](rt-storage.txt), [server](rt-server.txt) or another broker. A storage's events and `socketley.mqtt.publish` from any [script](lua.txt) reach its subscribers.

## Flags

Every flag a mqtt runtime takes, by group.

**Basics**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `-p` | int | Port: The port it listens on (a client: the port of its target). |
| `-s` |  | Start now: Start it as soon as it is made. |
| `-g` (--group) | text | Group: Puts it in a group; a proxy with --backend @group reaches every member. |
| `--lua` | path | Lua script: A script with the runtime's callbacks, run at start. |
| `--lua-ffi` |  | Lua FFI: Let the script require("ffi"): LuaJIT's calls into C and raw memory, where a wrong pointer ends the runtime's process. |

**Network**

| flag | value | what it does |

| `--shards` | int | Shards: Worker processes sharing the port: the way one runtime uses more than one core. |
| `--cpus` | text | CPUs: The CPUs its I/O may run on, as 0-3,6. |

**TLS**

| flag | value | what it does |

**Output**

|---|---|---|

| `--max-sessions` | int | Max sessions: The most sessions it keeps, connected or not; 100000 unless given. |
| `--keepalive-max` | int | Max keep alive: The longest keep alive a client is granted, in seconds; 1200 unless given. |

## Benchmarks

A ratio (×) is how many times better socketley did: more per second, or less time, memory or CPU; above 1× socketley is ahead. The range in brackets is the lowest and highest ratio across the passes.

### MQTT broker, deliveries per second

Mosquitto 2.0.22, 3 passes, 2026-11-10, socketley 0174a7a1.

| case | socketley | Mosquitto | socketley vs Mosquitto |
|---|---|---|---|
| fan-in: 16 publishers to 1 subscriber, QoS 0, 64 B | 7.23 M msg/s (0.95 cores) | 799 K msg/s (0.99 cores) | 9.06× (9.03–9.18) |
| fan-out: 1 publisher to 100 subscribers, QoS 0, 64 B | 11.80 M msg/s (1.00 cores) | 576 K msg/s (0.99 cores) | 20.50× (20.43–20.68) |
| fan-out: 1 publisher to 50 subscribers, QoS 1, 64 B | 1.50 M msg/s (1.00 cores) | 69 K msg/s (1.00 cores) | 21.64× (21.54–21.76) |
| round trip, QoS 1 publish to own delivery | 26.6 µs (0.91 cores) | 42.7 µs (0.67 cores) | 1.60× (1.59–1.60) |

How it was measured: mqbench (MQTT 3.1.1), 4 s a run; each broker on one core, mqbench on 20 others. MQTT 3.1.1, 64-byte payloads; Mosquitto with persistence off and unbounded queues, socketley --anonymous --session-queue 100000. A QoS 0 fan-out delivery costs Mosquitto about 2 µs of CPU, one write each; socketley coalesces the writes to a subscriber, which is the whole of the fan-out difference. The round trip is a QoS 1 publish to the publisher's own subscription.
