# proxy runtime

HTTP and TCP reverse proxy: routes by name and path, health checks, retries, mTLS, FastCGI

A **proxy** forwards HTTP or plain TCP to backends, balances them and steers around failing ones. Without `--backend` it is the **entrance**, routing each request by name to the runtime that has it.

```
socketley create proxy gw -p 8080 --backend 127.0.0.1:9000 -s          # /gw/... goes to the backend
socketley create proxy web -p 8081 --backend @web --strategy round-robin \
    --health-check http --health-path /health -s
socketley create proxy db-tcp -p 5433 --protocol tcp --backend 10.0.0.7:5432 -s
socketley create proxy php -p 8082 --backend fastcgi://127.0.0.1:9000 --root /var/www/site -s
```

> By default a backend has 2 seconds to start answering, or the request gets a 504. Raise `--backend-timeout` for slow applications.

## What it does

- **Routing**: A request for `/gw/x` on proxy `gw` reaches the backend as `/x`; any other path, `/` included, gets 404. Through the entrance, a request for a `--domain` name passes unchanged.
- **Any backend**: `host:port`, `https://`, `unix:`, a runtime, an `@group`, `fastcgi://`.
- **Resilience**: [Health checks](man-proxy-flags.txt), a [circuit breaker](man-proxy-flags.txt), [retries](man-proxy-flags.txt); `--sidecar` turns all on.
- **Sign-in first**: `--auth bearer:`, `basic:` or `idp:` before anything reaches a backend.
- **TLS on both legs**: Its own listener, [client certificates](man-proxy-flags.txt), verified `https://` backends.
- **Lua filters**: `on_route` picks backends; a [filter chain](man-lua-configuration.txt) rewrites traffic.
- **Modern HTTP**: The entrance speaks HTTP/2 and HTTP/3; every proxy relays WebSocket.

## Works with

A [dns](rt-dns.txt) runtime makes the entrance and its certificates. `--auth idp:` signs people in through an [idp](rt-idp.txt).

HAProxy runs one thread with http-reuse always; nginx keeps 256 idle backend connections (keepalive 256); socketley keeps as many backend connections as were busy at once. The kernel keeps at most 2,048 connections in TIME-WAIT for every arm (net.ipv4.tcp_max_tw_buckets, 131,072 by default), so a pass with a connection per request does not wait out the closed connections of the one before.

# server runtime

TCP, UDP, WebSocket and HTTP on one port, answered by Lua or by a built-in path

A **server** is one port for long-lived connections: TCP lines, WebSocket, HTTP and RESP on the same port, or UDP datagrams. Without a script it relays messages between clients; with Lua it answers them, as a chat room, a game server, a line protocol or an API.

```
socketley create server chat -p 9000 -s                    # every line reaches every other client
socketley create server echo -p 9001 --send-to sender -s   # answers whoever spoke
socketley create server room -p 9003 --lua room.lua -s     # the script decides who hears what
socketley create server site -p 8080 --http /srv/site --http-cache -s
socketley create server api -p 9002 --lua api.lua --cache store -s
```

```
-- room.lua: whoever sends "join" hears everything said in the room
function on_client_message(id, msg)
  if msg == "join" then self.join_group(id, "room") else self.group_send("room", msg) end
  return true   -- handled, so nothing is relayed on its own
end
```

> Warning: `--cache` also stores every ordinary message in the cache, under keys `1`, `2`, `3`… And `--http` injects a WebSocket script into every HTML page.

## What it does

- **One port, four protocols**: TCP lines, WebSocket, HTTP and RESP, [told apart by their first bytes](man-server-flags.txt); `--udp` for datagrams, where `on_client_message` names the peer and `self.send` answers it.
- **Lua per message**: `on_client_message` answers with `self.send` and returns `true` to keep the relay out; connects, disconnects, requests and upgrades have callbacks too. See [Lua](lua.txt).
- **Broadcast and rooms**: `self.broadcast` reaches everyone, `self.multicast` a list, `self.join_group` and `self.group_send` a room.
- **Relaying without code**: `--mode` and `--send-to` decide who hears a message; `--send-to sender` is an echo server.
- **HTTP on the same port**: `on_http_request` answers requests; `--http` serves a directory, `--http-cache` holds it in memory.
- **TLS and unix sockets**: `--tls --cert --key` encrypt the port, `--ca` asks for client certificates; `--listen unix:/path` serves a local socket.
- **Upstreams and a cache**: `-u host:port` dials other servers for `on_upstream`; with `--cache name`, clients send `cache <command>` ([cache access](man-server-flags.txt)).
- **Several cores**: `--shards N` runs N processes on one port, and a broadcast reaches every shard's clients; see [sharding](man-server-flags.txt).

## Works with

A [proxy](rt-proxy.txt) in front for names and TLS, a [cache](rt-cache.txt) behind for state, a [client](rt-client.txt) to chain servers. Its counters reach [metrics](rt-metrics.txt) without setup.

## Flags

Every flag a server runtime takes, by group.

**Basics**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `-p` | int | Port: The port it listens on (a client: the port of its target). |
| `-s` |  | Start now: Start it as soon as it is made. |
| `-g` (--group) | text | Group: Puts it in a group; a proxy with --backend @group reaches every member. |
| `--lua` | path | Lua script: A script with the runtime's callbacks, run at start. |
| `--lua-ffi` |  | Lua FFI: Let the script require("ffi"): LuaJIT's calls into C and raw memory, where a wrong pointer ends the runtime's process. |

**Network**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--bind` | text | Bind address: Bind the port to this address only, such as 127.0.0.1 when only a proxy on this machine should reach it. |
| `--listen` | text | Unix socket: Listen on a unix socket instead of a port. |
| `--shards` | int | Shards: Worker processes sharing the port: the way one runtime uses more than one core. |
| `--domain` | list | Names: The names it is reached by through the entrance; empty for its own name. |
| `--cpus` | text | CPUs: The CPUs its I/O may run on, as 0-3,6. |

**TLS**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--tls` |  | TLS: Encrypt its transport: terminate TLS on its port, or dial over it. |
| `--cert` | path | Certificate: The PEM certificate (chain allowed) a listener presents. |
| `--key` | path | Key: The PEM key of the certificate. |
| `--ca` | path | CA: On a listener: require client certificates from this CA (mutual TLS). On a client or proxy: the CA its servers are checked against. |
| `--acme` | list | ACME names: Names to get a Let's Encrypt certificate for, renewed by itself. |
| `--acme-email` | text | ACME e-mail: The address the CA writes to about the certificate. |

**Limits**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--max-connections` (--max-conn) | int | Max connections: The most clients at once. |
| `--rate-limit` | int | Rate limit: Messages a second per connection. |
| `--global-rate-limit` | int | Global rate limit: Messages a second over all connections. |
| `--congestion` | text | Congestion control: The kernel's congestion control for its connections, such as bbr, which keeps its rate up under packet loss. |
| `--idle-timeout` | duration | Idle timeout: Close a connection that has received nothing for this long; off unless given. |
| `--read-buffer` | size | Read buffer: How much data may pile up from one connection before it is refused; 1M unless given. |
| `--write-buffer` | size | Write buffer: How much unsent data may queue up for one connection before it is dropped; 8M unless given. |
| `--drain` |  | Drain on stop: Finish what is in flight before stopping. |

**Output**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--log` | path | State log: A file it appends each state change to. |
| `-w` | path | Message file: A file every received message is written to. |
| `-b` |  | Print messages: Print every received message. |
| `-bp` |  | …with name: Print them with the runtime's name before each. |
| `-bt` |  | …with time: Print them with the time before each. |
| `-bpt` (-btp) |  | …with time and name: Print them with the time and the name before each. |

**Server**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--mode` | one of inout, in, out, master | Mode: Who talks: both ways, in only, out only, or one master broadcasting. |
| `--send-to` | list | Answer to: Who the built-in path answers: sender, others, master. |
| `--udp` |  | UDP: Datagrams instead of a stream. |
| `--http` | path | Static files: Serve this directory over HTTP. |
| `--http-cache` |  | Files in memory: Read the static files into memory at start. |
| `--compress` |  | Compressed copies: Serve a file's .br or .gz copy next to it to clients that accept it, unless the copy is older than the file. |
| `--no-inject` |  | Pages as they are: Serve each page exactly as the file holds it, without the WebSocket script. |
| `--master-pw` | text | Master password: The password that claims master mode. |
| `--no-master-pw` |  | No master password: Take the master password away, which ends master mode. |
| `--cache` | text | Cache: A cache runtime its scripts and clients use. |
| `--origins` | list | Web origins: Other web origins whose pages may open a WebSocket to it; * for any. |
| `-u` (--upstream) | list | Upstreams: Servers it relays to, host:port each. |

## Benchmarks

A ratio (×) is how many times better socketley did: more per second, or less time, memory or CPU; above 1× socketley is ahead. The range in brackets is the lowest and highest ratio across the passes.

### WebSocket: echo and a chat room's fan-out

socketley, no script, ws 8.22.0 (Node 24.22.1), uWebSockets.js 20.71.0 (Node 24.22.1), 3 passes, 2026-11-10, socketley 81ffa51e.

| case | socketley | socketley, no script | ws 8.22.0 (Node 24.22.1) | uWebSockets.js 20.71.0 (Node 24.22.1) | socketley vs socketley, no script | socketley vs ws 8.22.0 (Node 24.22.1) | socketley vs uWebSockets.js 20.71.0 (Node 24.22.1) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| echo, 64 B messages, 256 connections, one in flight each | 303 K msg/s (1.00 cores) | 320 K msg/s (1.00 cores) | 151 K msg/s (1.00 cores) | 232 K msg/s (1.00 cores) | 0.95× (0.94–0.95) | 1.99× (1.97–2.03) | 1.31× (1.27–1.32) |
| room fan-out: 1 sender to 100 receivers, 64 B | 6.13 M msg/s (1.00 cores) | 6.15 M msg/s (1.00 cores) | 305 K msg/s (1.00 cores) | 5.40 M msg/s (1.00 cores) | 0.99× (0.99–1.00) | 20.00× (19.83–20.35) | 1.13× (1.12–1.14) |
| room fan-out: 1 sender to 1,000 receivers, 64 B | 6.26 M msg/s (1.00 cores) | 6.25 M msg/s (1.00 cores) | 293 K msg/s (1.00 cores) | 5.73 M msg/s (1.00 cores) | 1.00× (0.99–1.03) | 21.78× (21.32–22.57) | 1.09× (1.09–1.12) |

How it was measured: srvgen (Go), 4 s a run, every answer checked; each server on one core (ws and uWebSockets.js under Node 24), srvgen on 20 others. The same logic in each: an echo, and a room that a receiver enters by sending "join", with one sender's messages counted at every receiver. socketley runs it in Lua (join_group/group_send) and, as "no script", on its built-in relay; ws loops over the room with send(), uWebSockets.js publishes to a topic. Both socketley and uWebSockets.js build a room's frame once; socketley writes each receiver's share of a turn in one send, and uWebSockets.js corks its writes.

### TCP line protocol, answered by a handler

socketley, no script, Node 24.22.1 net, Go 1.24.6 net, 3 passes, 2026-11-10, socketley 81ffa51e.

| case | socketley | socketley, no script | Node 24.22.1 net | Go 1.24.6 net | socketley vs socketley, no script | socketley vs Node 24.22.1 net | socketley vs Go 1.24.6 net |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| line echo, 64 B, 256 connections, one in flight each | 313 K msg/s (1.00 cores) | 329 K msg/s (1.00 cores) | 199 K msg/s (1.00 cores) | 227 K msg/s (1.00 cores) | 0.95× (0.95–0.95) | 1.57× (1.57–1.60) | 1.38× (1.38–1.39) |
| line echo, 64 B, 64 connections, 16 pipelined each | 4.48 M msg/s (1.00 cores) | 4.63 M msg/s (1.00 cores) | 2.32 M msg/s (1.00 cores) | 3.24 M msg/s (1.00 cores) | 0.96× (0.95–0.97) | 1.94× (1.91–1.95) | 1.38× (1.37–1.39) |

How it was measured: srvgen (Go), 4 s a run, every answer checked; each server on one core, srvgen on 20 others. Every line is answered with itself by a handler: on socketley a Lua on_client_messages, handed a read's lines in one call and answering them with one self.send; on Node's net a function over the read's lines, written with one write a read; in Go a goroutine with bufio. With one line in flight the kernel's per-message cost dominates; 16 pipelined lines show each server's own per-line work, where a script with on_client_message, a call and a string a line, makes about 3.2 million a second.

### UDP datagrams answered

Node 24.22.1 dgram, Go 1.24.6 net, socketley, Lua, 3 passes, 2026-11-10, socketley 81ffa51e.

| case | socketley, no script | Node 24.22.1 dgram | Go 1.24.6 net | socketley, Lua | socketley vs Node 24.22.1 dgram | socketley vs Go 1.24.6 net | socketley vs socketley, Lua |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| datagram echo, 64 B, 128 sockets, one in flight each | 523 K datagrams/s (1.00 cores) | 162 K datagrams/s (1.00 cores) | 430 K datagrams/s (1.00 cores) | 447 K datagrams/s (1.00 cores) | 3.22× (3.12–3.22) | 1.20× (1.19–1.22) | 1.16× (1.15–1.17) |
| datagram echo, 1 KiB, 128 sockets, one in flight each | 497 K datagrams/s (1.00 cores) | 191 K datagrams/s (1.00 cores) | 413 K datagrams/s (1.00 cores) | 404 K datagrams/s (1.00 cores) | 2.60× (2.58–2.66) | 1.20× (1.20–1.22) | 1.23× (1.23–1.24) |

How it was measured: srvgen (Go), 4 s a run, every answer checked; each server on one core, srvgen (128 sockets) on 20 others. Node and Go are given the 1 MiB receive buffer socketley sets; at the kernel's default they lost datagrams at 1 KiB. No arm lost any.

### HTTP: static files and a fixed answer

nginx 1.28.3, 3 passes, 2026-11-10, socketley 0174a7a1.

| case | socketley | nginx | socketley vs nginx |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 KiB file, keep-alive, 256 connections | 271 K req/s (1.00 cores) | 50 K req/s (0.99 cores) | 5.46× (5.42–5.51) |
| 64 KiB file, keep-alive, 256 connections | 93 K req/s (1.00 cores) | 47 K req/s (0.99 cores) | 2.00× (1.98–2.16) |
| 1 KiB file, a connection per request, 64 at once | 83 K req/s (0.99 cores) | 35 K req/s (1.00 cores) | 2.36× (2.33–2.48) |
| fixed answer (Lua handler / nginx return), keep-alive | 246 K req/s (1.00 cores) | 77 K req/s (0.99 cores) | 3.22× (3.08–3.54) |

How it was measured: wrk 8 threads, 4 s a run; each server on one core, wrk on 20 others. socketley --http dir --http-cache against nginx with one worker, sendfile, open_file_cache and access logs off. Files are .txt: socketley adds a WebSocket script to every .html it serves, by design. The fixed answer is a Lua on_http_request on socketley and a return 200 on nginx, which runs no script at all. Read the 1 KiB keep-alive row with this machine in mind: nginx answers each request with its own write and wakeup, and on this VM waking a halted vCPU costs an exit, which costs a server that does that more than one that batches. A single unpublished pass on another VM (16 cores) read 1.85× for the same row. The kernel keeps at most 2,048 connections in TIME-WAIT for every arm (net.ipv4.tcp_max_tw_buckets, 131,072 by default), so a pass with a connection per request does not wait out the closed connections of the one before.

### HTTP on four cores

nginx 1.28.3, 3 passes, 2026-11-10, socketley 0174a7a1.

| case | socketley | nginx | socketley vs nginx |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 KiB file, keep-alive, 256 connections | 500 K req/s (3.99 cores) | 230 K req/s (3.99 cores) | 2.17× (2.15–2.25) |
| 64 KiB file, keep-alive, 256 connections | 229 K req/s (3.98 cores) | 166 K req/s (3.99 cores) | 1.38× (1.36–1.40) |
| 1 KiB file, a connection per request, 64 at once | 158 K req/s (3.94 cores) | 131 K req/s (3.90 cores) | 1.21× (1.21–1.21) |
| fixed answer (Lua handler / nginx return), keep-alive | 451 K req/s (3.99 cores) | 297 K req/s (3.98 cores) | 1.52× (1.46–1.54) |

How it was measured: wrk 16 threads, 4 s a run; socketley as four shards and nginx with four workers, each pinned to one of the same four cores; wrk (16 threads) on 20 others. The same rows as the one-core set, the same wrk for both. socketley spends about twice the CPU a request here that it does on one core, and most of that is the client, not the shards: wrk's threads each hold connections on all four shards, and waking a thread from another core is an interrupt the server's core pays for on loopback, a VM exit on this VM. With one wrk per quarter of the connections, four shards cost about 15% more a request than four separate one-core servers. A client on another machine costs neither. The kernel keeps at most 2,048 connections in TIME-WAIT for every arm (net.ipv4.tcp_max_tw_buckets, 131,072 by default), so a pass with a connection per request does not wait out the closed connections of the one before.

Every flag in full, and Sharding, Multi-Protocol Auto-Detection, Request Framing, Cache Access via Server: man-server-flags.txt

# storage runtime

S3 object storage over a directory, with versioning, replication, a web drive and git

A **storage** runtime serves the S3 API over one directory, so boto3, the AWS CLI, rclone and other S3 clients keep objects on this machine's disk. It adds a web drive with share links and media.

```
socketley create storage files -p 9000 --dir /srv/objects \
    --credentials /etc/socketley/storage.creds -s
aws --endpoint-url http://127.0.0.1:9000 s3 mb s3://photos
aws --endpoint-url http://127.0.0.1:9000 s3 cp beach.jpg s3://photos/
```

## What it does

- **The S3 API**: SigV4, multipart uploads, [S3 Select](man-storage-flags.txt); see [operations](man-storage-flags.txt).
- **Users and policies**: [Users](man-storage-flags.txt), [IAM](man-storage-flags.txt), [bucket policies](man-storage-flags.txt), [STS](man-storage-flags.txt).
- **Keeping versions**: [Versioning](man-storage-flags.txt), [object lock](man-storage-flags.txt), [lifecycle](man-storage-flags.txt), [tiers](man-storage-flags.txt).
- **Copies**: [Replication](man-storage-flags.txt) to other S3 endpoints, or a [cluster](man-storage-flags.txt) of nodes.
- **On disk**: [Compression](man-storage-flags.txt), [encryption](man-storage-flags.txt), and `--fsync` for [durability](man-storage-flags.txt).
- **Around the data**: [Webhooks](man-storage-flags.txt), [bucket websites](man-storage-flags.txt), [quotas](man-storage-flags.txt).
- **Web interface**: A [drive](man-storage-flags.txt), [git repositories](man-storage-flags.txt), sign-in through an [idp](rt-idp.txt).

## Works with

[sync](rt-sync.txt) carries directories into it, [mail](rt-mail.txt) keeps mailboxes in it, [metrics](rt-metrics.txt) archives to it.

## Flags

A ratio (×) is how many times better socketley did: more per second, or less time, memory or CPU; above 1× socketley is ahead. The range in brackets is the lowest and highest ratio across the passes.

### S3 over HTTP, SigV4

MinIO 2025-09-07, 3 passes, 2026-11-10, socketley 0174a7a1.

| case | socketley | MinIO | socketley vs MinIO |
|---|---|---|---|
| GET 4 KiB, 1 connection | 21 K obj/s (0.63 cores) | 3.9 K obj/s (1.28 cores) | 5.29× (5.22–5.31) |
| GET 4 KiB, 64 connections | 451 K obj/s (3.78 cores) | 25 K obj/s (3.99 cores) | 18.17× (17.98–18.73) |
| GET 4 KiB, 128 connections | 557 K obj/s (3.92 cores) | 24 K obj/s (3.99 cores) | 23.11× (22.69–23.75) |
| GET 4 KiB, 64 connections, from 50,000 objects | 251 K obj/s (3.96 cores) | 24 K obj/s (3.99 cores) | 10.42× (10.10–10.51) |
| GET 1 MiB, 64 connections | 42 K obj/s (3.95 cores) | 6.0 K obj/s (3.96 cores) | 7.05× (6.97–7.12) |
| PUT 4 KiB, 64 connections, into an empty store | 79 K obj/s (3.75 cores) | 15 K obj/s (3.98 cores) | 5.11× (4.92–5.31) |

How it was measured: s3gen (Go, one process, a request in flight per connection), 4s a run, SigV4 over plain HTTP, PUT bodies aws-chunked and signed; both servers on the same four cores (socketley as four shards), s3gen on 20 others. MinIO single node, single drive; both on tmpfs, so the comparison is the servers' work and not a disk. MinIO is a Go server that limits itself on one core, hence four for both. s3gen signs every request with SigV4 as warp does (PUTs as signed aws-chunked bodies) and checks every answer's status, length and ETag; from 64 connections both servers fill their four cores. The 4 KiB rows read 2,500 objects, which socketley keeps as in-memory copies; the 50,000-object row reads past them, where every GET opens its file as MinIO's always do. The PUT row starts both servers afresh on empty storage for every pass, because MinIO reclaims deleted objects in the background and its puts slow while it does.

# sync runtime

One job that carries a directory to a storage, from it, or both ways

A **sync** runtime is one job that carries files between a directory and a [storage](rt-storage.txt). Each job has its own line in `socketley ls`, its own log lines and alert.

```
socketley create sync photos --dir /srv/photos --storage ui/photos \
    --credentials /etc/socketley/sync.creds --mode out -s
socketley create sync offsite --dir /srv/photos \
    --storage https://files.example.com/photos --credentials /etc/socketley/offsite.creds \
    --every 1h --exclude '*.tmp,.git/*' -s
```

## What it does

- **Where**: `--storage`: a storage runtime (`ui/photos`), a host and port, or a URL, bucket last.
- **Which way**: `--mode` `out`, `in` or `inout`. Several targets only with `out`.
- **When**: On every change the kernel reports, plus a full walk every `--every`.
- **What**: All of `--dir` but the `--exclude` patterns, under `--prefix` in the bucket.

## Works with

A [storage](rt-storage.txt) runtime or any S3. A sync opens no port.

## Flags

Every flag a sync runtime takes, by group.

**Sync**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--dir` | path | Directory: The directory whose files are carried. Required. |
| `--storage` | list | Storage: Where they go: a runtime and a bucket, or a URL and one. Required. |
| `--mode` | one of out, in, inout | Direction: Direction: out to the storage, in from it, or inout for both. |
| `--credentials` | path | Credentials: A file holding access_key and secret_key. Required. |
| `--prefix` | text | Prefix: The key everything is written under, below the bucket. |
| `--every` | text | Walk every: How often the whole directory is rescanned; never to sync on changes only. |
| `--exclude` | list | Exclude: Patterns of paths, relative to the directory, that are not synced. |
| `--repositories` | path | Repositories: The file a storage writes for a user's own sync runtime, which pulls their git repositories. |

## Benchmarks

A ratio (×) is how many times better socketley did: more per second, or less time, memory or CPU; above 1× socketley is ahead. The range in brackets is the lowest and highest ratio across the passes.

### Carrying a directory to a storage and back

rclone v1.75.2, mc 2025-08-13, 3 passes, 2026-11-10, socketley 0174a7a1.

| case | socketley | rclone | mc | socketley vs rclone | socketley vs mc |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| first copy, 2000 files of 64 KiB and 50 of 1 MiB | 8.9 K files/s (0.21 cores) | 4.3 K files/s (1.76 cores) | 2.8 K files/s (1.18 cores) | 2.07× (2.06–2.11) | 3.18× (3.15–3.25) |
| 1000 files changed after it | 6.6 K files/s (0.40 cores) | 3.5 K files/s (1.56 cores) | 2.7 K files/s (1.19 cores) | 1.86× (1.86–1.88) | 2.46× (2.44–2.49) |
| first copy, 20,000 files of 4 KiB | 24 K files/s (0.52 cores) | 7.1 K files/s (1.66 cores) | 4.3 K files/s (1.37 cores) | 3.43× (3.30–3.44) | 5.72× (5.71–5.76) |
| first copy, 8 files of 256 MiB | 2.9 K MiB/s (0.08 cores) | 618.0 MiB/s (1.47 cores) | 2.0 K MiB/s (1.36 cores) | 4.68× (4.49–4.81) | 1.43× (1.42–1.43) |
| first copy, a tree 12 directories deep: 8,190 files of 4 KiB in 4,095 directories | 22 K files/s (0.57 cores) | 6.8 K files/s (1.69 cores) | 4.1 K files/s (1.34 cores) | 3.27× (3.24–3.27) | 5.49× (5.39–5.58) |
| checked again, 1 of 20,000 files deleted since: time | 73.9 ms (0.27 cores) | 219 ms (1.25 cores) | 270 ms (1.25 cores) | 2.93× (2.92–3.00) | 3.65× (3.57–3.67) |
| checked again, 1 of 20,000 files deleted since: requests sent | 1.0 requests (0.37 cores) | 21.0 requests (1.23 cores) | 22.0 requests (1.26 cores) | 21.00× (21.00–21.00) | 22.00× (22.00–22.00) |
| 1,000 files deleted | 41 K files/s (0.82 cores) | 11 K files/s (1.29 cores) | 7.0 K files/s (1.27 cores) | 3.70× (3.55–3.74) | 5.83× (5.76–6.08) |
| a directory of 1,000 files renamed | 7.7 K files/s (0.31 cores) | 3.4 K files/s (1.66 cores) | 2.0 K files/s (1.22 cores) | 2.27× (2.22–2.35) | 3.68× (3.67–3.82) |
| pulled into an empty directory, 2000 files of 64 KiB and 50 of 1 MiB | 21 K files/s (0.90 cores) | 6.7 K files/s (1.82 cores) | 4.1 K files/s (1.37 cores) | 3.03× (3.03–3.06) | 5.05× (4.95–5.11) |

How it was measured: the carriers themselves; the storage target is one socketley storage runtime on other cores; the carriers on two cores, the target storage runtime in a daemon of its own on four others. One socketley storage runtime on tmpfs is the target for all three, a fresh bucket a run, every run checked key for key and byte for byte. rclone 1.75.2 runs as its S3 docs advise (--transfers 8 --checkers 16 --fast-list --update --use-server-modtime), mc mirror with --overwrite --remove and eight workers. A socketley job walks once at start and then follows inotify, where the others walk both sides again; it checks a whole tree only when it starts, so the re-check row is a stop and a start, with one file deleted so its end can be seen.

### A change noticed while running

mc 2025-08-13, 3 passes, 2026-11-10, socketley 0174a7a1.

| case | socketley | mc | socketley vs mc |
|---|---|---|---|
| a 64 KiB file written, until it is in the storage | 0.87 ms (0.00 cores) | 1.57 ms (0.03 cores) | 1.83× (1.73–2.15) |

How it was measured: the carriers themselves; the storage target is one socketley storage runtime on other cores; the carrier on two cores, the storage on four others. Each file is timed from its write until a HEAD of its key answers with its MD5, one write at a time. rclone has no watch mode; mc mirror --watch is the nearest tool.

### Both ways at once

rclone v1.75.2, 3 passes, 2026-11-10, socketley 0174a7a1.

| case | socketley | rclone | socketley vs rclone |
|---|---|---|---|
| both ways: 500 files changed here and 500 in the storage | 12 K files/s (0.36 cores) | 2.3 K files/s (1.55 cores) | 5.30× (5.28–5.44) |

How it was measured: the carriers themselves; the storage target is one socketley storage runtime on other cores; the carrier on two cores, the storage on four others. A tree and a bucket in step, then 500 files rewritten here and 500 others replaced in the storage, then one run: socketley --mode inout against rclone bisync. mc mirror carries one way only.

# tunnel runtime

Makes a machine without an address of its own reachable through an edge it dials

A **tunnel** makes a machine with no address of its own reachable, such as one at home behind a router. An **agent** there dials out to an **edge** the internet reaches; nothing is opened on the router.

```
# on the machine with the address
socketley create tunnel edge --mode edge -p 9450 --domain edge --idp auth -s
# on the machine at home, signed in as an admin of auth
socketley tunnel join https://edge.example.com --http home=127.0.0.1:8123 \
    --tcp mc:25565=127.0.0.1:25565
```

## What it does

- **HTTP services**: Named beside the edge, such as `home.example.com`.
- **TCP services**: A port on the edge, carried unchanged to the agent.
- **Joining**: `socketley tunnel join` as an idp admin, or a one-time `invite` used with `--join`.
- **ssh through 443**: `--forward` carries a signed-in person to the named addresses, via `tunnel connect` or `tunnel ssh`.
- **Share a port**: `socketley tunnel share` publishes a local port for a while, optionally public.

## Works with

The edge machine needs what the [public HTTPS recipe](deploy.txt) sets up: a [dns](rt-dns.txt) runtime, which answers the services' names, and its entrance [proxy](rt-proxy.txt), which terminates TLS. It also needs an [idp](rt-idp.txt) runtime, here `auth`: its admins may join agents, and its users sign in for `--forward`.

## Flags

Every flag a tunnel runtime takes, by group.

**Basics**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `-p` | int | Port: The port it listens on (a client: the port of its target). |
| `-s` |  | Start now: Start it as soon as it is made. |

**Network**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--bind` | text | Bind address: Bind the port to this address only, such as 127.0.0.1 when only a proxy on this machine should reach it. |
| `--domain` | list | Names: The names it is reached by through the entrance; empty for its own name. |

**Output**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--log` | path | State log: A file it appends each state change to. |

**Tunnel**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--mode` | one of edge, agent | Mode: An edge agents dial out to, or an agent dialling one. |
| `--to` | text | Edge: The edge an agent dials, its https address. |
| `--join` | text | Invitation: What `socketley tunnel <edge> invite` printed, used once to join. |
| `--offer` | list | Offers: What an agent carries the edge's streams to: service=host:port each. |
| `--forward` | list | Forward: Where an edge forwards a signed-in user's stream, as ssh's ProxyCommand needs. |
| `--idp` | text | Identity provider: The idp runtime whose signed-in people may use --forward. |
| `--idp-audience` | list | Audiences: The clients whose access tokens --forward takes. |

## Benchmarks

A ratio (×) is how many times better socketley did: more per second, or less time, memory or CPU; above 1× socketley is ahead. The range in brackets is the lowest and highest ratio across the passes.

### A TCP service behind an edge

frp 0.71.1, 3 passes, 2026-11-10, socketley 0174a7a1.

| case | socketley | frp | socketley vs frp |
|---|---|---|---|
| round trip through the tunnel, 64 B echo | 90.0 µs (0.83 cores) | 167 µs (1.34 cores) | 1.86× (1.85–1.90) |
| throughput, 512 MiB echoed through the tunnel | 2.0 K MiB/s (1.91 cores) | 872.0 MiB/s (1.82 cores) | 2.27× (2.25–2.35) |

How it was measured: tb_client, one connection; agent and edge (frpc and frps) on the same two cores, the echo service on a third. socketley agent and edge against frpc and frps, the service an echo server, one connection. socketley answers a round trip in about half frp's time and moves bulk data at more than twice its rate.

# web runtime

Static site of files for browsers: a docs site, a blog, a single-page app; caching and compression built in

A **web** runtime serves a directory of files to browsers and does nothing else: no script, no WebSocket, no upload. Put a documentation site, a blog from a static site generator or a single-page app's build behind it.

```
socketley create web docs -p 9500 --root /srv/docs/current --domain docs -s
socketley create web www  -p 9501 --root /var/www/html --domain example.com -s
```

> It speaks plain HTTP and binds `127.0.0.1` unless `--bind` says otherwise. Visitors reach it through the entrance, which adds TLS and HTTP/2 for its `--domain` names. `--tls` and `--lua` are refused.

## What it does

- **Clean addresses**: `/guide/` serves `guide/index.html`, `/about` serves `about.html`, and a missing page gets the site's `404.html`.
- **Single-page apps**: `--fallback index.html` answers addresses with no file, while a missing `app.js` stays a 404.
- **Releases without a restart**: `--root` may be a symbolic link; swap it to a new build and the next request is served from it.
- **Caching done right**: ETag and Last-Modified on every file; names a build stamped with a hash are cached for a year, pages are revalidated.
- **Compression**: A `.br` or `.gz` copy next to a file is sent when the browser takes it; other text files are compressed once and kept.
- **Never waits on the disk**: Small files are kept in memory, large ones sent with `sendfile`; inotify sees every change at once.
- **Nothing leaks**: `..`, links pointing out of `--root` and hidden files (`.env`, `.git/`) are 404, `.well-known` excepted.

## Works with

The entrance [proxy](rt-proxy.txt) of a [dns](rt-dns.txt) runtime gives it HTTPS under its `--domain`; see the [public HTTPS recipe](deploy.txt). For a site that also needs WebSocket or a Lua handler, use a [server](rt-server.txt) with `--http`.

## Flags

Every flag a web runtime takes, by group.

**Basics**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `-p` | int | Port: The port it listens on (a client: the port of its target). |
| `-s` |  | Start now: Start it as soon as it is made. |
| `--lua-ffi` |  | Lua FFI: Let the script require("ffi"): LuaJIT's calls into C and raw memory, where a wrong pointer ends the runtime's process. |

**Network**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--bind` | text | Bind address: Bind the port to this address only, such as 127.0.0.1 when only a proxy on this machine should reach it. |
| `--shards` | int | Shards: Worker processes sharing the port: the way one runtime uses more than one core. |
| `--domain` | list | Names: The names it is reached by through the entrance; empty for its own name. |
| `--cpus` | text | CPUs: The CPUs its I/O may run on, as 0-3,6. |

**Limits**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--max-connections` (--max-conn) | int | Max connections: The most clients at once. |

**Output**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--log` | path | State log: A file it appends each state change to. |

**Web**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--root` | path | Document root: The directory whose files are the site. Required. |
| `--index` | text | Index page: The file a directory's address is answered with, index.html unless given. |
| `--fallback` | text | Fallback page: The page an address with no file is given, with 200, as a single-page app routes; 404.html, if there, otherwise. |
| `--backend` | text | PHP server: The FastCGI server a .php file under --root is run by: fastcgi://unix:/path or fastcgi://a.b.c.d:port. |
| `--fastcgi-root` | path | Server's root: --root as the FastCGI server sees it, when that is another path (a container). |
| `--lua-pages` |  | Lua pages: Run a .lua file under --root as a page, which answers its own address, rather than serving it. |

## Benchmarks

A ratio (×) is how many times better socketley did: more per second, or less time, memory or CPU; above 1× socketley is ahead. The range in brackets is the lowest and highest ratio across the passes.

### Static site: pages, assets, compression, revalidation

nginx 1.28.3, 3 passes, 2026-11-10, socketley 0174a7a1.

| case | socketley | nginx | socketley vs nginx |
|---|---|---|---|
| page 4 KiB, keep-alive, 256 connections | 237 K req/s (1.00 cores) | 48 K req/s (1.00 cores) | 4.94× (4.68–4.97) |
| page 4 KiB, a connection per request, 64 at once | 80 K req/s (1.00 cores) | 32 K req/s (1.00 cores) | 2.50× (2.46–2.74) |
| asset 64 KiB (hashed name), keep-alive, 256 connections | 81 K req/s (0.99 cores) | 42 K req/s (1.00 cores) | 1.89× (1.73–2.24) |
| file 1 MiB, keep-alive, 64 connections | 25 K req/s (1.00 cores) | 21 K req/s (1.00 cores) | 1.22× (1.16–1.24) |
| page 4 KiB as gzip, the .gz beside it | 272 K req/s (1.00 cores) | 48 K req/s (1.00 cores) | 5.66× (5.26–5.99) |
| page 4 KiB as brotli, the .br beside it | 277 K req/s (1.00 cores) | 47 K req/s (1.00 cores) | 5.99× (5.83–6.07) |
| page 4 KiB as gzip, no .gz on disk | 275 K req/s (1.00 cores) | 25 K req/s (1.00 cores) | 10.95× (10.69–11.06) |
| revalidation: If-None-Match, 304 | 283 K req/s (1.00 cores) | 59 K req/s (1.00 cores) | 4.73× (4.66–4.84) |
| missing file: the site's 404.html | 248 K req/s (1.00 cores) | 40 K req/s (1.00 cores) | 6.14× (6.13–6.25) |
| 10,000 pages of 4 KiB at random | 237 K req/s (1.00 cores) | 52 K req/s (1.00 cores) | 4.58× (4.57–4.85) |

How it was measured: wrk 8 threads, 4 s a run; each server on one core, wrk (8 threads) on 20 others. socketley create web --root with its defaults against nginx with one worker, sendfile, open_file_cache, gzip_static and brotli_static, both sending the same headers on plain HTTP (TLS and HTTP/2 are the entrance proxy's). The compressed rows send the same .gz and .br bytes; in the row with no .gz on disk socketley sends a copy it made once and nginx compresses every answer, so that row shows what each does with a site deployed without copies rather than a like-for-like speed. This VM halts idle vCPUs, which costs a server that writes each answer on its own more than one that batches: a single unpublished pass on another VM (16 cores) read 1.72x for the headline row. The kernel keeps at most 2,048 connections in TIME-WAIT for every arm (net.ipv4.tcp_max_tw_buckets, 131,072 by default), so a pass with a connection per request does not wait out the closed connections of the one before.

# All flags

Every flag of every runtime type, with the types that take it.

**Basics**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `-p` | int | Port: The port it listens on (a client: the port of its target). Types: server, client, proxy, cache, storage, dns, idp, db, mqtt, mail, tunnel, metrics, mcp, web. |
| `-s` |  | Start now: Start it as soon as it is made. Types: server, client, proxy, cache, storage, dns, idp, db, mqtt, mail, tunnel, metrics, mcp, web. |
| `-g` (--group) | text | Group: Puts it in a group; a proxy with --backend @group reaches every member. Types: server, client, proxy, cache, storage, dns, mqtt, mail. |
| `--lua` | path | Lua script: A script with the runtime's callbacks, run at start. Types: server, client, proxy, cache, storage, mqtt, mail, mcp. |
| `--lua-ffi` |  | Lua FFI: Let the script require("ffi"): LuaJIT's calls into C and raw memory, where a wrong pointer ends the runtime's process. Types: server, client, proxy, cache, storage, mqtt, mail, mcp, web. |

**Network**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--bind` | text | Bind address: Bind the port to this address only, such as 127.0.0.1 when only a proxy on this machine should reach it. Types: server, proxy, cache, storage, dns, idp, db, mqtt, mail, tunnel, metrics, mcp, web. |
| `--listen` | text | Unix socket: Listen on a unix socket instead of a port. Types: server, proxy, cache, storage. |
| `--shards` | int | Shards: Worker processes sharing the port: the way one runtime uses more than one core. Types: server, proxy, cache, storage, dns, idp, db, mqtt, mail, mcp, web. |
| `--domain` | list | Names: The names it is reached by through the entrance; empty for its own name. Types: server, proxy, cache, storage, idp, db, mail, tunnel, metrics, mcp, web. |
| `--cpus` | text | CPUs: The CPUs its I/O may run on, as 0-3,6. Types: server, client, proxy, cache, storage, dns, idp, db, mqtt, mail, metrics, mcp, web. |

**TLS**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--tls` |  | TLS: Encrypt its transport: terminate TLS on its port, or dial over it. Types: server, client, proxy, cache, storage, mqtt, mail. |
| `--cert` | path | Certificate: The PEM certificate (chain allowed) a listener presents. Types: server, client, proxy, cache, storage, mqtt, mail. |
| `--key` | path | Key: The PEM key of the certificate. Types: server, client, proxy, cache, storage, mqtt, mail. |
| `--ca` | path | CA: On a listener: require client certificates from this CA (mutual TLS). On a client or proxy: the CA its servers are checked against. Types: server, client, proxy, cache, storage, mqtt. |
| `--acme` | list | ACME names: Names to get a Let's Encrypt certificate for, renewed by itself. Types: server, proxy, cache, storage. |
| `--acme-email` | text | ACME e-mail: The address the CA writes to about the certificate. Types: server, proxy, cache, storage. |

**Limits**

| flag | value | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| `--max-connections` (--max-conn) | int | Max connections: The most clients at once. Types: server, proxy, cache, storage, idp, db, mqtt, mail, mcp, web. |
| `--rate-limit` | int | Rate limit: Messages a second per connection. Types: server, proxy, cache. |
| `--global-rate-limit` | int | Global rate limit: Messages a second over all connections. Types: server, proxy, cache. |
| `--congestion` | text | Congestion control: The kernel's congestion control for its connections, such as bbr, which keeps its rate up under packet loss. Types: server, proxy, cache, storage. |
| `--idle-timeout` | duration | Idle timeout: Close a connection that has received nothing for this long; off unless given. Types: server, proxy, cache, storage. |
| `--read-buffer` | size | Read buffer: How much data may pile up from one connection before it is refused; 1M unless given. Types: server, client, proxy, cache, storage. |
| `--write-buffer` | size | Write buffer: How much unsent data may queue up for one connection before it is dropped; 8M unless given. Types: server, client, proxy, cache, storage, mqtt. |
| `--drain` |  | Drain on stop: Finish what is in flight before stopping. Types: server, proxy, cache, storage. |
| `--reconnect` | int | Reconnect: Reconnect with backoff when the connection drops: the most attempts, 0 for no limit. Types: client. |

# Benchmarks

Each runtime against what people run instead, on one machine, in one run.

Each table below sets socketley beside reference servers doing the same work on one machine. A row gives a ratio, its range across passes, and the CPU spent. The data, with commit, versions and date of every set, is in [data/bench.json](data/bench.json); the harness is not in the repository.

## How these numbers are made

- **Interleaved on the same cores.** All arms run at once on the same pinned core, in a rotating order; the first pass is a discarded warm-up.
- **Median of per-pass ratios.** The range is shown beside it; a range that contains 1.00× is no difference.
- **CPU beside every rate.** A server at 1.00 core is saturated; a run whose load generator hits a full core is not published.
- **Checked answers.** HTTP body sizes are compared first, so a fast 404 is never measured.
- **A quiet machine.** No build, test or foreign server runs during a pass; a disturbed pass is run again.
- **Same work.** References run as a production install would, as each set's notes say.
- **The VM penalises wakeups.** It halts idle vCPUs, so a server that wakes a client per message (Redis at depth 1, nginx, Mosquitto's fan-out) takes VM exits more often than one that batches, as socketley does. Those rows swing, and the gap is smaller on hardware without the exit. Keeping vCPUs awake with spinners was refused: it delays clients' own wakeups.

A ratio (×) is how many times better socketley did: more per second, or less time, memory or CPU; above 1× socketley is ahead. The range in brackets is the lowest and highest ratio across the passes.

## Redis protocol, one command per round trip

Redis 8.0.5, Valkey 9.0.4, 3 passes, 2026-11-10, socketley 0174a7a1.

| case | socketley | Redis | Valkey | socketley vs Redis | socketley vs Valkey |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SET | 289 K /s (1.00 cores) | 165 K /s (1.00 cores) | 172 K /s (1.00 cores) | 1.78× (1.72–1.79) | 1.66× (1.55–1.86) |
| GET | 283 K /s (1.00 cores) | 167 K /s (1.00 cores) | 174 K /s (1.00 cores) | 1.63× (1.57–1.71) | 1.64× (1.49–1.76) |
| LPUSH | 272 K /s (1.00 cores) | 191 K /s (1.00 cores) | 169 K /s (1.00 cores) | 1.42× (1.42–1.44) | 1.70× (1.49–1.75) |
| LPOP | 275 K /s (1.00 cores) | 187 K /s (1.00 cores) | 174 K /s (1.00 cores) | 1.47× (1.43–1.72) | 1.60× (1.48–1.63) |
| SADD | 274 K /s (1.00 cores) | 178 K /s (1.00 cores) | 180 K /s (1.00 cores) | 1.58× (1.51–1.66) | 1.57× (1.52–1.84) |
| HSET | 282 K /s (1.00 cores) | 175 K /s (1.00 cores) | 164 K /s (1.00 cores) | 1.61× (1.36–1.72) | 1.73× (1.53–1.75) |
| ZADD | 196 K /s (1.00 cores) | 164 K /s (1.00 cores) | 163 K /s (1.00 cores) | 1.17× (1.13–1.26) | 1.19× (1.14–1.43) |

How it was measured: 3 redis-benchmark processes × 50 connections; servers on one core, clients on 20 others. Each server on one pinned core, every row at a full core: the rate is one core divided by the cost of an operation. SET and GET draw their keys at random from about a million, as a cache's clients spread them. At depth 1 that cost is mostly the kernel's per-message price, which all three pay alike, so the differences are small and the ranges wide; this VM halts idle vCPUs and every wakeup of a client costs the server a VM exit, which moves a server that answers each command with its own write more than one that batches.

## Redis protocol, 100 commands per message (pipelined)

Redis 8.0.5, Valkey 9.0.4, 3 passes, 2026-11-10, socketley 0174a7a1.

| case | socketley | Redis | Valkey | socketley vs Redis | socketley vs Valkey |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SET | 9.69 M /s (1.00 cores) | 2.31 M /s (1.00 cores) | 2.68 M /s (1.00 cores) | 4.18× (4.17–4.19) | 3.62× (3.60–3.63) |
| GET | 9.87 M /s (0.99 cores) | 2.52 M /s (1.00 cores) | 3.80 M /s (1.00 cores) | 3.91× (3.90–3.93) | 2.60× (2.57–2.61) |
| SADD | 5.76 M /s (1.00 cores) | 2.91 M /s (1.00 cores) | 2.55 M /s (1.00 cores) | 2.00× (1.96–2.04) | 2.23× (2.23–2.28) |
| HSET | 4.64 M /s (1.00 cores) | 2.33 M /s (1.00 cores) | 2.11 M /s (1.00 cores) | 1.99× (1.98–2.00) | 2.18× (2.18–2.21) |
| ZADD | 610 K /s (1.00 cores) | 473 K /s (1.00 cores) | 481 K /s (1.00 cores) | 1.29× (1.27–1.30) | 1.27× (1.25–1.28) |

How it was measured: 3 redis-benchmark processes × 50 connections; servers on one core, clients on 20 others. The per-message price divided by a hundred: what remains is parsing and executing commands, where the servers differ. SET and GET draw their keys at random from about a million, more than a core's caches hold, so each lookup waits on memory; SADD, HSET and ZADD put random members into one big collection each.

## Pipelined, one key

Redis 8.0.5, Valkey 9.0.4, 3 passes, 2026-11-10, socketley 0174a7a1.

| case | socketley | Redis | Valkey | socketley vs Redis | socketley vs Valkey |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SET | 14.39 M /s (1.00 cores) | 5.25 M /s (1.00 cores) | 2.94 M /s (1.00 cores) | 2.74× (2.72–2.75) | 4.88× (4.86–4.92) |
| GET | 14.78 M /s (1.00 cores) | 6.29 M /s (1.00 cores) | 4.31 M /s (1.00 cores) | 2.35× (2.33–2.36) | 3.43× (3.43–3.45) |
| LPUSH | 11.21 M /s (0.99 cores) | 4.99 M /s (0.99 cores) | 3.16 M /s (1.00 cores) | 2.25× (2.24–2.25) | 3.55× (3.54–3.55) |
| LPOP | 13.06 M /s (0.99 cores) | 4.27 M /s (1.00 cores) | 2.83 M /s (1.00 cores) | 3.06× (3.06–3.06) | 4.63× (4.61–4.64) |
| SADD | 13.84 M /s (0.99 cores) | 5.66 M /s (1.00 cores) | 3.74 M /s (1.00 cores) | 2.44× (2.44–2.45) | 3.69× (3.68–3.71) |
| HSET | 10.43 M /s (1.00 cores) | 4.36 M /s (1.00 cores) | 2.84 M /s (1.00 cores) | 2.39× (2.39–2.40) | 3.68× (3.67–3.68) |
| ZADD | 11.20 M /s (0.99 cores) | 4.29 M /s (1.00 cores) | 3.06 M /s (1.00 cores) | 2.61× (2.60–2.63) | 3.67× (3.60–3.69) |

How it was measured: 3 redis-benchmark processes × 50 connections; servers on one core, clients on 20 others. The same commands on one key, which stays in the core's cache: the easy case for every cache, kept to show parsing and executing alone.

| case | socketley | Redis Cluster 8.0.5, 4 masters | socketley vs Redis Cluster 8.0.5, 4 masters |
|---|---|---|---|
| SET | 24.96 M /s (3.25 cores) | 12.70 M /s (3.95 cores) | 1.97× (1.89–2.05) |
| GET | 27.23 M /s (3.35 cores) | 13.97 M /s (3.86 cores) | 1.95× (1.79–2.04) |
| LPUSH | 27.92 M /s (3.47 cores) | 13.97 M /s (3.91 cores) | 2.00× (2.00–2.00) |
| LPOP | 25.40 M /s (2.99 cores) | 12.15 M /s (3.92 cores) | 2.09× (2.09–2.09) |
| SADD | 28.53 M /s (3.17 cores) | 17.46 M /s (3.93 cores) | 1.63× (1.56–1.81) |

How it was measured: 3 redis-benchmark processes × 50 connections, 100 commands a message; socketley as four shards and Redis Cluster as four masters, each shard or master pinned to one of the same four cores; five redis-benchmark --cluster processes on 20 others. SET and GET draw their keys at random from 1,048,576, 64 behind each of the 16,384 slot tags, preloaded so every GET finds its key (the hit rate is counted every pass). Every shard's mesh counters are read around every timed run: no command crossed between shards in any pass, so the client sent each to its owner. redis-benchmark --cluster's threads spin while they wait, so its client cores are no reading of headroom.

## WebSocket: echo and a chat room's fan-out

socketley, no script, ws 8.22.0 (Node 24.22.1), uWebSockets.js 20.71.0 (Node 24.22.1), 3 passes, 2026-11-10, socketley 81ffa51e.

| case | socketley | socketley, no script | ws 8.22.0 (Node 24.22.1) | uWebSockets.js 20.71.0 (Node 24.22.1) | socketley vs socketley, no script | socketley vs ws 8.22.0 (Node 24.22.1) | socketley vs uWebSockets.js 20.71.0 (Node 24.22.1) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| echo, 64 B messages, 256 connections, one in flight each | 303 K msg/s (1.00 cores) | 320 K msg/s (1.00 cores) | 151 K msg/s (1.00 cores) | 232 K msg/s (1.00 cores) | 0.95× (0.94–0.95) | 1.99× (1.97–2.03) | 1.31× (1.27–1.32) |
| room fan-out: 1 sender to 100 receivers, 64 B | 6.13 M msg/s (1.00 cores) | 6.15 M msg/s (1.00 cores) | 305 K msg/s (1.00 cores) | 5.40 M msg/s (1.00 cores) | 0.99× (0.99–1.00) | 20.00× (19.83–20.35) | 1.13× (1.12–1.14) |

How it was measured: srvgen (Go), 4 s a run, every answer checked; each server on one core (ws and uWebSockets.js under Node 24), srvgen on 20 others. The same logic in each: an echo, and a room that a receiver enters by sending "join", with one sender's messages counted at every receiver. socketley runs it in Lua (join_group/group_send) and, as "no script", on its built-in relay; ws loops over the room with send(), uWebSockets.js publishes to a topic. Both socketley and uWebSockets.js build a room's frame once; socketley writes each receiver's share of a turn in one send, and uWebSockets.js corks its writes.

## TCP line protocol, answered by a handler

socketley, no script, Node 24.22.1 net, Go 1.24.6 net, 3 passes, 2026-11-10, socketley 81ffa51e.

| case | socketley | socketley, no script | Node 24.22.1 net | Go 1.24.6 net | socketley vs socketley, no script | socketley vs Node 24.22.1 net | socketley vs Go 1.24.6 net |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| line echo, 64 B, 256 connections, one in flight each | 313 K msg/s (1.00 cores) | 329 K msg/s (1.00 cores) | 199 K msg/s (1.00 cores) | 227 K msg/s (1.00 cores) | 0.95× (0.95–0.95) | 1.57× (1.57–1.60) | 1.38× (1.38–1.39) |
| line echo, 64 B, 64 connections, 16 pipelined each | 4.48 M msg/s (1.00 cores) | 4.63 M msg/s (1.00 cores) | 2.32 M msg/s (1.00 cores) | 3.24 M msg/s (1.00 cores) | 0.96× (0.95–0.97) | 1.94× (1.91–1.95) | 1.38× (1.37–1.39) |

How it was measured: srvgen (Go), 4 s a run, every answer checked; each server on one core, srvgen on 20 others. Every line is answered with itself by a handler: on socketley a Lua on_client_messages, handed a read's lines in one call and answering them with one self.send; on Node's net a function over the read's lines, written with one write a read; in Go a goroutine with bufio. With one line in flight the kernel's per-message cost dominates; 16 pipelined lines show each server's own per-line work, where a script with on_client_message, a call and a string a line, makes about 3.2 million a second.

## HTTP: static files and a fixed answer

nginx 1.28.3, 3 passes, 2026-11-10, socketley 0174a7a1.

| case | socketley | nginx | socketley vs nginx |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 KiB file, keep-alive, 256 connections | 271 K req/s (1.00 cores) | 50 K req/s (0.99 cores) | 5.46× (5.42–5.51) |
| 64 KiB file, keep-alive, 256 connections | 93 K req/s (1.00 cores) | 47 K req/s (0.99 cores) | 2.00× (1.98–2.16) |
| 1 KiB file, a connection per request, 64 at once | 83 K req/s (0.99 cores) | 35 K req/s (1.00 cores) | 2.36× (2.33–2.48) |
| fixed answer (Lua handler / nginx return), keep-alive | 246 K req/s (1.00 cores) | 77 K req/s (0.99 cores) | 3.22× (3.08–3.54) |

How it was measured: wrk 8 threads, 4 s a run; each server on one core, wrk on 20 others. socketley --http dir --http-cache against nginx with one worker, sendfile, open_file_cache and access logs off. Files are .txt: socketley adds a WebSocket script to every .html it serves, by design. The fixed answer is a Lua on_http_request on socketley and a return 200 on nginx, which runs no script at all. Read the 1 KiB keep-alive row with this machine in mind: nginx answers each request with its own write and wakeup, and on this VM waking a halted vCPU costs an exit, which costs a server that does that more than one that batches. A single unpublished pass on another VM (16 cores) read 1.85× for the same row. The kernel keeps at most 2,048 connections in TIME-WAIT for every arm (net.ipv4.tcp_max_tw_buckets, 131,072 by default), so a pass with a connection per request does not wait out the closed connections of the one before.

## HTTP on four cores

nginx 1.28.3, 3 passes, 2026-11-10, socketley 0174a7a1.

| case | socketley | nginx | socketley vs nginx |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 KiB file, keep-alive, 256 connections | 500 K req/s (3.99 cores) | 230 K req/s (3.99 cores) | 2.17× (2.15–2.25) |
| 64 KiB file, keep-alive, 256 connections | 229 K req/s (3.98 cores) | 166 K req/s (3.99 cores) | 1.38× (1.36–1.40) |
| 1 KiB file, a connection per request, 64 at once | 158 K req/s (3.94 cores) | 131 K req/s (3.90 cores) | 1.21× (1.21–1.21) |
| fixed answer (Lua handler / nginx return), keep-alive | 451 K req/s (3.99 cores) | 297 K req/s (3.98 cores) | 1.52× (1.46–1.54) |

How it was measured: wrk 16 threads, 4 s a run; socketley as four shards and nginx with four workers, each pinned to one of the same four cores; wrk (16 threads) on 20 others. The same rows as the one-core set, the same wrk for both. socketley spends about twice the CPU a request here that it does on one core, and most of that is the client, not the shards: wrk's threads each hold connections on all four shards, and waking a thread from another core is an interrupt the server's core pays for on loopback, a VM exit on this VM. With one wrk per quarter of the connections, four shards cost about 15% more a request than four separate one-core servers. A client on another machine costs neither. The kernel keeps at most 2,048 connections in TIME-WAIT for every arm (net.ipv4.tcp_max_tw_buckets, 131,072 by default), so a pass with a connection per request does not wait out the closed connections of the one before.

MinIO single node, single drive; both on tmpfs, so the comparison is the servers' work and not a disk. The PUT row starts both servers afresh on empty storage for every pass, because MinIO reclaims deleted objects in the background and its puts slow while it does.

How it was measured: loadgen, 4s a run, 100,000 documents, data on tmpfs; all three on the same four cores (socketley as four shards), loadgen on 20 others. 100,000 documents, data on tmpfs. MongoDB through its wire protocol with journaled writes, PocketBase over its REST API with request logs off, socketley over its HTTP API with a key. A sharded socketley db hands every write to shard 0, so its writes are at most what one shard takes, at more cores; reads and queries spread over all four.

A socketley job walks once at start and then follows inotify, where the others walk both sides again; it checks a whole tree only when it starts, so the re-check row is a stop and a start, with one file deleted so its end can be seen.

## OpenID Connect provider

Keycloak 26.8.1, 3 passes, 2026-11-10, socketley 0174a7a1.

| case | socketley | Keycloak | socketley vs Keycloak |
|---|---|---|---|
| sign-in: authorization code with a password, 16 clients | 265.0 req/s (3.95 cores) | 223.0 req/s (3.90 cores) | 1.19× (1.18–1.24) |
| refresh token, 256 clients | 59 K req/s (2.91 cores) | 2.4 K req/s (3.86 cores) | 24.85× (24.10–25.84) |
| userinfo, 512 clients | 513 K req/s (3.75 cores) | 21 K req/s (3.83 cores) | 24.87× (24.11–26.34) |
| JWKS, 256 connections (wrk) | 510 K req/s (3.99 cores) | 29 K req/s (3.91 cores) | 17.30× (15.83–17.73) |

How it was measured: idpgen, 4s a run, 200 accounts; both on the same four cores (socketley as four shards; Keycloak with its PostgreSQL), idpgen and wrk on 20 others. 200 accounts. A sign-in is the authorization code flow with PKCE and a password, so it also compares the password hashes each uses by default: scrypt here, PBKDF2 in Keycloak. Keycloak's CPU includes PostgreSQL's. Refresh and userinfo come from four idpgen processes and JWKS from wrk, with as many clients as fill socketley's four cores; refresh stays near the same rate from 256 to 512 clients, bound by the durable write of each rotated token family through shard 0. Sign-ins come four at a time from each of four addresses: socketley refuses a fifth from one address while four are being checked, and four connections alone may land on two of its four shards, which would measure where the kernel put them. Both are warmed with sign-ins before the passes until a 5 s run gains under 3% on the best before it: Keycloak's JIT compiles the flow over its first half minute, from about 100 to 190 sign-ins a second.

|---|---|---|---|
| SMTP in, 4 KiB messages, 64 connections, 10 a connection | 569.0 msg/s (0.14 cores) | 129.0 msg/s (0.30 cores) | 4.43× (3.88–4.43) |
| SMTP in, 64 KiB messages, 64 connections, 10 a connection | 345.0 msg/s (0.23 cores) | 75.5 msg/s (0.21 cores) | 4.62× (3.98–5.25) |
| IMAP: LOGIN and LOGOUT, 8 clients | 127.0 sign-ins/s (0.99 cores) | 65.2 sign-ins/s (0.99 cores) | 1.94× (1.94–1.95) |
| IMAP: LOGIN, SELECT, FETCH every header of 10,000, 8 clients | 484 K msg/s (0.99 cores) | 125 K msg/s (0.99 cores) | 3.88× (3.87–3.94) |
| IMAP: LOGIN, SELECT, FETCH 1,000 whole 64 KiB messages, 8 clients | 21 K msg/s (0.99 cores) | 14 K msg/s (0.99 cores) | 1.51× (1.43–1.56) |

How it was measured: smtp-source (64 processes x 1 connections); mailload.py (8 asyncio processes x 1 connection), 4 s a run; every process of each on the same one core (socketley's daemon, idp, storage and mail; Postfix and Dovecot); smtp-source and mailload on 20 others; data on the VM's ext4 disk. Postfix hands each message over LMTP to Dovecot's Maildir and index; socketley's mail runtime writes it into its storage runtime. Both sync to disk (about 4 ms a sync here) before a message counts, so the SMTP rows are bound by syncs, not cores, and are timed until the last message is in its mailbox. Every sign-in hashes the password: scrypt in socketley, yescrypt in Dovecot. Dovecot 2.4's lmtp_user_concurrency_limit is set to unlimited, 2.3's default, since 10 made Postfix wait out five-minute retries.

| connect: 200 TLS connections, each a full verified handshake | 5.6 K conn/s (2.02 cores) | 2.7 K conn/s (1.28 cores) | 2.1 K conn/s (1.96 cores) | 2.5 K conn/s (2.27 cores) | 2.14× (1.97–2.14) | 2.61× (2.56–2.65) | 2.26× (2.21–2.40) |
| held: 200 idle connections, memory per connection | 62.8 KiB (0.00 cores) | 23.9 KiB (0.00 cores) | 269.0 KiB (0.00 cores) | 78.6 KiB (0.00 cores) | 0.38× (0.37–0.43) | 4.28× (4.14–4.81) | 1.25× (1.21–1.41) |
| held: 10,000 idle connections, memory per connection | 2.3 KiB (0.00 cores) | 9.6 KiB (0.00 cores) | 9.6 KiB (0.00 cores) | 9.5 KiB (0.00 cores) | 4.14× (4.06–4.17) | 4.17× (4.15–4.17) | 4.12× (4.04–4.14) |

How it was measured: clientgen target (Go) on 2-5, every client arm on core 8, 3 s windows; every client arm on one core, the Go target (clientgen) on four others. Every client on the same one core, the target (a Go program) on four others with headroom: every row records the target's cores, and none used all four. socketley is one client runtime holding every connection (--connections N) with its Lua on_message as the handler; the others are one process with the same logic. Every count is taken at the target: a consumer's count must equal the lines sent, every request's size is checked, and a round trip is the interval between one connection's requests as the target sees them. The firehose rows are bound by the client's core, and every line differs (each carries its index). socketley's script reads them with on_read, walking a view of the read buffer with view:lines(), which makes no string, as Go's ReadSlice hands out a slice of its buffer; Node and Python make a string or a bytes object per line. Written with on_message instead, a Lua string per line, the 64 B row makes about 12.7 million lines a second, and with on_messages, one string per read, about 52 million. Over TLS the 64 B row is bound by the target, whose one goroutine encrypting the stream uses a whole core while socketley's runtime decrypts at about four fifths of its own; the target's cores beside the row say so. Connecting is that one runtime dialling all of them, as the others dial from one process; the memory row is socketley's daemon and the runtime's process together, by proportional set size, divided by the connections, so at 200 it is mostly the two processes' fixed cost. One runtime per connection instead, each made with socketley create ... -s from a shell loop, is a process each: 386 created and connected a second, 243 with TLS, and 1,546 KiB each held.

| case | socketley | tcpkali | Go | socketley vs tcpkali | socketley vs Go |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| send: 64 B lines as fast as the connection takes them, TCP | 126.03 M lines/s (1.00 cores) | 102.03 M lines/s (1.00 cores) | 67.64 M lines/s (1.00 cores) | 1.15× (1.07–1.27) | 1.86× (1.63–1.86) |
| send: 4 KiB lines, TCP | 2.45 M lines/s (1.00 cores) | 1.62 M lines/s (1.00 cores) | 1.35 M lines/s (1.00 cores) | 1.48× (1.45–1.57) | 1.94× (1.74–2.83) |

How it was measured: clientgen target (Go) on 2-5, every client arm on core 8, 3 s windows; every sender on one core, the Go sink on four others. Sending as fast as the connection takes it, counted at a sink on other cores. socketley paces with self.pending() and on_writable and sends one line per self.send call; tcpkali repeats its message into large writes; Go makes one buffered write call per line. All are bound by the client's core.

## Driving a Redis-protocol server

redis-benchmark 8.0.5, 3 passes, 2026-11-10, socketley 0174a7a1.

| case | socketley | redis-benchmark | socketley vs redis-benchmark |
|---|---|---|---|
| pipelined INCR to a socketley cache, depth 32, 1 connection | 966 K /s (0.57 cores) | 916 K /s (0.62 cores) | 1.06× (1.05–1.06) |
| pipelined INCR to a socketley cache, depth 32, 4 connections | 5.91 M /s (0.84 cores) | 6.89 M /s (0.99 cores) | 0.86× (0.81–0.86) |

How it was measured: clientgen target (Go) on 2-5, every client arm on core 8, 3 s windows; each client on one core, the socketley cache on another. A socketley client runtime sending 32 INCR commands as one message and the next 32 on the 32nd reply, the replies counted with on_read and view:lines() as redis-benchmark counts them in C, against redis-benchmark -P 32 with one thread, both to the same socketley cache on its own core, counted by the cache's own counter. At one connection both wait on the round trip; at four, socketley's runtime holds four connections, as redis-benchmark's one thread does, and the cache is the bound under socketley's client at a whole core, where redis-benchmark is at its own.
